# ArkType

> TypeScript's 1:1 validator

# Setup

> Install ArkType, define a Type and precompile it in your bundler.

## Install

```bash
npm install arktype
```

```bash
npm install -D @ark/aot
```

`arktype` is a dependency and `@ark/aot` a dev dependency. `arktype` defines and validates Types. [`@ark/aot`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) precompiles them when you build, so arktype's parser never ships and nothing compiles at runtime. Skip it for a script or REPL with no build step: every Type works without it.

## Define a Type

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

export const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

const out = User({ name: "Alan", age: -1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) console.error(out.summary)
```

## Add the plugin

**Vite**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
})
```

Vitest runs your tests through the same plugin.

**Next.js**

```js
export default {
	turbopack: {
		rules: {
			"*.ts": { loaders: ["@ark/aot/turbopack"] },
			"*.tsx": { loaders: ["@ark/aot/turbopack"] }
		},
		resolveAlias: {
			arktype: "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/codecs": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/config": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/errors": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/mutatesInput": "arktype/runtime"
		}
	}
}
```

For `next build --webpack`, see [Next.js](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next).

**esbuild**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { build } from "esbuild"

await build({
	entryPoints: ["src/main.ts"],
	bundle: true,
	outfile: "dist/main.js",
	plugins: [precompile.esbuild()]
})
```

**Rolldown**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "rolldown"

export default defineConfig({
	input: "src/main.ts",
	output: { file: "dist/main.js" },
	plugins: [precompile.rolldown()]
})
```

**Rollup**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { nodeResolve } from "@rollup/plugin-node-resolve"
import typescript from "@rollup/plugin-typescript"

export default {
	input: "src/main.ts",
	output: { file: "dist/main.js", format: "es" },
	plugins: [
		precompile.rollup(),
		nodeResolve({ extensions: [".ts", ".js"] }),
		typescript()
	]
}
```

**webpack**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

export default {
	entry: "./src/main.ts",
	resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] },
	module: {
		rules: [
			{ test: /\.ts$/, loader: "ts-loader", options: { transpileOnly: true } }
		]
	},
	plugins: [precompile.webpack()]
}
```

**Bun**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

await Bun.build({
	entrypoints: ["src/main.ts"],
	outdir: "dist",
	plugins: [precompile.bun()]
})
```

Bun's bundler needs Bun 1.2.22 or later. To precompile as `bun test` or `bun run` loads your code, see [Bun](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bun).

**Node**

```ts
import { register } from "@ark/aot/node"

register()
```

```sh
node --import ./register.ts src/main.ts
```

Node 22.15 or later. A program `tsc` compiles for production precompiles with [`arktype-precompile --emit`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#tsc).

Rspack, Rsbuild, Farm and the rest are in [Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup).

## Run it

Build or start your dev server as you already do. `User` is now a standalone validator, and the program prints:

```
age must be non-negative
```

A precompiled error says what failed without printing the value, which arktype at runtime adds as `(was -1)`.

To see what the build makes of each definition without bundling, run:

```sh
npx arktype-precompile --check
```

```
src/user.ts:3:21  accepted
1 site in 2 files: 1 accepted (100.0%)
```

A definition the build can't precompile fails it, naming the file, the line and the fix. See [Troubleshooting](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting).

## Configure TypeScript

TypeScript `>=5.1`, including TypeScript 7, with:

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"strict": true,
		"skipLibCheck": true,
		"exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true
	}
}
```

- [`strict`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strict), or at least [`strictNullChecks`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strictNullChecks), is required for inference to work.
- [`skipLibCheck`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#skipLibCheck) is recommended. It avoids harmless errors from differences between your config and ours (see [FAQ](https://arktype.io/docs/faq#why-do-i-see-type-errors-in-an-arktype-package-in-node_modules)) and speeds up your editor.
- [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#exactOptionalPropertyTypes) is recommended. It makes your inferred types match runtime behavior. ArkType rejects `undefined` for an optional key unless its value allows it, so without this flag, `typeof User.infer` accepts `{ age: undefined }` while `User` rejects it.

ArkType is ESM-only, but a CommonJS project can `require` it on runtimes that support `require(esm)`, like Node `>=20.19` or `>=22.12`. TypeScript allows that `require` under `"module": "nodenext"` from 5.8, where `node16` reports TS1479. `@ark/aot` runs on Node 22.12 or later.

## Runtimes

ArkType runs in Node, Deno, Bun, browsers and edge runtimes like Cloudflare Workers. A precompiled validator never generates code, so it runs under a Content-Security-Policy that blocks `eval`. Without precompiling, ArkType validates without compiling where `new Function` is blocked; under a strict policy, enable [`jitless`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#jitless) so it never tries `new Function`, which the policy would report.

## Next

- Set up [your editor](https://arktype.io/docs/editor), and give your agent the [ArkType skill](https://arktype.io/docs/agents).
- Learn the syntax, starting with [your first type](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/your-first-type).
- Configure ArkType globally in a module that loads before anything creates a Type. See [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).
- Coming from Zod or another validator? See [Migrating](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating). From an earlier ArkType? See [Upgrading](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading).

# Your first type

> Define a type with TypeScript syntax, compose it, and validate data with it.

If you already know TypeScript, you already know most of ArkType's syntax.

## Define

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"versions?": "(number | string)[]"
})

// { name: string; platform: "android" | "ios"; versions?: (number | string)[] }
type User = typeof User.infer
```

A key ending in `?` is optional, as in TypeScript. String literals like `'android'` need their own quotes inside the definition.

Definitions are checked by TypeScript, so a mistake is an error in your editor, with autocomplete to help fix it:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "strng"
	// TypeScript: 'strng' is unresolvable
})
```

## Compose

Suppose we want to move `platform` and `versions` from our original type to a new `device` property.

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	// nested definitions don't need to be wrapped
	device: {
		platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
		"versions?": "(number | string)[]"
	}
})
```

To decouple `device` from `User`, move it to its own type and reference it.

```ts
const Device = type({
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"versions?": "(number | string)[]"
})

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	device: Device
})
```

## Validate

Call a type with `unknown` data to get back either the validated data or an `ArkErrors` object describing every problem.

```ts
const out = User({
	name: "Alan Turing",
	device: {
		platform: "enigma",
		versions: [0, "1", 0n]
	}
})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: device.platform must be "android" or "ios" (was "enigma")
	//            device.versions[2] must be a number or a string (was a bigint)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// out is narrowed to the validated User
	console.log(`Hello, ${out.name}`)
}
```

Calling a type never throws for invalid data. Each problem is in `out.issues`, with its `path`, `code` and `message`; see [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors).

Where invalid data is a bug rather than something to handle, use `.assert`. It returns the validated data or throws a `TraversalError` describing the same problems.

```ts
// TraversalError: name must be a string (was missing)
const user = User.assert({})
```

You now know how to define a `Type` and use it to check your data at runtime.

Next, we'll look at how ArkType extends TypeScript's type system with runtime constraints like `string.email` or `number.integer < 100`.

# Adding constraints

> Narrow types beyond what TypeScript can express, with keywords, ranges, divisors and custom predicates.

TypeScript can represent types like `string` or `number`, but what about `email` or `integer less than 100`?

In ArkType, conditions that narrow a type beyond its **basis** are called **constraints**. They compose with TypeScript's operators like any other part of a definition.

## Define

Let's create a new `Contact` Type that enforces our example constraints.

```ts
const Contact = type({
	// many common constraints are available as built-in keywords
	email: "string.email",
	// others can be written as type-safe expressions
	score: "number.integer < 100"
})

// infer the TypeScript type as usual
type Contact = typeof Contact.infer
```

> **number excludes NaN and Infinity**
>
> `number` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` by default. To allow them,
> see `number.NaN`, `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` in
> [Keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords), or the `numberAllowsNaN` and
> `numberAllowsInfinity` options in [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).

## Compose

Imagine we want to define a new Type representing a non-empty list of `Contact`.

Definitions create new types. Chained methods refine or transform types you already have.

```ts
// a non-empty list of Contact
const Contacts = Contact.array().atLeastLength(1)

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
const out = Contacts([])
```

## Narrow

Structured constraints like divisors and ranges will only take us so far. For anything else, add your own logic with `.narrow`.

```ts
// there's no "not divisible" expression - need to narrow
const Odd = type("number").narrow((n, ctx) =>
	// if even, add a customizable error and return false
	n % 2 === 0 ? ctx.mustBe("odd") : true
)

const FavoriteNumbers = type({
	even: "number % 2",
	odd: Odd
})

const out = FavoriteNumbers({
	even: 7,
	odd: 8
})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: even must be even (was 7)
	//            odd must be odd (was 8)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	console.log(out.odd)
}
```

You now know how to refine your types to enforce additional constraints at runtime.

But what if once your input is fully validated, you still need to make some adjustments before it's ready to use?

The final section of the intro covers **morphs**, which transform data as part of a Type.

# Morphs

> Transform data as part of validation by piping it through functions and other Types.

Sometimes, data at the boundaries of your code needs more than validation before it's ready to use.

**Morphs** transform your data. You can **pipe** them before, after or between validators, and chain them to other morphs.

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<object>>
const parseJson = type("string").pipe((s): object => JSON.parse(s))

// { ark: "type" }
const out = parseJson('{ "ark": "type" }')

// ArkErrors: must be a string (was an object)
const badOut = parseJson(out)
```

This is a good start, but what happens if we pass a string that isn't valid JSON?

```ts
// Uncaught SyntaxError: Expected property name ☠️
const badOut = parseJson('{ unquoted: "keys" }')
```

By default, ArkType assumes that if one of your morphs or narrows throws, you intend to crash. For a function you don't trust, use `pipe.try`, which turns what it throws into an error:

```ts
const parseJson = type("string").pipe.try((s): object => JSON.parse(s))

const out = parseJson('{ unquoted: "keys" }')

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: must be valid according to an anonymous predicate (was aborted due to error:
	//                SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 2 (line 1 column 3)
	//            )
	console.error(out.summary)
}
```

A validated `object` still isn't very useful, though. Since a Type can be called like a function, it can be a step in a pipe too. For JSON, the built-in `string.json.parse` keyword does the parsing, and `.to` validates its output:

```ts
// .to is a sugared .pipe for a single parsed output validator
const parseJson = type("string.json.parse").to({
	name: "string",
	version: "string.semver"
})

const out = parseJson('{ "name": true, "version": "v2.0.0" }')

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: name must be a string (was boolean)
	//            version must be a semantic version (see https://semver.org/) (was "v2.0.0")
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// { name: string; version: string }
	console.log(`${out.name}:${out.version}`)
}
```

> **Morphs receive your data, not a copy**
>
> A morph is passed the validated value itself. If it mutates its argument, it
> mutates the caller's data, so return a new value instead.

```ts
const addTag = type({ tags: "string[]" }).pipe(o => ({
	...o,
	tags: [...o.tags, "new"]
}))
```

When you're ready to ship, [precompile](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) your Types: the same definitions, compiled when you build into standalone validators that carry only the checks they need.

You now have the fundamentals you need to bring your types to runtime. The rest of the docs cover each part of the API in depth, starting with [primitives](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives).

# Cheat sheet

> ArkType's most common syntax, patterns and gotchas on one page.

A quick reference for ArkType's most common patterns. The [skill for agents](https://arktype.io/docs/agents) covers the same ground.

## Syntax kinds

ArkType offers several ways to define the same type. Use whichever fits your context.

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

// string expression, the most concise
const StringSyntax = type("string | number")

// tuple expression, for operands that aren't strings
const TupleSyntax = type(["string", "|", "number"])

// chained, to compose existing types
const Chained = type("string").or("number")
```

## Keywords

Keywords follow a `typescriptType.constraint.subconstraint` pattern. See [Keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords) for the full list.

```ts
// string keywords
type("string.email") // email address
type("string.uuid") // UUID
type("string.url") // parsable URL
type("string.trim") // morph: trims whitespace
type("string.json.parse") // morph: string → parsed JSON
type("string.date.parse") // morph: string → Date

// number keywords
type("number.integer") // whole numbers
type("number.safe") // between MIN_SAFE_INTEGER and MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, not necessarily an integer
type("number.epoch") // integer ms timestamp a Date can hold
```

`number` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`. Add `number.NaN`, `number.Infinity` or `number.NegativeInfinity` to allow them.

## Operators

```ts
type("string | number") // union
type("string.email & /@arktype\\.io$/") // intersection
type("number > 0") // exclusive min
type("number >= 0") // inclusive min
type("string <= 255") // max length
type("number != 0") // excludes 0
type("number % 2") // divisible by 2
```

## Objects

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"email?": "string.email", // optional: '?' goes on the key
	age: "number >= 0 = 0" // defaultable, so optional in the input
})

// index signatures (Record types)
const Env = type({
	"[string]": "string" // Record<string, string>
})

// undeclared keys are allowed by default; reject or remove them
const Strict = type({ "+": "reject", name: "string" })
const Stripped = type({ "+": "delete", name: "string" })
```

## Arrays and tuples

```ts
const Strings = type("string[]") // string expression
const Numbers = type.number.array() // chained

// tuples: fixed length, a type per position
const Pair = type(["string", "number"])

// type([X]) is a 1-element tuple, not an array
const Item = type({ id: "string" })
const Wrong = type([Item]) // tuple of exactly [Item]
const Right = Item.array() // Item[]

// readonly
const Ids = type("string[]").readonly() // readonly string[]
```

## Enumerations

```ts
const Role = type("'admin' | 'member'") // literals need their own quotes
const Size = type.enumerated(1, 2, 3)

enum Color {
	Red = "red",
	Blue = "blue"
}
const ColorValue = type.valueOf(Color)
```

## Composition

```ts
const Device = type({
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"version?": "string"
})

// reference in another type by passing it directly
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	device: Device
})

// fluent composition
const Admin = User.and({ role: "'admin'" })
const Guest = type({ name: "string" }).or({ token: "string" })
const Draft = User.partial()
const Name = User.pick("name")
```

## Recursive types

```ts
import { scope } from "arktype"

const types = scope({
	TreeNode: {
		value: "number",
		children: "TreeNode[]"
	}
}).export()

const tree = types.TreeNode({ value: 1, children: [] })
```

## Morphs and pipes

```ts
// .to(): parse, then validate the output
const parsePort = type("string.integer.parse").to("0 < number <= 65535")

// .pipe(): validate, then transform
const toUpper = type("string").pipe(s => s.toUpperCase())

// built-in parse morphs
const parseDate = type("string.date.parse") // string → Date
const parseJson = type("string.json.parse") // string → parsed JSON
const trim = type("string.trim") // string → trimmed string
```

## Custom rules

```ts
const Signup = type({
	password: "string >= 8",
	confirmPassword: "string"
}).narrow(
	(data, ctx) =>
		data.password === data.confirmPassword ||
		ctx.reject({
			expected: "identical to password",
			actual: "",
			path: ["confirmPassword"]
		})
)
```

## Matching

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const sizeOf = match({
	string: s => s.length,
	number: n => n,
	default: "assert"
})

sizeOf("abc") // 3
```

## Type inference

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number"
})

// extract the TypeScript type
type User = typeof User.infer
// { name: string; age?: number }
```

## Error handling

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number"
})

const out = User({ name: "Alan", age: "not a number" })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: age must be a number (was a string)
	console.error(out.summary)
	// plain objects, each with its path, code and message
	out.issues[0].path
} else {
	// out is typed as { name: string; age?: number }
	console.log(out.name)
}

// returns the validated data or throws
const user = User.assert({ name: "Alan" })
```

## Interop

```ts
// a Standard Schema, accepted by tRPC, Hono, oRPC, the MCP SDK and others
User["~standard"]

// { $schema: "...", type: "object", properties: { ... }, required: ["name"] }
User.toJsonSchema()
```

Global configuration goes through `configure` from `arktype/config`, in a file that runs before anything imports `arktype`. See [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).

## Precompile

```ts
// vite.config.ts: every Type becomes a standalone validator at build time
export default {
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
}
```

## Common gotchas

| Mistake | Fix |
| - | - |
| `name: "string \| undefined"` for optional | Use `"name?": "string"`: `?` goes on the **key** |
| `type([Schema])` for arrays | Use `Schema.array()`: brackets create tuples |
| ``type(`${Schema}[]`)`` | Use `Schema.array()` or `[Schema, "[]"]`, never interpolate a Type |
| `"Record<string, T>"` with `T` a variable | Use `type.Record("string", T)` or `{ "[string]": T }` |
| `type("number = 0")` | Defaults only work as object values or tuple elements |
| `out[0]` or `out.map(...)` on errors | Use `out.issues[0]` or `out.issues.map(...)` |
| Mutating the argument in `.pipe` | Return a new value; a morph receives the caller's data, not a copy |
| `type User = typeof Schema.t` | Use `typeof Schema.infer` for the output type |
| Precompiled: `User.and(...)` called at runtime | Compose inside a definition: `const Admin = User.and(...)` |
| Precompiled: `type()` from a runtime value | Make it static, mark it `// @ark-runtime`, or build with `runtime: "arktype"` |

# Agents

> Help Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents write ArkType.

Every error ArkType reports names its fix: `tsc`'s as a definition is written, a [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) build's and validation's. An agent can close each loop on its own, which is also why precompiling is free with one: the build step is one more loop it already runs.

## Skill

The ArkType [skill](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/skills/arktype/SKILL.md) tells agents when to reach for ArkType, how its syntax maps to TypeScript, and which mistakes to avoid. Add it to your project with:

```bash
npx skills add arktypeio/arktype
```

This installs the skill from the repository's default branch, which tracks the latest release. The `arktype` package also includes the skill at `skills/arktype/SKILL.md`, so tools like [skills-npm](https://github.com/antfu/skills-npm) can link the copy that matches your installed version.

Agents read two references the skill links when a task needs them: the [migration guide](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating), when they convert schemas from Zod, Valibot, TypeBox, Yup, Joi, Effect Schema or JSON Schema, and a precompile guide with the setup for each bundler, Next.js and test runner and the fix for each build error.

## Migrate from Zod

With the skill installed, ask for a migration in one prompt:

```
Migrate this project from Zod to ArkType.
```

The agent rewrites each schema where it is, keeps Zod's removal of undeclared keys, swaps integrations like `zodResolver` for their Standard Schema versions, removes `zod` with your package manager and runs your typecheck and tests. Where a dependency accepts only Zod, like the MCP SDK before v2, it keeps Zod for that call. Review its summary, which lists what still behaves differently and any test it updated, like a JSON Schema snapshot whose keys are now in canonical order. [Migrating a project](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#migrating-a-project) lists the steps it follows.

## Docs as Markdown

Every page of these docs is available as Markdown by adding `.md` to its URL, e.g. [/docs/intro/setup.md](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/setup.md). The Copy page button beside each page's title copies it, and its menu opens it in Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor.

[/llms.txt](https://arktype.io/llms.txt) is an index of every page, with a link to its Markdown and a one-line description, following the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention. [/llms-full.txt](https://arktype.io/llms-full.txt) has the full text of every ArkType page in one file. Precompile, ArkRegex, Attest, JSON Schema, ArkSets and Internals each have a file like it at their section's URL plus `/llms.txt`, like [/docs/precompile/llms.txt](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/llms.txt).

## Precompile

Precompiling used to cost a build step and its errors. An agent runs the build, reads the error and fixes it, so your users get the speed and size and you don't pay for them. A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) build reports each definition it can't precompile with its file, line and column, the reason and the fix. [With agents](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile#with-agents) shows one and the tools that shorten the loop: `arktype-precompile --check`, the ESLint rule and shadow mode. [Troubleshooting](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting) lists the fix for each report.

## AGENTS.md

Agents that don't load skills still read your `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. Paste this in to keep them on ArkType when they add validation:

```md
## Validation

- Validate untrusted input, like request bodies, form data, env vars and JSON, with ArkType. Docs: https://arktype.io/llms.txt
- Derive each TypeScript type from its validator with `typeof T.infer` rather than writing it by hand.
```

If you precompile, add:

```md
- ArkType definitions are precompiled by @ark/aot when the app builds. Fix each precompile error as its last line says, and don't set allowUnsafe or runtime: "arktype" to get past one. `npx arktype-precompile --check "src/**/*.ts"` lists them without building. Setup and fixes: https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/llms.txt
```

## Building agents

ArkType types are [Standard Schemas](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema) that can also produce JSON Schema, so libraries that need both accept them directly. For example, the [MCP TypeScript SDK](https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/advanced/schema-libraries) (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`) takes an ArkType type as a tool's `inputSchema` as-is. It derives the JSON Schema the model sees from it, and validates the model's arguments before your handler runs:

```ts
// server is an McpServer from @modelcontextprotocol/server
server.registerTool(
	"greet",
	{
		description: "Greet someone by name",
		inputSchema: type({ name: "string", "times?": "1 <= number.integer <= 5" })
	},
	async ({ name, times }) => ({
		content: [{ type: "text", text: `Hello, ${name}! `.repeat(times ?? 1) }]
	})
)
```

Calling `greet` with `times: 99` returns an error result to the model with ArkType's message, `times must be at most 5 (was 99)`, so it knows what to fix.

A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) validator ships `~standard.jsonSchema`, which the SDK reads to describe the tool, only when you ask for it, so set it in `ark.json`:

```json
{ "precompile": { "members": { "~standard.jsonSchema": true } } }
```

# Editor setup

> Highlighting, inline errors and autocomplete for ArkType definitions in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and other editors.

ArkType works in any editor with TypeScript support. These extensions make definitions read like the rest of your code.

## VS Code

Install [ArkType](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=arktypeio.arkdark) (`arktypeio.arkdark`). It's also on [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/arktypeio/arkdark) for Cursor, VSCodium and Windsurf. It adds:

- syntax highlighting for strings in ArkType definitions, in `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mdx`, `.svelte`, `.vue`, `.astro` and Markdown files
- one-line summaries of ArkType's type errors at the end of the line, through [ErrorLens](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=usernamehw.errorlens), which it installs as a dependency
- the setting `"editor.quickSuggestions": { "strings": "on" }`, so you get completions while typing an expression like `"string | num"`

It also sets ErrorLens to show the message of the problem closest to your cursor, with no delay and without the hover buttons, and to show only the part of an ArkType error that names the fix, like `"number | string"` for `"number | strin"`. Each is an ordinary default, so a value in your own settings for `errorLens.followCursor`, `errorLens.delay`, `errorLens.editorHoverPartsEnabled` or `errorLens.replace` overrides it.

To have auto-import pick ArkType's `type` instead of the `type` function from Node's `os` module, add this to `.vscode/settings.json`:

```json
{
	"typescript.preferences.autoImportSpecifierExcludeRegexes": ["^(node:)?os$"]
}
```

### Themes

[ArkThemes](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=arktypeio.arkthemes) (`arktypeio.arkthemes`, also on [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/arktypeio/arkthemes)) is a separate extension with **ArkDark**, which these docs use for code, and **ArkLight**, each with an italic variant. They highlight TypeScript generics distinctly. You don't need them for the ArkType extension to work.

## JetBrains IDEs

The [ArkType plugin](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/27099-arktype), maintained by Jan-Niklas Wortmann, adds syntax highlighting for ArkType definitions to WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA and other JetBrains IDEs.

## Other editors

There's no official extension for other editors yet. For Neovim, a community [tree-sitter grammar](https://github.com/jeffrom/tree-sitter-arktype) covers the most common syntax. If you'd like to help add support for another editor, see [this issue](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/989).

Completions and type errors come from TypeScript, so they work in every editor without an extension.

# Migrating

> Migrate a project from Zod with one prompt, or convert schemas from Zod, Valibot, TypeBox, Yup, Joi, Effect Schema and JSON Schema to ArkType, and the defaults that differ between them.

To migrate a project from Zod, add the [ArkType skill](https://arktype.io/docs/agents#skill) and ask your agent:

```
Migrate this project from Zod to ArkType.
```

It follows [Migrating a project](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#migrating-a-project). This page is also part of the skill, as `references/migrating.md`, so agents read it when they convert schemas.

## Zod side by side

A Zod schema and its ArkType equivalent:

```ts
import { z } from "zod"

const User = z.object({
	name: z.string().min(1),
	email: z.email(),
	age: z.number().int().nonnegative().optional(),
	role: z.enum(["admin", "member"]).default("member")
})

type User = z.infer<typeof User>

const result = User.safeParse(data)

if (!result.success) console.error(result.error.issues)
```

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	// z.object() removes undeclared keys
	"+": "delete",
	name: "string >= 1",
	email: "string.email",
	// .optional() accepts undefined too
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0 | undefined",
	role: "'admin' | 'member' = 'member'"
})

type User = typeof User.infer

const out = User(data)

if (out instanceof type.errors) console.error(out.issues)
```

`.parse(data)` is `User.assert(data)`. The [Zod table](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#zod) maps the rest of the API, and [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ) lists what to write where the two libraries' defaults disagree, like `"+": "delete"` above. One the example leaves as is: Zod also applies `role`'s default when the key is present as `undefined`, which ArkType rejects.

## Adopt incrementally

You don't have to convert a project at once. ArkType and Zod both implement [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), so each can stand in for the other while you convert:

- **A Zod schema works inside an ArkType definition**, so convert the schemas that use it first and the shared one later:

```ts
import { z } from "zod"

// not converted yet
const Address = z.object({ street: z.string(), city: z.string() })

const User = type({ name: "string", address: Address })
```

- **An ArkType Type works wherever a library accepts Standard Schema**, like tRPC, TanStack Form, Hono's `sValidator` or react-hook-form's `standardSchemaResolver`, so call sites can switch one at a time. [Swap integrations](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#migrating-a-project) has each.

A Valibot schema embeds the same way. Yup's validates asynchronously, so it can't.

## Precompile

Once your schemas are Types, [add `@ark/aot`](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/setup#add-the-plugin) to your bundler, so each Type ships as a standalone validator with no parser. Your definitions don't change.

A definition that still embeds a Zod or Valibot schema can't be precompiled yet, so the build fails, naming it. Until you've converted it, build with `runtime: "arktype"`, which ships arktype, so what the build can't precompile runs as it did before:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.vite({ runtime: "arktype" })]
})
```

To see what's left, run `npx arktype-precompile --check`, which lists each definition the default build would refuse. See [Dynamic vs Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/dynamic-vs-precompiled).

## Migrating a project

To move a whole project off Zod, or another library below, work through it in this order.

1. **Take stock.** Find every import of the old library (`zod`, `zod/v4`, `zod/mini`) and of packages built on it, like `@hookform/resolvers/zod` or `zod-to-json-schema`, and every use of the schemas, including files that call `.safeParse()` or read `.shape` without importing the library. Run the project's typecheck and test scripts once, so you know what passes before you start.
2. **Convert each schema in place.** Keep its name, its file and what it takes and returns, so imports and call sites keep working: a `.transform()` stays in the schema as a `.pipe()`, not in its callers. `z.infer<typeof X>` and `z.output` become `typeof X.infer`, and `z.input` becomes `typeof X.inferIn`.
3. **Keep behavior identical.** The migrated schemas should accept, reject and return what the old ones did. These rules are for Zod, and [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ) has them for the other libraries:
   - `z.object()` removes undeclared keys, and so should the migrated objects, even where the code reads only declared keys, since parsed data often reaches a database or a response whole. Call `configure({ onUndeclaredKey: "delete" })` from `arktype/config` in one file, like `src/arktype.config.ts`, and import it first in every file that creates a Type, so it applies whichever file loads first, tests included. If the project [precompiles](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile), also name that file as the build's `config` in [`ark.json`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#ark-json), which the CLI and test drivers read as the bundler does. Then `.passthrough()` and `z.looseObject()` become `"+": "ignore"`, and `.strict()` becomes `"+": "reject"`.
   - Without that setting, write `"+": "delete"` in every object instead, nested ones included. `.merge()` takes `"+"` from the object merged in, so write `.merge({ "+": "delete", ... })`; with the global setting, merged objects keep deleting.
   - A union of such objects throws a `ParseError` saying it's indeterminate unless a key tells them apart. Follow [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ) for it, and keep the global setting: `"+": "ignore"` belongs only on the union's branches.
   - `.optional()` also accepts `undefined`, so write `"key?": "T | undefined"`. Before Zod 4.4, any key whose schema accepts `undefined` may be missing, so a `z.unknown()` key is `"key?": "unknown"`; from 4.4, only `.optional()` and defaults let a key be missing, so it stays `key: "unknown"`. Check the version the project installs. In Zod 4, `.default(x).optional()` still fills in `x`, so it's `key: T.default(x)`.
   - `z.any()` is `"unknown.any"`, or `"key?": "unknown.any"` as a key before Zod 4.4. It infers `any` as Zod's did, so refinements that read its properties type-check without casts.
   - Translate coercions and refinements literally, as in [Coercion is a parse](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#semantics-to-check). `z.coerce.number()` takes any input, `null` included, so its input stays `"unknown"`, in a tool's input schema too. Keywords like `string.numeric.parse` reject inputs Zod accepted, like `" 1"`, so suggest them rather than substituting them. A `.refine()` after a `.transform()` is a `.narrow()` after a `.pipe()`: `.to("number > 0")` would also check the type, and `number` rejects `Infinity` and `NaN`. An object's `.refine()` stays on that object as a `.narrow()`, not in a second schema.
   - `string.email` and Zod 4's `z.email()` disagree on some addresses: Zod rejects `a..b@x.co` and `.a@x.co` and accepts `a'b@x.co`, and ArkType does the opposite. Where that matters, keep Zod's pattern as a regex.
   - Keep custom messages. `.min(1, "Name is required")` becomes `type("string >= 1").configure({ message: "Name is required" })`.
4. **Update call sites.**
   - `X.parse(data)` becomes `X.assert(data)`, which throws.
   - `X.safeParse(data)` becomes `const out = X(data)`, then check `out instanceof type.errors`. `parseAsync` and `safeParseAsync` become the same, since ArkType is synchronous.
   - `ZodError` becomes `type.errors`. Its `issues` keep their `path` and `message`, and `error.format()` becomes `out.summary`. `error.flatten().fieldErrors` becomes `flatByPath(out)`, which maps each path to its errors; read each error's `message`, which is the custom one where you configured it. `X.assert` throws a `TraversalError`, whose `arkErrors` holds them.
   - Don't add casts or `any`, not even `as unknown`. A helper typed with `z.ZodTypeAny` or `z.ZodSchema` takes `type.Any`. To keep the output type, use `<T extends type.Any>(schema: T): T["infer"]`, not `type.Any<t>`. A function that builds a schema from another becomes a generic, like `type("<t>", { data: "t" })`.
5. **Swap integrations.** Most accept an ArkType type directly, through [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema):

| With Zod | With ArkType |
| - | - |
| `zodResolver(schema)` (react-hook-form) | `standardSchemaResolver(schema)` from `@hookform/resolvers/standard-schema` |
| tRPC `.input(schema)`, `@t3-oss/env-*`, TanStack Form | the same call, given the ArkType type |
| AI SDK 6 `tool({ inputSchema })`, MCP SDK v2 `registerTool` | the same call, given the ArkType type, which also supplies the JSON Schema |
| AI SDK 5 `tool({ inputSchema })` | `jsonSchema<typeof T.infer>(T.toJsonSchema(), { validate })`, where `validate` returns `{ success: true, value }` or `{ success: false, error }` |
| `zValidator` from `@hono/zod-validator` | `sValidator` from `@hono/standard-validator` |
| `@hono/zod-openapi` | `hono-openapi`: `describeRoute`, `validator` and `resolver` |
| `zod-to-json-schema`, `z.toJSONSchema(schema)` | `schema.toJsonSchema()` |
| `@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi` | `schema.toJsonSchema({ target: "openapi-3.0" })` for each Schema Object in your OpenAPI document; see below |
| `drizzle-zod` | `drizzle-arktype` |
| a library that accepts only Zod | keep Zod for that call, and say so |

Without casts:

- `toJsonSchema()` returns a `JsonSchema`, the type to give the document's Schema Objects (`import type { JsonSchema } from "arktype"`). Build path and query parameters from an object type's `.props`, which lists each key, whether it's required, and its Type.
- A `fallback` declared apart from the `toJsonSchema()` call is a `ToJsonSchema.FallbackOption` (`import type { ToJsonSchema } from "arktype"`).
- The MCP SDK finds a prompt argument's completer through Zod's `.shape`, so give `argsSchema` one, as below.

```ts
import { completable } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server"
import { type } from "arktype"

const Args = type({ language: "string" })
const argsSchema = {
	"~standard": Args["~standard"],
	shape: {
		language: completable({ "~standard": type("string")["~standard"] }, value =>
			["typescript", "python"].filter(l => l.startsWith(value))
		)
	}
}
```

6. **Swap dependencies.** Remove `zod` and the packages that existed only for it, and add their replacements, with the project's package manager, like `pnpm remove zod` or `npm uninstall zod`. Editing `package.json` by hand leaves the lockfile stale, and some package managers then refuse to run scripts. If `arktype` is already a dependency, keep that version. Don't upgrade another dependency to a new major version, like the MCP SDK to v2, so it takes ArkType; keep Zod for it as the table says.
7. **Verify.** Run the `typecheck` and `test` scripts in `package.json` until both pass; `npx tsc` alone can miss a second tsconfig. Search again for imports of the old library, and check that every file importing `arktype`, `.js` files included, imports the config first if it creates a Type. Change a test only where it asserts the old library itself, like a Zod error message or `instanceof ZodError`. Never delete a test, weaken an assertion or change an expected value to match new output. The exception is a snapshot of generated JSON Schema, which ArkType writes in a canonical order: required keys, then optional ones, each sorted, and enum and union members sorted. Reorder such a snapshot only when order is its only difference.
8. **Report** what still behaves differently, if anything, such as error message text, and any snapshot you reordered.

## How to convert

1. Write each schema as the TypeScript type it validates. Most constructs become a string or an object definition; the tables below map them library by library.
2. Check every row of [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ). A translation that looks right can still accept or return different data.
3. Confirm the types match. While the old schema still exists, a line like this fails to compile until they do:

```ts
type Equals<a, b> =
	[a] extends [b] ?
		[b] extends [a] ?
			true
		:	false
	:	false
const outputMatches: Equals<typeof User.infer, z.output<typeof OldUser>> = true
const inputMatches: Equals<typeof User.inferIn, z.input<typeof OldUser>> = true
```

4. Run both on the same inputs, valid and invalid, and compare which they accept and what they return.

You can migrate one schema at a time. A Zod or Valibot schema is a [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), so it can appear inside an ArkType definition while the rest is converted: `type({ name: "string", address: zodAddress })`. Yup's Standard Schema validates asynchronously, so it can't.

## Defaults that differ

| Behavior | ArkType | Zod | Valibot | TypeBox `Value.Check` | Yup | Joi | Effect Schema |
| - | - | - | - | - | - | - | - |
| Undeclared object keys | kept | removed | removed | allowed | kept | rejected | removed |
| Optional key present with the value undefined | rejected | accepted | accepted | accepted | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| Default applied when the value is undefined | no, only if absent | yes | yes | only `Value.Default` | yes | yes | yes |
| Converts input types, e.g. `"12"` to `12` | only when parsing | only in `z.coerce` | no | only `Value.Convert` | yes, unless strict | yes, unless convert false | no |
| `number` accepts `Infinity` | no | v4: no, v3: yes | yes | no | yes | no | yes |
| `number` accepts `NaN` | no | no | no | no | no | no | yes |
| An array where an object is expected | accepted | rejected | accepted | rejected | rejected | rejected | rejected |
| Empty string for a plain string | accepted | accepted | accepted | accepted | rejected if required | rejected | accepted |

What to write when the old behavior matters:

```ts
// remove undeclared keys like Zod, Valibot and Effect, for this object only
const Stripped = type({ "+": "delete", name: "string" })

// reject them like Joi or Zod's .strict()
const Strict = type({ "+": "reject", name: "string" })

// accept an explicit undefined as well as a missing key
const Patch = type({ "nickname?": "string | undefined" })

// apply a default when the key is missing or undefined
const Settings = type({
	theme: type("'light' | 'dark' | undefined")
		.pipe(v => v ?? "light")
		.default(undefined)
})

// allow non-finite numbers
const Measurement = type(
	"number | number.Infinity | number.NegativeInfinity | number.NaN"
)
```

`"+"` applies to its own object, not to nested ones, and `.merge()` takes it from the object merged in, so repeat it there. To remove undeclared keys everywhere, as Zod does, set `onUndeclaredKey: "delete"` with `configure` from `arktype/config`, in a file imported before anything imports `arktype`.

Either way, an object that deletes keys transforms its input, so a union of such objects needs a key that tells them apart, like a literal `type`. Without one, data with both objects' keys could come out as either, so the union throws a `ParseError`. Where the old schema has no such key, delete outside the union. The result keeps every key either object declares, where Zod keeps only those of the first object that matches:

```ts
// z.union([z.object({ uri, text }), z.object({ uri, blob })])
const Contents = type({ "+": "ignore", uri: "string", text: "string" })
	.or({ "+": "ignore", uri: "string", blob: "string" })
	.to({ "+": "delete", uri: "string", "text?": "string", "blob?": "string" })
```

With `"delete"` or `"reject"`, from `"+"` or `configure`, an object's undeclared keys are `never`, so `.and()` with an object that has other keys throws. Add keys with `.merge()`.

## Semantics to check

**Transforms run in order.** `.pipe(fn)` transforms after validation, `.to(definition)` validates the result, and a `.narrow()` after a `.pipe()` sees the transformed value, like Zod's `.transform().refine()`. A narrow on an object whose properties transform sees the transformed properties.

```ts
// Zod: z.string().transform(s => s.length).refine(n => n > 2)
const Length = type("string")
	.pipe(s => s.length)
	.narrow(n => n > 2)

// Zod: z.preprocess(v => (typeof v === "string" ? v.split(",") : v), z.array(z.string()))
const Tags = type("string | string[]")
	.pipe(v => (typeof v === "string" ? v.split(",") : v))
	.to("string[]")
```

**Coercion is a parse.** ArkType never converts a value unless the definition says so, so write the conversion the old library did. `string.numeric.parse`, `string.integer.parse`, `string.date.parse`, `string.json.parse` and `string.url.parse` accept only strings, and accept fewer of them than `Number()` or `new Date()`:

```ts
// z.coerce.number(), which is Number(value) for any input
const Count = type("unknown").pipe(Number).to("number")

// z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(8080) in an object
const Server = type({
	port: type("unknown").pipe(Number).to("number.integer > 0").default(8080)
})

// z.coerce.date(), which is new Date(value) for any input, so null is 1970-01-01
const When = type("unknown")
	.pipe(
		v => new Date(v instanceof Date || typeof v === "string" ? v : Number(v))
	)
	.to("Date")

// stricter, for strings only: rejects " 1", "0x10" and ""
const Page = type("string.numeric.parse")

// z.stringbool() accepts "true", "1", "yes", "on" and their opposites; write the set you need
const Flag = type("'true' | 'false'").pipe(s => s === "true")
```

**Refinements with a path or several errors.** A `.narrow()` returns `true` or calls `ctx.reject()`, which takes a `path` and a full `message`. To report several errors, call `ctx.error()` for each, then return `true`:

```ts
// Zod: .superRefine((d, ctx) => ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", message: "...", path: ["end"] }))
const Range = type({ start: "number", end: "number" }).narrow(
	(d, ctx) =>
		d.start <= d.end ||
		ctx.reject({ message: "end must not be before start", path: ["end"] })
)
```

**Discriminated unions are plain unions.** ArkType finds the discriminant itself, so `z.discriminatedUnion("type", [A, B])`, `v.variant("type", [...])` and `Schema.Union(A, B)` are `A.or(B)`, or `"A | B"` in a scope.

**Recursion needs no annotation.** Replace `z.lazy`, `v.lazy`, `Type.Recursive`, `yup.lazy`, `Joi.link` and `Schema.suspend` with a scope, or `this` for a type that refers to itself:

```ts
const Category = type({ name: "string", subcategories: "this[]" })

const types = scope({
	Json: "string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | JsonObject",
	JsonObject: { "[string]": "Json" },
	Filter: { "[string]": "Json | Filter" }
}).export()
```

Delete the hand-written TypeScript type that `z.lazy` needed; `typeof types.Filter.infer` replaces it.

**Composing objects.** `.merge()` replaces keys like Zod's `.extend()`, `v.object({ ...a.entries })` or `Type.Composite`. `.and()` intersects, and throws when a key's types conflict. `.pick()`, `.omit()`, `.partial()`, `.required()` and `.keyof()` keep their names.

**Records with literal keys.** `Record<"a" | "b", T>` must be written as named keys, `{ a: T, b: T }` (add `?` for Zod v3, whose enum-keyed records are partial). An index signature like `"[string]": "number"` applies to every key, including declared ones, so a catch-all like Zod's `.catchall(z.number())` next to a string key becomes `"[string]": "string | number"`.

**Brands.** `.brand("UserId")` or `"string#UserId"` infers `Brand<string, "UserId">`, which is not assignable to or from the old library's brand type. Change code that names the old brand type to `typeof UserId.infer`.

**Errors.** Errors are values: `T(data)` returns the data or an `ArkErrors`, and `T.assert(data)` throws. To change a message, `.describe("a strong password")` gives `must be a strong password (was ...)`, and `.configure({ message: "Choose a stronger password" })` replaces the whole message. Zod's and Valibot's `description` is documentation, but ArkType's `.describe()` is what errors say the value must be, so keep documentation in a comment or `.configure({ title })`.

**Dates and formats.** `z.string().datetime()` rejects offsets and date-only strings unless configured; `string.date.iso` accepts both. In JSON Schema, `format` is an annotation and validates nothing unless the validator, like ajv with `ajv-formats`, checks it; `string.email` always validates.

**Synchronous only.** ArkType doesn't await. Move an async `refine`, Yup `test` or Joi `external` out of the schema and run it after validation.

## Zod

Zod Mini spells most methods as functions, so `z.optional(z.string())` maps like `z.string().optional()`, and `z.string().check(z.minLength(1))` like `z.string().min(1)`.

| Zod | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `z.string()`, `z.number()`, `z.boolean()`, `z.null()` | `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"null"` |
| `z.unknown()`, `z.any()`, `z.never()` | `"unknown"`, `"unknown.any"`, `"never"` |
| `z.literal("a")`, `z.literal(0.5)` | `"'a'"`, `"0.5"` |
| `z.enum(["a", "b"])` | `"'a' \| 'b'"` or `type.enumerated("a", "b")` |
| `z.nativeEnum(E)`, `z.enum(E)` | `type.valueOf(E)` |
| `z.object({ ... })` | `type({ ... })`, nested objects as plain objects |
| `.optional()` on a property | `"key?": "T \| undefined"` |
| `.nullable()`, `.nullish()` | `"string \| null"`; `"key?": "string \| null \| undefined"` |
| `.default(x)` on a property | `"key": "number = 0"` or `key: T.default(x)` |
| `z.array(T)`, `.min(1)`, `.nonempty()` | `"T[]"` or `T.array()`, `"string[] >= 1"` |
| `z.array(T).min(1)`, `T` a Type in a variable | `T.array().atLeastLength(1)` |
| `z.tuple([A, B])`, `.rest(C)` | `[A, B]`, `[A, B, "...", "C[]"]` |
| `z.union([A, B])`, `A.or(B)`, `z.discriminatedUnion` | `A.or(B)`, `"A \| B"` |
| `z.intersection(A, B)`, `A.and(B)` | `A.and(B)` |
| `z.record(z.string(), T)` | `"Record<string, T>"` or `{ "[string]": T }` |
| `.extend({ ... })`, `.merge(B)` | `.merge({ ... })` |
| `.pick`, `.omit`, `.partial`, `.required`, `.keyof` | same names |
| `.strict()`, `z.strictObject` | `"+": "reject"` |
| `.passthrough()`, `z.looseObject` | the default |
| `.strip()`, the default `z.object` | `"+": "delete"` |
| `z.lazy(() => T)` | a scope or `this` |
| `.min(n)` / `.max(n)` / `.length(n)` on strings | `"string >= n"`, `"string <= n"`, `"string == n"` |
| `.int()`, `.positive()`, `.nonnegative()`, `.gt(n)` | `"number.integer"`, `"number > 0"`, `"number >= 0"`, `"number > n"` |
| `.multipleOf(n)` | `"number % n"` |
| `.email()`, `.url()`, `.uuid()`, `.regex(r)` | `"string.email"`, `"string.url"`, `"string.uuid"`, `/r/` |
| `.ip()` (Zod 3), `z.ipv4()`, `z.ipv6()` | `"string.ip"`, `"string.ip.v4"`, `"string.ip.v6"` |
| `.datetime()`, `z.iso.datetime()` | `"string.date.iso"` |
| `.trim()`, `.toLowerCase()` | `"string.trim"`, `"string.lower"` |
| `z.date()`, `z.instanceof(C)` | `"Date"`, `type.instanceOf(C)` |
| `.refine(fn, msg)`, `.superRefine(fn)` | `.narrow((v, ctx) => fn(v) \|\| ctx.reject({ message: msg }))` |
| `.transform(fn)`, `.pipe(T)` | `.pipe(fn)`, `.to(T)` |
| `z.preprocess(fn, T)` | `type("unknown").pipe(fn).to(T)` |
| `z.coerce.number()`, `z.coerce.date()` | `type("unknown").pipe(Number).to("number")`, see above |
| `z.custom<T>(fn)` | `type("unknown").narrow((v): v is T => fn(v))` |
| `.brand<"Id">()` | `.brand("Id")` or `"string#Id"` |
| `.describe(text)` | a comment or `.configure({ title: text })` |
| `{ message }`, `{ error }`, `required_error` | `.configure({ message })`, or `.describe(...)` for "must be ..." |
| `z.infer`, `z.output`, `z.input` | `typeof T.infer`, `typeof T.inferIn` |
| `.parse(x)`, `.safeParse(x)` | `T.assert(x)`, `T(x)` then `instanceof type.errors` |
| `ZodError`, `.flatten().fieldErrors` | `type.errors`, `flatByPath(out)` |
| `z.ZodTypeAny` in a helper's signature | `type.Any` |

## Valibot

| Valibot | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `v.object`, `v.looseObject`, `v.strictObject` | `"+": "delete"`, the default, `"+": "reject"` |
| `v.objectWithRest(entries, rest)` | an index signature, `"[string]": ...` |
| `v.optional(T)`, `v.exactOptional(T)` | `"key?": "T \| undefined"`, `"key?": "T"` |
| `v.optional(T, default)` | `"key": "T = default"`, which applies it only where the key is missing; Valibot also applies it to `undefined`, so see [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ) |
| `v.nullable(T)`, `v.nullish(T)` | `"T \| null"`, `"key?": "T \| null \| undefined"` |
| `v.picklist(["a", "b"])`, `v.enum(E)` | `"'a' \| 'b'"`, `type.valueOf(E)` |
| `v.union`, `v.variant("type", [...])`, `v.intersect` | `A.or(B)`, `A.or(B)`, `A.and(B)` |
| `v.array`, `v.tuple`, `v.tupleWithRest`, `v.record` | `"T[]"`, `[A, B]`, `[A, "...", "B[]"]`, `"Record<string, T>"` |
| `v.lazy` | a scope or `this` |
| `v.pipe(v.string(), v.email(), v.maxLength(255))` | `"string.email <= 255"` |
| `v.minLength`, `v.maxLength`, `v.length`, `v.nonEmpty` | `"string >= n"`, `"string <= n"`, `"string == n"`, `"string > 0"` |
| `v.minValue`, `v.maxValue`, `v.integer`, `v.multipleOf` | `"number >= n"`, `"number <= n"`, `"number.integer"`, `"number % n"` |
| `v.url`, `v.uuid`, `v.isoDateTime`, `v.regex(r)` | `"string.url"`, `"string.uuid"`, `"string.date.iso"`, `/r/` |
| `v.trim()`, `v.toLowerCase()`, `v.toNumber()`, `v.toDate()` | `"string.trim"`, `"string.lower"`, `"string.numeric.parse"`, `"string.date.parse"` |
| `v.check(fn, msg)`, `v.rawCheck` | `.narrow((x, ctx) => fn(x) \|\| ctx.reject({ message: msg }))` |
| `v.forward(v.partialCheck(...), ["key"])` | `.narrow(...)` with `ctx.reject({ path: ["key"] })` |
| `v.transform(fn)` | `.pipe(fn)` |
| `v.brand("Id")` | `.brand("Id")` |
| `v.instance(C)`, `v.date()`, `v.custom(fn)` | `type.instanceOf(C)`, `"Date"`, `type("unknown").narrow(fn)` |
| `v.fallback(T, x)` | none; handle the `ArkErrors` result |
| `v.InferOutput`, `v.InferInput` | `typeof T.infer`, `typeof T.inferIn` |
| `v.parse(S, x)`, `v.safeParse(S, x)` | `T.assert(x)`, `T(x)` |

## TypeBox

TypeBox schemas are JSON Schema, so [JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#json-schema-and-ajv) also applies.

| TypeBox | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `Type.Object({...})`, `{ additionalProperties: false }` | `type({...})`, `"+": "reject"` |
| `Type.Optional(T)` | `"key?": "T \| undefined"` |
| `Type.String({ minLength, maxLength, pattern })` | `"1 <= string <= 255"`, `/pattern/` |
| `Type.String({ format: "email" })` | `"string.email"` |
| `Type.Number({ minimum, exclusiveMaximum })`, `Type.Integer()` | `"0 <= number < 10"`, `"number.integer"` |
| `Type.Literal`, `Type.Union`, `Type.Enum(E)` | `"'a'"`, `A.or(B)`, `type.valueOf(E)` |
| `Type.Array(T, { minItems })`, `Type.Tuple` | `"T[] >= 1"`, `[A, B]` |
| `Type.Record(Type.String(), T)` | `"Record<string, T>"` |
| `Type.Intersect`, `Type.Composite` | `A.and(B)`, `A.merge(B)` |
| `Type.Partial`, `Type.Pick`, `Type.Omit`, `Type.KeyOf` | `.partial()`, `.pick()`, `.omit()`, `.keyof()` |
| `Type.Recursive(This => ...)` | `this` or a scope |
| `Type.Date()`, `Type.Unknown()`, `Type.Any()` | `"Date"`, `"unknown"`, `"unknown.any"` |
| `Type.Transform(T).Decode(f).Encode(g)` | `codec(T, Out, { decode: f, encode: g })` |
| `Value.Decode(T, x)`, `Value.Encode(T, x)` | `T.assert(x)`, `T.encode.assert(x)` |
| `{ default: x }` with `Value.Default` | `"key": "T = x"` |
| `Static<typeof T>`, `StaticDecode`, `StaticEncode` | `typeof T.infer`, `typeof T.infer`, `typeof T.inferIn` |
| `Value.Check(T, x)`, `Value.Parse`, `TypeCompiler.Compile` | `T.allows(x)`, `T.assert(x)`, nothing to compile |

## Yup

Yup converts values unless `.strict()`, and treats a field as optional unless `.required()`. Translate what the data actually is: a form posting strings needs `"string.numeric.parse"` where Yup's `number()` converted. Like Joi, Yup applies a default to a key present as `undefined`, where `"key": "T = x"` rejects it; [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ) has the pattern that keeps it.

| Yup | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `object({...})`, `.shape({...})` | `type({...})`, `.merge({...})` |
| `string()` (not required) | `"key?": "string \| undefined"` |
| `.required()`, `.defined()`, `.nullable()` | `"key": "string > 0"` for strings, `"key": "T"`, `"T \| null"` |
| `.default(x)` | `"key": "T = x"` |
| `.email()`, `.url()`, `.uuid()`, `.matches(r)` | `"string.email"`, `"string.url"`, `"string.uuid"`, `/r/` |
| `.min(n)`, `.max(n)`, `.length(n)` on strings, arrays | `"string >= n"`, `"T[] <= n"`, `"string == n"` |
| `.integer()`, `.positive()`, `.moreThan(n)` | `"number.integer"`, `"number > 0"`, `"number > n"` |
| `.trim()`, `.lowercase()` | `"string.trim"`, `"string.lower"` |
| `.oneOf(["a", "b"])` | `"'a' \| 'b'"` |
| `array().of(T)`, `tuple([A, B])` | `T.array()`, `[A, B]` |
| `.test(name, message, fn)` | `.narrow((x, ctx) => fn(x) \|\| ctx.reject({ message }))` |
| `.oneOf([ref("password")])` | a `.narrow()` on the object comparing the keys, which runs only once every key is valid, where Yup reports the mismatch beside other errors |
| `.transform(fn)` | `.pipe(fn)` |
| `.when("other", ...)` | a union of the cases, or a `.narrow()` on the object |
| `lazy` | a scope or `this` |
| `.noUnknown()`, `stripUnknown: true` | `"+": "reject"`, `"+": "delete"` |
| `InferType<typeof S>` | `typeof T.infer` |
| `validateSync(x)`, `isValidSync(x)`, `validate(x)` | `T.assert(x)`, `T.allows(x)`, `T(x)` |

## Joi

Joi rejects undeclared keys, rejects empty strings, and converts strings to numbers, booleans and dates unless `convert: false`. ArkType reads an ISO date-time without an offset as UTC, where Joi reads it in local time. Joi also applies a default to a key present as `undefined`; see [Defaults that differ](https://arktype.io/docs/migrating#defaults-that-differ). It infers no types, so `typeof T.infer` replaces the interfaces written next to Joi schemas.

| Joi | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `Joi.object({...})`, `.unknown(true)` | `type({ "+": "reject", ... })`, `type({...})` |
| `Joi.string()` (optional), `.required()` | `"key?": "string > 0 \| undefined"`, `"key": "string > 0"` |
| `.allow("")`, `.allow(null)` | `"string"`, `"string \| null"` |
| `.valid("a", "b")` | `"'a' \| 'b'"` |
| `.email()`, `.uri()`, `.guid()`, `.pattern(r)` | `"string.email"`, `"string.url"`, `"string.uuid"`, `/r/` |
| `.min(n)`, `.max(n)`, `.length(n)` | `"string >= n"`, `"string <= n"`, `"string == n"` |
| `Joi.number().integer().positive()` | `"number.integer > 0"` |
| `Joi.number()` reading strings | `"number \| string.numeric.parse"` |
| `Joi.boolean()` reading strings | `type("boolean \| 'true' \| 'false'").pipe(v => v === true \|\| v === "true")` |
| `Joi.date()`, `Joi.date().iso()` | `"Date \| string.date.parse"`, `"string.date.iso.parse"` |
| `Joi.array().items(T)`, `.min(1)` | `T.array()`, `"T[] >= 1"` |
| `.unique()` | `.narrow((a, ctx) => new Set(a).size === a.length \|\| ctx.reject("unique"))` |
| `Joi.alternatives().try(A, B)` | `A.or(B)` |
| `.default(x)` | `"key": "T = x"` |
| `.custom(fn)` | `.narrow()` or `.pipe()` |
| `.messages({...})` | `.configure({ message })` |
| `Joi.link("#id")` | a scope or `this` |
| `.when(...)` | a union of the cases, or a `.narrow()` on the object |
| `schema.validate(x)`, `.attempt(x, schema)` | `T(x)`, `T.assert(x)` |

## Effect Schema

Names are Effect 3's. Effect 4 renames some: `Schema.filter` is `Schema.check`, `Schema.transform` is `Schema.decodeTo` and `Schema.Enums` is `Schema.Enum`.

| Effect Schema | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `Schema.Struct({...})` | `type({ "+": "delete", ... })` |
| `Schema.optional(T)`, `Schema.optionalWith(T, { exact: true })` | `"key?": "T \| undefined"`, `"key?": "T"` |
| `Schema.optionalWith(T, { default: () => x })` | `"key": "T = x"` |
| `Schema.NullOr`, `Schema.NullishOr` | `"T \| null"`, `"T \| null \| undefined"` |
| `Schema.Literal("a", "b")`, `Schema.Enums(E)` | `"'a' \| 'b'"`, `type.valueOf(E)` |
| `Schema.Union(A, B)`, `Schema.TaggedStruct` | `A.or(B)`, an object with a literal `_tag` |
| `Schema.Array`, `Schema.NonEmptyArray`, `Schema.Tuple` | `"T[]"`, `"T[] >= 1"`, `[A, B]` |
| `Schema.Record({ key: Schema.String, value: T })` | `"Record<string, T>"` |
| `Schema.suspend(() => T)` | a scope or `this` |
| `Schema.Int`, `Schema.Positive`, `Schema.between(a, b)` | `"number.integer"`, `"number > 0"`, `"a <= number <= b"` |
| `Schema.minLength`, `Schema.pattern(r)`, `Schema.UUID` | `"string >= n"`, `/r/`, `"string.uuid"` |
| `Schema.NumberFromString`, `Schema.DateFromString` | `"string.numeric.parse"`, `"string.date.parse"` |
| `Schema.Trim`, `Schema.Lowercase`, `Schema.parseJson(T)` | `"string.trim"`, `"string.lower"`, `type("string.json.parse").to(T)` |
| `Schema.filter(fn)` | `.narrow(fn)` |
| `Schema.transform(From, To, { decode, encode })` | `codec(From, To, { decode, encode })` |
| `Schema.brand("Id")` | `.brand("Id")` |
| `Schema.Type<typeof S>`, `Schema.Encoded<typeof S>` | `typeof T.infer`, `typeof T.inferIn` |
| `Schema.decodeUnknownSync`, `decodeUnknownEither` | `T.assert(x)`, `T(x)` |
| `Schema.encodeSync`, `encodeEither` | `T.encode.assert(x)`, `T.encode(x)` |
| `onExcessProperty: "error"` | `"+": "reject"` |

`codec` comes from `arktype/codecs`, and importing it is what makes `.encode` available. A `Schema.Class` becomes a Type plus, if you need methods, your own class constructed from its output.

## JSON Schema and ajv

To keep a schema as JSON, convert it at runtime with `jsonSchemaToType` from `@ark/json-schema`; it accepts exactly what a JSON Schema 2020-12 validator accepts, except that lengths count UTF-16 code units, with `format` as an annotation. To rewrite it as definitions:

| JSON Schema | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `{ type: "string", minLength: 1, maxLength: 255 }` | `"1 <= string <= 255"` |
| `{ type: "string", pattern: "^a" }` | `/^a/` |
| `{ type: "integer", minimum: 0, exclusiveMaximum: 10 }` | `"0 <= number.integer < 10"` |
| `{ multipleOf: 5 }` | `"number % 5"` |
| `{ enum: ["a", "b"] }`, `{ const: "a" }` | `"'a' \| 'b'"`, `"'a'"` |
| `{ type: ["string", "null"] }`, `anyOf`, `oneOf` | `"string \| null"`, `A.or(B)` |
| `allOf` | `A.and(B)` |
| `properties` with `required` | keys, with `?` on those not required |
| `additionalProperties: false`, `additionalProperties: T` | `"+": "reject"`, `"[string]": "T \| A"`, `A` the declared keys' types |
| `patternProperties: { "^x-": T }` | `"[/^x-/]": T` |
| `{ type: "array", items: T, minItems: 1 }` | `"T[] >= 1"` |
| `prefixItems` | `[A, B]` |
| `$defs` with `$ref` | a scope |
| `format: "email"`, `"uuid"`, `"date-time"`, `"uri"` | `"string.email"`, `"string.uuid"`, `"string.date.iso"`, `"string.url"` |
| `default` | `"key": "T = x"` |

ajv options map too: `removeAdditional` is `"+": "delete"`, `useDefaults` is a default in the definition, and `coerceTypes` is a parse keyword like `string.numeric.parse`. `T.toJsonSchema()` converts back.

# Upgrading

> What to change when upgrading from ArkType 2.2, with each breaking change before and after.

Each section is one change since 2.2.9, with code that behaves differently before and after it. The full list of changes, including fixes and new features, is in the CHANGELOGs of [arktype](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/CHANGELOG.md), [@ark/aot](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/aot/CHANGELOG.md), [arksets](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/sets/CHANGELOG.md), [@ark/json-schema](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/json-schema/CHANGELOG.md), [@ark/fast-check](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/fast-check/CHANGELOG.md), [arkregex](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/regex/CHANGELOG.md) and [@ark/attest](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/attest/CHANGELOG.md).

## Checklist

Go down the list. Each question your code answers yes to links to what to change.

- Do you ship arktype to a browser without a build step that precompiles? [It's larger](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#unprecompiled-arktype-is-larger).
- Do you install `@ark/type`, `@ark/regex` or an `@arktype/*` package? [Rename it](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#package-names).
- Do you read `ArkErrors` as an array, like `out[0]`, `out.length`, `out.map()` or `[...out]`? [Read `out.issues`](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#arkerrors-is-no-longer-an-array).
- Do you call methods on an error, like `hasCode()`, `toString()` or `instanceof ArkError`? [Errors are plain objects](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#errors-are-plain-objects).
- Do you switch on error `code`s, or configure text for `predicate`? See [undeclared](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#undeclared-keys-have-the-undeclared-code), [discriminant](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#union-misses-have-the-discriminant-code) and [notEqual](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#excluded-values-have-the-notequal-codes).
- Do you snapshot or assert error messages, or their order? See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#errors): objects, dates and union misses print differently, errors follow the order keys are declared, and configured messages apply to more errors.
- Do you show the messages of Standard Schema issues, as a form library does? [They leave out the path](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#standard-schema-messages-leave-out-the-path).
- Do you configure an `expected`, `actual` or `message` writer? [Writers take the error](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#error-writers-receive-the-error-and-the-locale).
- Do you call `configure()` after a Type is created, or pass a global-only option to a Scope? See [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#configuration).
- Do you use `number` for data that can be `Infinity`? [Allow it](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#number-rejects-infinity).
- Do you write date literals or limits without a time zone, or parse ISO dates without an offset? See [date literals](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#date-literals-need-a-time-zone) and [`string.date.iso.parse`](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#stringdateisoparse-reads-dates-in-utc).
- Do you use `"@"` or `"[k]?"` as a literal key? [Escape it](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#-holds-an-objects-metadata).
- Do you set `clone`, or rely on output being a copy of its input? [Output shares unchanged values](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#the-clone-option-is-removed).
- Do you write `"+": "delete"` or `"+": "reject"` and care about key order or symbol keys? See [delete](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#-delete-removes-symbol-keys-and-lists-keys-as-declared) and [reject](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#-reject-checks-string-keys-only).
- Do you use function defaults, or morphs on defaults? [They run on each call](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#defaults-run-each-time-theyre-applied).
- Do you chain two right bounds, like `number < 5 < 6`? [Group them](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#a-second-right-bound-throws).
- Do you embed an async Standard Schema, like a Zod schema with an async refinement? [It throws](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#standard-schemas-must-validate-synchronously).
- Do you store or snapshot `toJsonSchema()`, `.expression` or `.json`, or convert `NaN` or `Infinity` literals to JSON Schema? See [Output](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#output).
- Do you rely on what `.required()`, `.map()` or arkregex infer? See [Inference](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#inference) and [ArkRegex](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#arkregex).
- Do you import from `@ark/schema`, `@ark/util` or a deep path like `arktype/internal/...`? See [@ark/schema](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#arkschema), [@ark/util](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#arkutil) and [Deep imports](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#deep-imports).
- Do you use `@ark/json-schema`, `@ark/fast-check` or attest, or run attest on TypeScript 7? See their sections below.

## Bundle size

### Unprecompiled arktype is larger

`import { type } from "arktype"` bundles more than it did, mostly for copy-on-write transforms, cyclic data, errors and their English text, and the set algebra that reduces unions and intersections. The [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/CHANGELOG.md#precompile-to-ship-less) has the sizes.

To ship less than before, [precompile](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/setup#add-the-plugin). Each Type becomes a standalone validator on `arktype/runtime`, so arktype's parser never ships. Your definitions don't change.

## Errors

### ArkErrors is no longer an array

`ArkErrors` was an `Array` subclass. It's now a plain class whose `issues` is a plain array with one error per path. Indexing, iteration, `length` and array methods move to `issues`:

```ts
const out = type({ name: "string" })({ name: 5 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// before: out[0], out.map(e => e.message), for (const e of out), out.length
	out.issues[0]
	out.issues.map(e => e.message)
	for (const error of out.issues) console.log(error.message)
	out.issues.length
}
```

`Array.isArray(out)` is now `false`, and `[].concat(out)` nests the errors instead of spreading them, so pass `out.issues`. A [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema) failure is no longer the `ArkErrors`, but `{ issues }`, as [below](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#standard-schema-messages-leave-out-the-path).

`ArkErrors` keeps `issues`, `count`, `summary`, `throw()`, `toJSON()`, `toString()` and `toLocaleString(locale)`. `message` and `toTraversalError()` are gone: read `summary`, and call `throw()`. `byPath`, `flatByPath`, `flatProblemsByPath` and `byAncestorPath` are functions `arktype` exports:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type } from "arktype"

const out = type({ name: "string" })({ name: 5 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// before: out.flatProblemsByPath
	flatProblemsByPath(out)
}
```

A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators#errors) build's `arktype/runtime` doesn't export them, and its errors have no `propString` or `problem`, so there group `out.issues` by `issue.path` instead.

A callback adds an error with `ctx.error` or `ctx.reject` rather than `ctx.errors.add`.

### Standard Schema messages leave out the path

A [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema) failure is `{ issues }`, a plain array with a copy of each error whose `message` leaves its path out, since a consumer like a form library shows it beside the field or prints the path before it:

```ts
const T = type({ name: "string > 1" })

// [{ message: "must be at least length 2 (was 1)", path: ["name"], ... }]
// before: "name must be at least length 2 (was 1)"
T["~standard"].validate({ name: "x" })
```

Update snapshots of those messages, and read `summary` from the errors calling the Type returns for one line naming each path.

### Errors are plain objects

The errors in `issues` are plain objects without getters or methods, holding the keys their JSON had. `ArkError` is exported only as a type, which comparing `code` narrows as `hasCode` did, and `messageIn` writes one in a locale:

```ts
import { messageIn, type } from "arktype"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

const out = type({ n: "number % 2" })({ n: 1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	for (const error of out.issues) {
		// before: error.hasCode("divisor")
		if (error.code === "divisor") console.log(error.rule)
		// before: error.toLocaleString(de)
		messageIn(error, de)
	}
}
```

`hasCode`, `flat`, `throw`, `toString`, `toJSON` and `toLocaleString` are gone from errors, so `error instanceof ArkError` is false and `` `${error}` `` is `[object Object]`. `path` is a plain array. An error's text is written when its `ArkErrors`' issues are first read, so a configured writer is called once per error. A Type that calls no narrow or morph may also find the issues themselves at that read, so [read them before the data you validated changes](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#arkerrors).

### Objects print by their kind

An error's `actual` prints an object as `an object`, an array as `an array` and a function as `a function`, where it printed an object or array as compact JSON, a Date as its date and another instance by its class's name. A message no longer grows with the data, and nothing an object holds reaches a log through it:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be "a" or "b" (was an object)
// before: (was {"x":1})
type("'a' | 'b'")({ x: 1 })
```

A value an `instanceof` check rejects is described as a domain error describes it, or by its class's name if it's a builtin's instance:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a Date (was a number), before: (was number)
type("Date")(5)

// ArkErrors: must be a Date (was Map), as before
type("Date")(new Map())
```

### Undeclared keys have the undeclared code

A key that `"+": "reject"` disallows was a `predicate` error. Its code is now `undeclared`, and its `data` is the key's value rather than the object:

```ts
const T = type({ "+": "reject", a: "string" })

const out = T({ a: "x", b: 1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	out.issues[0].code // "undeclared", before: "predicate"
	out.issues[0].data // 1, before: { a: "x", b: 1 }
}
```

Configure its text under `undeclared` instead of `predicate`.

### Union misses have the discriminant code

A value that matches no branch of a union ArkType checks by its type or by a literal value, like `number | null`, `"a" | "b" | "c"` or objects with a discriminant key, was a `predicate` error, and one of two literals, like `boolean`, was a `union` error. Its code is now `discriminant`, and its `data` is the discriminating value:

```ts
const out = type("number | null")("x")

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	out.issues[0].code // "discriminant", before: "predicate"
}
```

A described union's miss is at the union's own path, with the union's value as its `data`. A union reports `union` rather than `discriminant` where its discriminant can't tell the branches apart: for data that can't hold it, like `5` for a union of objects, for data matching none of its values when some branches don't have its key, and for a miss of a union discriminated by its value whose branch is described.

Configure its text under `discriminant` instead of `predicate`.

Where every object a union discriminated by type expects is an array, its `cases` holds `"Array"` in place of `"object"`, and its message says `an array`:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a string or an array (was a number)
// before: must be a string or an object (was a number)
type("string | string[]")(5)
```

A `switch` over `cases` must handle `"Array"`.

### Excluded values have the notEqual codes

`!=` excludes one value from a range, like `number != 0`, and unions of ranges one value apart reduce to it. Its errors have the codes `notEqual` and `notEqualLength`, so with `undeclared` and `discriminant`, an exhaustive `switch` over `ArkErrorCode`, or a `Record<ArkErrorCode, ...>`, must handle four new codes:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be other than 0 (was 0)
type("number != 0")(0)
```

### Unions report each branch their discriminant can't rule out

A discriminated union whose discriminant can't place the data, because the data can't hold it, or matches none of its values while some branches don't have its key, reports as an undiscriminated union does, listing each branch's error. Each path a union lists reads as its own error would:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be an object (was a number)
// before: kind must be "circle" or "square" (was missing)
type({ kind: "'circle'", r: "number" }).or({
	kind: "'square'",
	side: "number"
})(5)

// ArkErrors: value at [0] must be a number (was a string) or value at [1] must be a string (was a number)
// before: value at [0] must be a number (was a string) or [1] must be a string (was a number)
type("number[] | string[]")(["a", 1])
```

Objects alike but for one key's value are now one object (see [Output](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#output)), so data they reject is reported as any object's is, each failing key on its own, and a message configured on the union no longer replaces the error at that key.

### Errors follow the order keys are declared

An object's errors are reported in the order its definition declares its keys, where they were required keys first, then optional ones, each sorted. On a failed call, each morph whose input is valid runs as it's reached, so its errors are in that order too:

```ts
import { firstIssue, type } from "arktype"

const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number", "nick?": "string" })

const out = User({ nick: 0 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// "name must be a string (was missing)"
	// before: "age must be a number (was missing)"
	firstIssue(out).message
}
```

Declared keys are still checked before an index signature's and undeclared keys, which follow the data's order.

### Configured messages apply to more errors

A `message` configured on a pipe applies to errors validating its output, and a union or intersection whose failing branches or constraints were all configured with one `message` reports it:

```ts
const Port = type("string.numeric.parse | number")
	.to("0 < number <= 65535")
	.configure({ message: "Enter a port number." })

// ArkErrors: Enter a port number.
// before: must be at most 65535 (was 99999)
Port("99999")

const Email = type("string.email > 0").configure({
	message: "Email is not valid"
})

// ArkErrors: Email is not valid
// before: ("") must be...
//   ◦ an email address
//   ◦ non-empty
Email("")
```

`Port.out` keeps its own errors. Constraints described alike are described once, so `type("string.email > 0", "@", "Email is not valid")("")` says `must be Email is not valid (was "")`.

### Error writers receive the error and the locale

An `expected` writer receives the error rather than its context, an `actual` writer receives `(data, error, locale)`, and every writer receives the [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n) last. In an `expected` writer, `meta` may be `undefined`, since an error from `ctx.reject` has none:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({
	predicate: {
		// before: ctx => ctx.meta.title!
		expected: error => error.meta?.title ?? "valid"
	}
})
```

A writer's argument no longer has `toJSON`, `toString` or the text getters that could read the text it writes.

### pipe.try errors reference the morph

An error from a `pipe.try` morph that threw has the function as `morph` and what it threw as `cause`. Before, it had them as `predicate` and its own `actual`. Its `code` is still `predicate`, and its message is unchanged:

```ts
const Parse = type("string").pipe.try((s): object => JSON.parse(s))

const out = Parse("{")

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	const error = out.issues[0]
	// error.morph is the function, before: error.predicate
	// error.cause is the SyntaxError it threw, before: error.actual
}
```

### Keyword parse errors are data
