The errors `string.integer.parse`, `string.date.parse`, `string.url.parse`, `string.json`, `string.json.parse` and `string.regex` raise while parsing carry `meta.keyword`, a `description` and what was thrown as `cause`, instead of their own English `expected` text. Their messages are unchanged, and `predicate` config now applies to them:

```ts
const out = type("string.json.parse")("{")

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	const error = out.issues[0]
	// error.meta is { keyword: "string.json.parse" }
	// error.cause is the SyntaxError JSON.parse threw
}
```

### assert throws when a root morph fails

When a Type's root is a morph that returns `ArkErrors`, `.assert` throws instead of returning them, and a configured `onFail` is called:

```ts
const N = type("number")
const T = type("string").pipe(s => N(s))

// before: returned ArkErrors
// throws TraversalError: must be a number (was a string)
T.assert("x")
```

### Dates are described in UTC

Dates in descriptions and error messages are written in UTC instead of local time. A date at midnight is written as its calendar date:

```ts
const T = type("Date < d'2000-01-01T12:30:00Z'")

// ArkErrors: must be January 1, 2000, 12:29:59.999 PM UTC or earlier (was June 1, 2001)
// before, in New York: must be 7:29:59.999 AM, January 1, 2000 or earlier
T(new Date("2001-06-01"))
```

## Validation

### "@" holds an object's metadata

An object definition's `"@"` key is its description or meta object, as `"@"` is in a tuple expression. It was an ordinary key. Escape it as `"\\@"` to keep the key:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a user (was a number)
type({ "@": "a user", name: "string" })(5)

// Type<{ "@": string }>
const At = type({ "\\@": "string" })
```

### Date literals need a time zone

A date literal, or a string passed as a date limit, must be the same instant on every machine: an ISO date (UTC) like `2025-01-01`, an ISO date-time with `Z` or an offset, or epoch milliseconds. A date-time without an offset or a non-ISO string was read in the local time zone, and now throws a `ParseError`:

```ts
// throws ParseError: Date literal '2025-01-01T12:00' must be an ISO date like 2025-01-01, an ISO date-time with Z or an offset like 2025-01-01T12:00Z, or epoch milliseconds
// before: noon in the machine's time zone
type("Date > d'2025-01-01T12:00'")

// unchanged
type("Date > d'2025-01-01'")
type("Date > d'2025-01-01T12:00Z'")
```

### string.date.iso.parse reads dates in UTC

`string.date.iso.parse` reads an ISO date or date-time without an offset as UTC, so one string is one instant on every machine, and a date that doesn't exist fails rather than rolling over. `string.date.parse` and `string.date` read the strings `string.date.iso` accepts the same way:

```ts
const parse = type("string.date.iso.parse")

// 2025-01-01T12:00:00.000Z
// before, in New York: 2025-01-01T17:00:00.000Z
parse("2025-01-01T12:00")

// ArkErrors: must be an ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ) date (was "2025-02-29")
// before: 2025-03-01T00:00:00.000Z
parse("2025-02-29")
```

### Merging an array throws

`.merge`, `type.merge` and `Merge` extend an object, so an array, a tuple or another class's instance on either side throws a `ParseError`, where merging an array gave an object:

```ts
// throws ParseError: merge operand must resolve to an object literal type (was string[])
type({ a: "string" }).merge("string[]")
```

Spread the array's Type into a tuple, or merge objects only.

### A second right bound throws

A range takes at most one right bound, so a second throws a `ParseError`, as its type already failed:

```ts
// throws ParseError: Expression number must have at most one right bound
// before: number < 5
type("number < 5 < 6")

// intersect a second comparator
type("0 < number < 10 & number != 5")
```

### number rejects Infinity

`number` rejects `Infinity` and `-Infinity`, as it already rejected `NaN`:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a number (was Infinity)
// before: Infinity
type.number(Infinity)
```

Allow them everywhere with `configure({ numberAllowsInfinity: true })`, or in one Type with the `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` keywords:

```ts
const T = type("number | number.Infinity | number.NegativeInfinity")
```

### object.json accepts only plain objects and arrays

`object.json` rejects an object whose prototype isn't `Object.prototype` or `null`, unless it's an array, so a `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, function or class instance, which `JSON.stringify` doesn't write as itself, fails anywhere in the data:

```ts
// ArkErrors: at must be a plain object or array (was an object)
// before: { at: Date }
type("object.json")({ at: new Date() })
```

### string.numeric accepts exponents

`string.numeric` and `string.numeric.parse` accept an exponent, as `Number()` does:

```ts
// 100000, before: ArkErrors: must be a well-formed numeric string (was "1e5")
type("string.numeric.parse")("1e5")
```

To keep rejecting them, intersect a pattern: `"string.numeric & /^[^eE]*$/"`.

### .and checks props against index signatures

`.and` checks each prop against the other side's index signatures as an object literal does, so a required prop they exclude throws a `ParseError`, and an optional one becomes `never`:

```ts
// throws ParseError: Intersection at a of string and number results in an unsatisfiable type
// before: { [string]: number, a: string }
type({ a: "string" }).and({ "[string]": "number" })
```

Widen the index signature's value to include the prop's, like `"[string]": "string | number"`.

### Integer keys past an array's last index are undeclared

An integer key from 4294967295 up can't be an array index, so `"+": "reject"` rejects it and `"+": "delete"` deletes it:

```ts
const T = type("string[]").onUndeclaredKey("reject")

// ArkErrors: value at ["4294967295"] must be removed, before: valid
T(Object.assign(["a"], { 4294967295: "b" }))
```

### Standard Schemas must validate synchronously

A Standard Schema in a definition whose `validate` returns a Promise, like a Zod schema with an async refinement, throws when it's validated, where it gave `undefined`:

```ts
import { z } from "zod"

const T = type({ name: z.string().refine(async s => s.length > 1) })

// throws: Standard Schema definitions must validate synchronously (zod returned a Promise)
// before: { name: undefined }
T({ name: "x" })
```

### .allows is false when a narrow adds an error

A narrow that adds an error through `ctx` and returns a truthy value failed validation, but `.allows` returned `true`:

```ts
const T = type("number").narrow((n, ctx) => n > 0 || !!ctx.error("positive"))

T.allows(-1) // false, before: true
```

### .extends ignores meta

`.extends` and `.subsumes` compare Types without their meta, so a described Type extends its undescribed self. `.equals` still compares meta:

```ts
type("string | number").describe("a key").extends("string | number") // true, before: false
```

### Optional index signatures throw

A key like `"[k]?"` was the literal key `"[k]"`, made optional. It now throws a `ParseError`, since it reads as an optional index signature. Escape its `[` to keep the literal key:

```ts
// throws ParseError: Index signature [k] can't be optional. Escape its '[' with a backslash for an optional key named '[k]'
type({ "[k]?": "string" })
// TypeScript: Index signature [k] can't be optional. Escape its '[' with a backslash for an optional key named '[k]'

// Type<{ "[k]"?: string }>
type({ "\\[k]?": "string" })
```

### The clone option is removed

Transforming no longer clones the input first. Output shares every value nothing transformed with the input, and a morph receives the validated value itself, so a morph that mutates its argument mutates your data. Remove `clone` from your config.

```ts
const T = type({ a: "string.trim", b: { c: "string" } })
const input = { a: " x ", b: { c: "y" } }

T.assert(input).b === input.b // true, before: false
```

### "+": "delete" removes symbol keys and lists keys as declared

`"+": "delete"` also removes undeclared symbol keys, and its output lists keys in the order the definition declares them, as Zod does, rather than the input's order:

```ts
const T = type({ "+": "delete", b: "string", a: "string" })

T({ a: "1", z: 0, b: "2" }) // { b: "2", a: "1" }, before: { a: "1", b: "2" }
```

### "+": "reject" checks string keys only

`"+": "reject"` allows undeclared symbol keys, so `rejectAllowsSymbolKeys` is gone. Reject types that differ only by a symbol key now overlap, so a union of them with a morph is indeterminate:

```ts
const T = type({ "+": "reject", a: "string" })

// valid, before: ArkErrors: value at [Symbol(s)] must be removed
T({ a: "x", [Symbol("s")]: 1 })
```

### Defaults run each time they're applied

A function default is called each time the default is applied, and its result is validated like input at that key, where it was called once when the Type was defined. A morph on a primitive default runs on each call too:

```ts
let calls = 0

const T = type({ count: ["number", "=", () => ++calls] })

// calls is 0, before: 1, from checking the default when T was defined
T({}) // { count: 1 }
```

### Smaller fixes that change results

Each was a bug, but code may depend on it:

- `string[] & number[]` is `[]`, where it allowed any array: `type("string[] & number[]").expression` is `[]`, before: `unknown[]`.
- Intersecting an object that rejects or deletes undeclared keys with an index signature keeps its optional keys optional: `type({ "+": "reject", "a?": "number" }).and({ "[string]": "number" })` accepts `{}`, before: rejected it.
- With `jitless`, a `g` or `y` pattern checks from the start of the string every time, where the same input alternated between valid and invalid.
- An optional key in an intersection allows `undefined` only where both sides do, so a Scope configured with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes: false` no longer loosens a Type from one that isn't.
- With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes: false`, a defaulted key given `undefined` gets the default, before: kept `undefined`.
- A tuple expression's `:` after a morph throws `ParseError: Predicate operand must be unknown (was a morph)`, where it threw a TypeError.
- `Exclude` and `Extract` over a definition still being defined throw `ParseError: Extract can't filter a type still being defined`.
- `type(["string", "toString"])` throws that `'toString'` is unresolvable, where it threw an internal TypeError.

### Shallow cycles throw

An alias that resolves to itself without passing through an object, array or morph accepted every value. It now throws a `ParseError`:

```ts
// throws ParseError: Alias 'a' has a shallow resolution cycle: a->a
scope({ a: "a" }).export()
// TypeScript: Alias 'a' has a shallow resolution cycle: a->a
```

## Configuration

### Configure before any Type is created

Global config is fixed when the first Type is created, whether by a definition or by referencing a keyword like `type.number`, and `configure` throws after that, where it used to apply to scopes created later but not to `type` or keywords. Call it in a file of its own, and import that file before anything creates a Type:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ onUndeclaredKey: "delete" })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"
```

### Global-only options throw in a Scope

`onUndeclaredKey`, `numberAllowsNaN`, `numberAllowsInfinity`, `dateAllowsInvalid`, `keywords` and `locale` can only be set with `configure()`. A Scope's type already rejected them, but a cast config passing one was honored for `onUndeclaredKey` and ignored for the rest. Each now throws:

```ts
// throws ParseError: numberAllowsInfinity can only be configured globally, with configure()
// before: ignored
scope({}, { numberAllowsInfinity: true } as never)
```

### onUndeclaredKey: "delete" rejects overlapping object unions

With `onUndeclaredKey: "delete"` configured, a union of objects whose inputs overlap throws a `ParseError`, as it already did with `"+": "delete"` in each object. Before, data both allowed came out as whichever branch sorted first:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ onUndeclaredKey: "delete" })
```

```ts
// throws ParseError: An unordered union of a type including a morph and a type with overlapping input is indeterminate
// before: { uri: "u", blob: "b" } for { uri: "u", text: "t", blob: "b" }
type({ uri: "string", text: "string" }).or({ uri: "string", blob: "string" })
```

Give the branches a key that tells them apart, like a literal `kind`, or delete outside the union.

### meta.keyword is reserved

Built-in keywords set `meta.keyword` on the constraints they add, so a [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n) can find their phrase. Rename your own meta named `keyword`. A keyword's meta in `.json` holds it beside its description:

```ts
// { domain: "string", pattern: [{ rule: "...", meta: { description: "an email address", keyword: "string.email", format: "email" } }], ... }
// before: the pattern's meta was its description, "an email address"
type("string.email").json
```

## Output

These change what `toJsonSchema()`, `.expression` and `.json` return, which matters if you store or snapshot them.

- `jsonSchema` meta is the Type's JSON Schema, replacing what its constraints imply, where it was written into the schema as an ordinary `jsonSchema` key. See [Your own schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#your-own-schema).

- Unions of ranges that overlap, meet or leave out one value, and of objects alike but for one key's value, are one range or object: `1 < number < 10 | 10 <= number < 100` is `1 < number < 100`, `number < 0 | number > 0` is `number != 0`, and `{ kind: "a", x: string } | { kind: "b", x: string }` is `{ kind: "a" | "b", x: string }`.

- `string.date.iso` writes `format: "date-time"` beside its `pattern`, whose groups no longer capture, and a format keyword constrained further keeps its `format`: `"string.email < 255"` writes `format: "email"`, before: none. The [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/CHANGELOG.md#write-string-keywords-formats-in-json-schema) lists each keyword's.

- A union of literals with configured meta becomes `enum`: `type("'a' | 'b'").configure({ title: "Letter" }).toJsonSchema()` is `{ type: "string", enum: ["a", "b"], title: "Letter" }` instead of an `anyOf` of `const`s.

- A literal's JSON Schema has its `type` beside its `const` or `enum`: `'a' | 'b'` is `{ type: "string", enum: ["a", "b"] }`, and `'a' | 'b' | null` is `{ anyOf: [{ type: "string", enum: ["a", "b"] }, { type: "null" }] }`.

- A cyclic Type's `$defs` hold only its cyclic aliases, named by the alias, like `user`, with everything else inline, where every object, array and union was a def named like `user1` or `intersection1`.

- A string index signature beside declared keys becomes `patternProperties: { "": ... }` instead of `additionalProperties`.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws for a regex flag JSON Schema can't express, instead of leaving it out: `type(/^a/i).toJsonSchema()` throws (code `patternFlags`), before: `{ type: "string", pattern: "^a" }`, which rejects `"A"`.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws for an index signature key it can't express, instead of leaving out the index signature: `type({ "[string <= 3]": "number" }).toJsonSchema()` throws (code `indexKey`), before: `{ type: "object" }`. See [JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#how-types-map) for the keys it can write.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws for a `NaN`, `Infinity` or `-Infinity` literal, like `number.NaN` or `number.Infinity`, since JSON can't hold one, where it wrote `const: Infinity`, which serializes as `null`. [Handle the `unit` code](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes), e.g. `unit: ctx => (typeof ctx.unit === "number" ? { type: "number" } : ctx.base)`.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws for `object.json` and the Types it's part of, like `string.json.parse`'s output, since its check that an object is plain is a `predicate`. [Handle that code](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) to write it as before.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws a `ParseError` for a `target` other than `"draft-2020-12"`, `"draft-07"` or `"openapi-3.0"`, where it wrote draft 2020-12: `type("string").toJsonSchema({ target: "draft-04" })`, before: `{ type: "string" }`.

- Expressions keep length bounds and protos beside a structure: `type("number[] > 1").expression` is `number[] >= 2`, before: `number[]`.

- Optional keys are listed by name, whether or not they have a default: `{ bar?: number, foo: string = "foo" }`, before: `{ foo: string = "foo", bar?: number }`.

- The `$ark.x` names that functions get in `.json` and `.expression` are names only and no longer resolve through `$ark`.

- Keys are ordered by code unit, where they were ordered as `JSON.stringify` writes them, which moves only keys that first differ at a character JSON escapes or where one ends: `"a"` now precedes `"a b"`.

## Inference

- `.required()` makes a defaulted key required in `inferIn`, as it already did at runtime: `type({ foo: "string = 'bar'" }).required()` infers `{ foo: string }` as input, before: `{ foo?: string }`.
- `.map()` on a union infers each branch: `type({ kind: "'a'", a: "string" }).or({ kind: "'b'", b: "number" }).map(p => p)` is `Type<{ kind: "a"; a: string } | { kind: "b"; b: number }>`, before: `Type<{ kind: "a" | "b" }>`, and the callback's argument holds each branch's props, not only those every branch shares.
- A morph that returns `any` infers `any` as its output: `type({ a: ["string", "=>", s => JSON.parse(s)] }).infer` is `{ a: any }`, before: `{ a: (In: string) => Out<any> }`.

## @ark/schema

- `BaseNode.compiledMeta` is removed, and `BaseScope.resolutions` holds an unresolved alias's parse context instead of its id.
- `$.node(kind, input)` takes a node's inner, with children already nodes: `$.node("min", 5)` is now `$.node("min", { rule: 5 })`. Parse the schema format with `rootSchema` or `$.schema`.
- Call a node's `traverseAllows`, `traverseApply` and `traverseTransform` on the node, as in `node.traverseAllows(data, ctx)`, not detached, as in `[x].every(node.traverseAllows)`, until the JIT compiles it.
- `NodeParseContext`, what `parseNode` takes, is `{ kind, def, $, id, alias, prereduced }`.
- Internal members have short names, each spelled out by its JSDoc, like `is` (before: `hasKind`), `alters` (before: `hasTransform`) and `errCount` (before: `currentErrorCount`). The CHANGELOG lists every one.
- A morph's input is the first of its `morphs`: its `json` is `{ morphs: ["string", "$ark.trim"] }`, before: `{ in: "string", morphs: ["$ark.trim"] }`, and a schema with `in` still parses to it. Read the input as `head` (before: `inner.in` or `knownIn`), what it pipes to as `piped` and the node it ends with as `tail` (before: `lastMorphNode`). A node's `rawIn` and `rawOut` are `_in` and `_out`.
- An alias's `resolutionId` (read `resolution.id`), a node's `assertHasKindIn`, `isConstraint` and `isRefinement`, a root's `shortDescription`, a morph's `declareIn` and `serializedMorphs` and a structure's `optionalKeys` are removed.
- A constraint's `compiledCondition`, a predicate's `compiledNegation`, a morph's `compiledMorphs`, a sequence's `optionalsLength` and the `PrecompiledReferences` type are removed. A leaf writes its check with `compileCondition(js, data)`.
- Derived keys like the flags `hasAlias` and `hasMorph` (before: `includesAlias`, `includesMorph`), `innerEntries` and `propsByKey` moved from a node's own enumerable keys to `node.cache`, so spreading or iterating a node no longer includes them.

## @ark/util

- `Scanner`'s `jumpToIndex` is removed.
- `isNumericString` and `isWellFormedInteger` read only strings: `isNumericString(5)` throws, before: `true`.
- `$ark.filename` is removed. `$ark.version` still names the `@ark/util` version that created the registry.

## Deep imports

A deep import like `arktype/internal/parser/string.ts` keeps its module's types but loads `arktype/internal` at runtime, which exports the names of every arktype module. Import from `arktype/internal` itself. `@ark/schema`, `@ark/util`, `arkregex` and `arksets` each have an `./internal` entry like it.

## ArkRegex

A capture in one alternation branch is `undefined` in every other branch, so the inferred tuples line up with what `exec` returns:

```ts
const R = regex("^(?:(1)|(2))$")

// before: ["1"] | [undefined, "2"]
type Captures = typeof R.inferCaptures // ["1", undefined] | [undefined, "2"]
```

Other patterns infer what they match more exactly, which can widen or narrow an inferred type:

- `\s` is `string`, before: `" " | "\n" | "\t"`.
- An unbounded run of digits, like `\d+`, is `string`, before: `` `${number}` ``.
- With the `m` flag, `^` and `$` don't anchor: `regex("^abc$", "m")` is `` `${string}abc${string}` ``, before: `"abc"`.
- In a character set, `[\b]` is a backspace and `[\/]` is `/`, before: `""` and an error message.
- A capture inside a lookaround is counted: `regex("^(?=(a))a(b)$")` captures `["a", "b"]`, before: `["b"]`.

## @ark/json-schema

`arktype` is a peer dependency at the version released with `@ark/json-schema`, where it was a dependency, so install the two together. `jsonSchemaToType` reads a schema as a 2020-12 validator does, which changes what some schemas accept:

- `prefixItems` makes its elements optional: `{ type: "array", prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }] }` is `[string?, number?, ...unknown[]]` and accepts `[]`, before: `[string, number, ...unknown[]]`.
- `{ type: "object" }` rejects arrays.
- A `uniqueItems` error reads `must be an array of unique items (was an array)`, before: `(was an array with 2 duplicates: 1, and 3)`.
- The `writeJsonSchema*Message` functions, like `writeJsonSchemaInsufficientKeysMessage`, are no longer exported.

## @ark/fast-check

`arktype` is a peer dependency at the version released with `@ark/fast-check`, where it was a dependency, so install the two together.

## Attest

Under TypeScript 7, attest analyzes with its native API, which needs 7.1 or later, so 7.0.x throws `@ark/attest requires TypeScript 7.1+`. Where attest runs, install TypeScript 7.1 or later, or keep TypeScript 6, which it analyzes with its JS API as before.

Runtime benches run in a loop compiled for each bench, after a warmup, so their times don't compare with earlier versions'. Re-record stored runtime baselines.

- A bench should return the result it computes, so V8 can't drop the work. attest warns when a bench returns `undefined`.
- `until.count` and `until.ms` bound the samples taken after the warmup. Before, they counted sets of 1000 calls and time from the bench's start.
- Instantiation counts include evaluating the type a bench returns as fully as displaying it would. Re-record type benches whose results weren't already fully evaluated.

## Package names

Each package publishes under one name. The others, which published the same code, are no longer published, and `@ark/type` and `@ark/regex` are deprecated on npm, so installing one warns with the name to use:

| Install | Instead of |
| - | - |
| `arktype` | `@ark/type`, `@arktype/type` |
| `arkregex` | `@ark/regex`, `@arktype/regex` |
| `@ark/<name>` | `@arktype/<name>`, e.g. `@arktype/schema` |

# Primitives

> Define strings, numbers, bigints, symbols, booleans, null and undefined, with literals, patterns, lengths, ranges and divisors.

## string

### keywords

Reference a keyword anywhere a definition is expected:

```ts
const User = type({
	email: "string.email",
	ids: "string.uuid.v4[]"
})
```

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `string` | a string |
| `string.alpha` | only letters |
| `string.alphanumeric` | only letters and digits 0-9 |
| `string.base58` | base58-encoded |
| `string.base64` | base64-encoded |
| `string.base64.url` | base64url-encoded |
| `string.capitalize` | a morph from a string to capitalized |
| `string.capitalize.preformatted` | capitalized |
| `string.creditCard` | a credit card number |
| `string.date` | a parsable date |
| `string.date.epoch` | an integer string representing a safe Unix timestamp |
| `string.date.epoch.parse` | a morph from an integer string representing a safe Unix timestamp to a Date |
| `string.date.iso` | an ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ) date |
| `string.date.iso.parse` | a morph from an ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ) date to a Date |
| `string.date.parse` | a morph from a parsable date to a Date |
| `string.digits` | only digits 0-9 |
| `string.email` | an email address |
| `string.hex` | hex characters only |
| `string.integer` | a well-formed integer string |
| `string.integer.parse` | a morph from a well-formed integer string to an integer |
| `string.ip` | an IP address |
| `string.ip.v4` | an IPv4 address |
| `string.ip.v6` | an IPv6 address |
| `string.json` | a JSON string |
| `string.json.parse` | safe JSON string parser |
| `string.lower` | a morph from a string to lowercase |
| `string.lower.preformatted` | lowercase |
| `string.normalize` | a morph from a string to NFC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFC` | a morph from a string to NFC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFC.preformatted` | NFC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFD` | a morph from a string to NFD-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFD.preformatted` | NFD-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKC` | a morph from a string to NFKC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKC.preformatted` | NFKC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKD` | a morph from a string to NFKD-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKD.preformatted` | NFKD-normalized unicode |
| `string.numeric` | a well-formed numeric string |
| `string.numeric.parse` | a morph from a well-formed numeric string and finite to a number |
| `string.regex` | a regex pattern |
| `string.semver` | a semantic version (see <https://semver.org/>) |
| `string.trim` | a morph from a string to trimmed |
| `string.trim.preformatted` | trimmed |
| `string.upper` | a morph from a string to uppercase |
| `string.upper.preformatted` | uppercase |
| `string.url` | a URL string |
| `string.url.parse` | a morph from a URL string to a URL instance |
| `string.uuid` | a UUID |
| `string.uuid.v1` | a UUIDv1 |
| `string.uuid.v2` | a UUIDv2 |
| `string.uuid.v3` | a UUIDv3 |
| `string.uuid.v4` | a UUIDv4 |
| `string.uuid.v5` | a UUIDv5 |
| `string.uuid.v6` | a UUIDv6 |
| `string.uuid.v7` | a UUIDv7 |
| `string.uuid.v8` | a UUIDv8 |

Every keyword, including those for other types, is listed on the [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords) page.

### literals

Quote a string inside a definition to allow exactly that string. Single and double quotes are equivalent:

```ts
const Literals = type({
	singleQuoted: "'typescript'",
	doubleQuoted: '"arktype"'
})
```

### patterns

A regex literal requires the string to match it. Like a `RegExp`, it is unanchored unless you anchor it with `^` and `$`.

**string**

```ts
const AToZ = type("/^a.*z$/")

// ArkErrors: must be matched by ^a.*z$ (was "abc")
AToZ("abc")
```

**fluent**

```ts
const AToZ = type.string.matching(/^a.*z$/)

// ArkErrors: must be matched by ^a.*z$ (was "abc")
AToZ("abc")
```

A `RegExp` works as a definition too, e.g. `type({ code: /^a.*z$/ })`.

Regex literals are typed with [ArkRegex](https://arktype.io/docs/regex), so a pattern that constrains the string's shape narrows the inferred type:

```ts
// Type<string>
const Hex = type("/^[0-9a-fA-F]+$/")

// Type<`${number}.${number}.${number}`>
const Semver = type("/^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$/")
```

#### e(x)ec mode

Prefix a regex literal with `x` to transform the string into the result of `RegExp.prototype.exec`. The output is the match, not the string, and its capture groups are typed:

```ts
const User = type({
	birthday: "x/^(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})-(?<year>\\d{4})$/"
})

const data = User.assert({ birthday: "05-21-1993" })

data.birthday.groups.month // "05"
data.birthday.groups.year // "1993"
```

### lengths

Constrain a string's length with `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==` or `!=`:

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: "string > 0",
	atMost10: "string <= 10",
	exactly5: "string == 5"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: type.string.moreThanLength(0),
	atMost10: type.string.atMostLength(10),
	exactly5: type.string.exactlyLength(5)
})
```

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
// 4 to 6 digits
const Pin = type("4 <= string.digits <= 6")

// ArkErrors: must be at least length 4 (was 3)
Pin("123")
```

**fluent**

```ts
// 4 to 6 digits
const Pin = type.keywords.string.digits.atLeastLength(4).atMostLength(6)

// ArkErrors: must be at least length 4 (was 3)
Pin("123")
```

## number

`number` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`. Allow them in one type with the `number.NaN`, `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` keywords:

```ts
const MaybeInfinite = type("number | number.Infinity | number.NegativeInfinity")
```

To allow them everywhere, configure [`numberAllowsNaN`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#numberallowsnan) or [`numberAllowsInfinity`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#numberallowsinfinity).

### keywords

```ts
const User = type({
	createdAt: "number.epoch",
	age: "number.integer >= 0"
})
```

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `number` | a number |
| `number.Infinity` | Infinity |
| `number.NaN` | NaN |
| `number.NegativeInfinity` | -Infinity |
| `number.epoch` | an integer representing a safe Unix timestamp |
| `number.integer` | an integer |
| `number.safe` | at least -9007199254740991 and at most 9007199254740991 |

### literals

A number in a definition allows exactly that number:

```ts
const Literals = type({
	number: "1337"
})
```

### ranges

Constrain a number with `>`, `>=`, `<` or `<=`:

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	positive: "number > 0",
	atMost5: "number <= 5"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	positive: type.number.moreThan(0),
	atMost5: type.number.atMost(5)
})
```

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
const Percentage = type("0 <= number <= 100")

// ArkErrors: must be at most 100 (was 101)
Percentage(101)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Percentage = type.number.atLeast(0).atMost(100)

// ArkErrors: must be at most 100 (was 101)
Percentage(101)
```

`!=` excludes one value:

```ts
const NonZero = type("number != 0")

// ArkErrors: must be other than 0 (was 0)
NonZero(0)
```

### divisors

Constrain a number to a multiple of an integer with `%`:

**string**

```ts
const Even = type("number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
Even(3)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Even = type.number.divisibleBy(2)

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
Even(3)
```

## bigint

**string**

```ts
const Bigints = type({
	foo: "bigint"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bigints = type({
	foo: type.bigint
})
```

### literals

Add the suffix `n` to a [number literal](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives#number-literals) to allow exactly that `bigint`:

```ts
const Literals = type({
	bigint: "1337n"
})
```

A [unit expression](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#unit) like `type.unit(1337n)` does the same.

## symbol

**string**

```ts
const Symbols = type({
	key: "symbol"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Symbols = type({
	key: type.symbol
})
```

To allow one specific symbol, use a [unit expression](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#unit).

Symbol keys need no special syntax, e.g. `{ [mySymbol]: "string" }`. See [properties](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties) to make them optional or defaultable.

## boolean

**string**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	key: "boolean"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	key: type.boolean
})
```

### literals

**string**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	a: "true",
	b: "false",
	// equivalent to "boolean"
	c: "true | false"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	a: type.true,
	b: type.false,
	// equivalent to type.boolean
	c: type.true.or(type.false)
})
```

## null

`"null"` allows exactly `null`, usually in a [union](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#union):

**string**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	foo: "number | null"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	foo: type.number.or(type.null)
})
```

## undefined

`"undefined"` allows exactly `undefined`, usually in a [union](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#union):

**string**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: "number | undefined",
	"optionalKey?": "number | undefined"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: type.number.or(type.undefined),
	optionalKey: type.number.or(type.undefined).optional()
})
```

> **Allowing undefined does not make a key optional**
>
> Like in TypeScript, a required key that allows `undefined` must still be present:
>
> ```ts
> const MyObj = type({
> 	key: "number | undefined"
> })
>
> // { key: undefined }
> MyObj({ key: undefined })
>
> // ArkErrors: key must be a number or undefined (was missing)
> MyObj({})
> ```

# Objects

> Define objects, arrays, tuples, dates and class instances, and derive new object types from existing ones.

## properties

An object definition can combine required, optional and defaultable keys with index signatures.

### required

**string**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: "string",
	// nested definitions don't need their own type call
	[symbolicKey]: {
		nested: "unknown"
	}
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: type.string,
	// nested definitions don't need their own type call
	[symbolicKey]: {
		nested: type.unknown
	}
})
```

### optional

**string**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	"optionalKey?": "number[]",
	[symbolicKey]: "string?"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	optionalKey: type.number.array().optional(),
	[symbolicKey]: type.string.optional()
})
```

**tuple**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	optionalKey: ["number[]", "?"],
	[symbolicKey]: ["string", "?"]
})
```

> **Key or value syntax?**
>
> Prefer the key syntax, `"key?"`. It mirrors TypeScript and reads as what it is: a constraint on whether the key is present, not on its value.
>
> Put `?` on the value when the key is a symbol, when you want go-to-definition and JSDoc on an unquoted key, or when you'd rather not quote keys.

> **An optional key doesn't allow undefined**
>
> ArkType checks optional keys the way TypeScript does with [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#exactOptionalPropertyTypes): a missing key is valid, but a key set to `undefined` must allow `undefined`.
>
> ```ts
> const MyObj = type({
> 	"key?": "number"
> })
>
> // {}
> MyObj({})
>
> // ArkErrors: key must be a number (was undefined)
> MyObj({ key: undefined })
> ```
>
> To allow it, add `undefined` to the value: `"key?": "number | undefined"`. You can also set [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#exactoptionalpropertytypes) to `false` globally.

### defaultable

A defaultable key is optional in the input. When it is missing, the output has its default.

**string**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	defaultableKey: "boolean = false"
})

// { defaultableKey: false }
MyObj({})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	defaultableKey: type.boolean.default(false)
})

// { defaultableKey: false }
MyObj({})
```

**tuple**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	defaultableKey: ["boolean", "=", false]
})

// { defaultableKey: false }
MyObj({})
```

`= []` and `= {}` give each output its own new array or object, so mutating one never changes another:

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	values: "string[] = []",
	meta: "object = {}"
})
```

For any other object, default to a function that returns it, e.g. `type.Date.default(() => new Date())`.

> **Optional and default only work in objects and tuples**
>
> `number.optional()` and `number.default(0)` don't return a `Type`. They return the tuple definitions `[Type<number>, "?"]` and `[Type<number>, "=", 0]`, which are only valid as a property or a tuple element. `type("string?")` throws a `ParseError`.
>
> For a `Type` that accepts `undefined`, use a union like `type("string | undefined")`. To replace `undefined` with a value, add a morph:
>
> ```ts
> const FallbackString = type("string | undefined").pipe(v => v ?? "")
> ```

### index

An index signature constrains every key that matches it:

```ts
const Scores = type({
	"[string]": "number"
})
```

The key can be any string or symbol type, like `symbol`, `string | symbol`, a keyword like `string.uuid` or a regex literal:

```ts
const DataAttributes = type({
	"[/^data-/]": "string"
})

// ArkErrors: value at ["data-id"] must be a string (was a number)
DataAttributes({ "data-id": 1 })
```

A union of literal keys becomes those named keys, so `"['a' | 'b']": "number"` is `{ a: number, b: number }`.

`Record` is available as a [generic keyword](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords), e.g. `type("Record<string, number>")` or `type.Record("string", "number")`.

### undeclared

By default, ArkType allows keys you didn't declare, like TypeScript does. That lets you validate an object you already have without copying it, and skipping the check for extra keys is faster.

To reject or delete undeclared keys, set `"+"` in the object, or [configure](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#onundeclaredkey) a different default for every object:

**string**

```ts
// fail if any string key other than "onlyAllowedKey" is present
const MyClosedObject = type({
	"+": "reject",
	onlyAllowedKey: "string"
})

// delete every key other than "onlyPreservedKey"
const MyStrippedObject = type({
	"+": "delete",
	onlyPreservedKey: "string"
})

// allow and keep undeclared keys (the default)
const MyOpenObject = type({
	"+": "ignore",
	nonexclusiveKey: "number"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
// fail if any string key other than "onlyAllowedKey" is present
const MyClosedObject = type({
	onlyAllowedKey: "string"
}).onUndeclaredKey("reject")

// delete every key other than "onlyPreservedKey"
const MyStrippedObject = type({
	onlyPreservedKey: "string"
}).onUndeclaredKey("delete")

// allow and keep undeclared keys (the default)
const MyOpenObject = type({
	nonexclusiveKey: "number"
}).onUndeclaredKey("ignore")
```

`"ignore"` only matters if you configured a different default.

A rejected key is an error with the code `undeclared`:

```ts
const MyClosedObject = type({
	"+": "reject",
	onlyAllowedKey: "string"
})

// ArkErrors: extraKey must be removed
MyClosedObject({ onlyAllowedKey: "ok", extraKey: 1 })
```

Both act on string keys: `"reject"` checks only an object's string keys, and `"delete"` builds a new object holding only its declared keys. So an undeclared symbol key passes `"reject"` and is dropped by `"delete"`, and reject types that differ only by a symbol key overlap, so a union of them with a morph is indeterminate.

`"delete"`'s output lists the declared keys in the order the definition declares them, as Zod does, then any keys matching an index signature in the input's order.

`.onDeepUndeclaredKey()` applies the same behavior to every nested object:

```ts
const MyDeeplyStrippedObject = type({
	preserved: "string",
	nested: {
		preserved: "string"
	}
}).onDeepUndeclaredKey("delete")

// { nested: { preserved: "b" }, preserved: "a" }
MyDeeplyStrippedObject({
	preserved: "a",
	extra: 1,
	nested: { preserved: "b", extra: 2 }
})
```

> **Prefer in-object syntax where possible**
>
> `.onUndeclaredKey()` and `.configure()` rebuild the whole type they're called on, so creating a type with them is slower than writing `"+"` in the object. Validation is equally fast either way. Methods like `.or()` and `.pipe()` reference the original type rather than rebuilding it, so they have no such cost.

### merge

Merging adds properties to an object or replaces existing ones, like JavaScript's [spread syntax](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Spread_syntax). Write it as a `"..."` key in the object, `.merge()` or the `Merge` generic:

**string**

```ts
const User = type({ isAdmin: "false", name: "string" })

// Type<{ name: string; isAdmin: true; permissions: string[] }>
const Admin = type({
	"...": User,
	isAdmin: "true",
	permissions: "string[]"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const User = type({ isAdmin: "false", name: "string" })

// Type<{ name: string; isAdmin: true; permissions: string[] }>
const Admin = User.merge({
	isAdmin: "true",
	permissions: "string[]"
})
```

**generic**

```ts
const types = type.module({
	User: { isAdmin: "false", name: "string" },
	AdminProps: { isAdmin: "true", permissions: "string[]" },
	// { name: string; isAdmin: true; permissions: string[] }
	Admin: "Merge<User, AdminProps>"
})
```

A key in both objects takes its value from the merged object. An [intersection](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#intersection) would instead intersect the two values, and `false & true` would throw a `ParseError`. When the keys don't overlap, the two give the same type, but merging is less work to compute, both when the type is created and in your editor, so prefer it for combining properties.

Like the other [structural transformations](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-structural), `merge` builds a new object from the properties, so a root narrow or metadata is not carried over.

#### n-ary

`type.merge` merges any number of objects, each overriding the ones before it:

```ts
// Type<{ b: number; a?: 1 }>
const Merged = type.merge({ a: "string" }, { b: "number" }, { "a?": "1" })
```

### escapes

Escape a key's `?`, the `[` of a key in brackets, or a key that is exactly `+`, `...` or `@`, with a backslash to use it literally:

```ts
// Type<{ "isAdmin?": boolean; "+": string; "[id]"?: string }>
const Escaped = type({
	"isAdmin\\?": "boolean",
	"\\+": "string",
	"\\[id]?": "string"
})

// ArkErrors: value at ["isAdmin?"] must be boolean (was missing)
Escaped({ "+": "x" })
```

An index signature can't be optional, so a key like `"[id]?"` throws a `ParseError` unless its `[` is escaped.

### keyof

Like in TypeScript, `keyof` extracts an object's keys as a union:

**string**

```ts
const types = type.module({
	UsedCar: {
		originallyPurchased: "string.date",
		remainingWheels: "number"
	},
	// "originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels"
	UsedCarKey: "keyof UsedCar"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const UsedCar = type({
	originallyPurchased: "string.date",
	remainingWheels: "number"
})

// Type<"originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels">
const UsedCarKey = UsedCar.keyof()
```

**tuple**

```ts
const UsedCar = type({
	originallyPurchased: "string.date",
	remainingWheels: "number"
})

// Type<"originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels">
const UsedCarKey = type(["keyof", UsedCar])
```

**args**

```ts
const UsedCar = type({
	originallyPurchased: "string.date",
	remainingWheels: "number"
})

// Type<"originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels">
const UsedCarKey = type("keyof", UsedCar)
```

Also like in TypeScript, a `[string]` index signature absorbs the named keys, so `keyof` is `string`:

```ts
const RecordWithSpecialKeys = type({
	"[string]": "unknown",
	verySpecialKey: "number"
})

// true
RecordWithSpecialKeys.keyof().equals("string")
```

> **ArkType's keyof never includes number**
>
> TypeScript's `keyof` can include `number`, but JavaScript has no numeric keys: `{ 4: true }` and `{ "4": true }` are the same object, and `Object.keys` returns `["4"]` for both. ArkType's `keyof` only returns `string` and `symbol` keys, the two kinds of key an object can have.
>
> **Why ArkType diverges from TypeScript here**
>
> In a set-based type system, two types that describe the same values need the same representation. TypeScript keeps separate numeric and string representations of the same key, which leads to results like this:
>
> ```ts
> type Thing1 = {
> 	[x: string]: unknown
> }
>
> // Thing2 describes the same values as Thing1
> type Thing2 = Record<string, unknown>
>
> type Key1 = keyof Thing1
> // type Key1 = string | number
>
> type Key2 = keyof Thing2
> // type Key2 = string
> ```

### get

Like an indexed access type in TypeScript (`User["name"]`), `get` extracts the type of the value at a key:

```ts
const Manatee = type({
	isFriendly: "true",
	snorf: {
		uses: "string[]"
	}
})

// Type<true>
const IsFriendly = Manatee.get("isFriendly")

// pass more keys to access nested properties
// Type<string[]>
const SnorfUses = Manatee.get("snorf", "uses")
```

The key can also be a union, a literal or an index signature, and the object can be a union with optional keys. The [`get` tests](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/__tests__/get.test.ts) cover each case.

> **Extracting part of a type can be an antipattern**
>
> Before using `get`, `pick` or `omit` on a type you defined, consider defining that part as its own type and referencing it. Composing small types is usually clearer and faster than extracting parts of a large one.

### structural transformations

`merge`, `pick`, `omit`, `required`, `partial` and `map` each return a **new object built from the properties** of the `Type` they're called on, rather than referencing that `Type`.

> **Only properties are carried over**
>
> Anything attached to the object itself is dropped: most importantly a root [narrow](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) or [filter](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#filter), but also [metadata](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#metadata) like `.describe(...)`. Constraints on the properties are kept.
>
> ```ts
> const User = type({
> 	name: "string",
> 	email: "string"
> }).narrow(user => user.email.includes("@"))
>
> // the narrow is not a property, so PartialUser doesn't have it
> const PartialUser = User.partial()
>
> // { email: "not an email" }
> PartialUser({ email: "not an email" })
> ```
>
> Reapply what you still need to the result:
>
> ```ts
> const PartialUser = type({
> 	name: "string",
> 	email: "string"
> })
> 	.partial()
> 	.narrow(user => user.email?.includes("@") ?? true)
> ```
>
> A root [morph](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe) can't be reduced to properties, so transforming a type like `type({ name: "string" }).pipe(user => user)` throws a `ParseError` instead of dropping it.

### pick / omit

Keep or remove specific properties:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	email: "string.email",
	"age?": "number"
})

// Type<{ name: string; email: string }>
const NameAndEmail = User.pick("name", "email")

// Type<{ name: string; age?: number }>
const WithoutEmail = User.omit("email")
```

In a definition, use the `Pick` and `Omit` [generics](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords). Their keys are definitions, so quote each one:

```ts
const types = type.module({
	User: {
		name: "string",
		email: "string.email",
		"age?": "number"
	},
	NameAndEmail: "Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>",
	WithoutEmail: "Omit<User, 'email'>"
})
```

### required / partial

Make every named property required or optional:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"email?": "string.email",
	"age?": "number"
})

// Type<{ name: string; email: string; age: number }>
const RequiredUser = User.required()

// Type<{ name?: string; email?: string; age?: number }>
const PartialUser = User.partial()
```

`required` also removes defaults, so a defaulted key becomes a plain required key:

```ts
// Type<{ foo: string }>
const T = type({ foo: "string = 'bar'" }).required()

// ArkErrors: foo must be a string (was missing)
T({})
```

In a definition, use the `Required` and `Partial` [generics](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords), e.g. `"Partial<User>"` in a scope.

> **Arrays and tuples mirror TypeScript's Required and Partial**
>
> Like the mapped types they're named for, `required` and `partial` apply to an array's or tuple's elements:
>
> ```ts
> // Type<[string?, number?]>
> const PartialPair = type(["string", "number"]).partial()
>
> // Type<[string, number]>
> const RequiredPair = type(["string", "number?"]).required()
> ```
>
> They only change whether an element must be present, never the values it allows. TypeScript also adds `undefined` to variadic elements and index signature values, since it has no way to mark them optional. ArkType doesn't, so `type("string[]").partial()` is still `string[]`.
>
> A postfix element can't follow an optional one, in ArkType or in TypeScript, so `partial` throws a `ParseError` on a tuple like `[string, ...number[], boolean]`.

### readonly

Mark every property as `readonly`. This only affects the inferred type; the output isn't frozen.

```ts
// Type<{ readonly id: number; readonly name: string }>
const Frozen = type({
	id: "number",
	name: "string"
}).readonly()
```

### map

`map` transforms each property of an object. The function receives a prop with its `key`, `value` (a `Type`) and `kind` (`"required"` or `"optional"`), and returns a `{ key, value }` object, optionally with `kind`:

```ts
const Name = type({
	first: "string",
	last: "string"
})

// Type<{ first: string | null; last: string | null }>
const NullableName = Name.map(prop => ({
	key: prop.key,
	value: prop.value.or("null")
}))
```

Return `[]` to remove a property, or several props to add more than one:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number"
})

// Type<{ name: string }>
const NameOnly = User.map(prop => (prop.key === "age" ? [] : prop))
```

### props

`props` lists an object's properties, with required keys first, then optional keys, each sorted by name:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number",
	role: "'admin' | 'user' = 'user'"
})

for (const prop of User.props) {
	console.log(prop.kind) // "required", "optional", "optional"
	console.log(prop.key) // "name", "age", "role"
	console.log(prop.value.expression) // "string", "number", '"admin" | "user"'
	if ("default" in prop) console.log(prop.default) // "user"
}
```

## arrays

**string**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: "string[]"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: type.string.array()
})
```

**tuple**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: ["string", "[]"]
})
```

**args**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: type("string", "[]")
})
```

### lengths

Constrain an array's length with `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==` or `!=`:

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: "string[] > 0",
	atMost5: "boolean[] <= 5",
	pair: "number[] == 2"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: type.string.array().moreThanLength(0),
	atMost5: type.boolean.array().atMostLength(5),
	pair: type.number.array().exactlyLength(2)
})
```

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
const Tags = type("0 < string[] <= 10")

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
Tags([])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Tags = type.string.array().moreThanLength(0).atMostLength(10)

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
Tags([])
```

## tuples

Like objects, tuples are structures whose values are nested definitions. Like TypeScript, ArkType supports prefix, defaultable, optional, variadic and postfix elements, with the same rules for combining them.

### prefix

**string**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	"string",
	// object definitions can be nested in tuples, and vice versa
	{
		coordinates: ["number", "number"]
	}
])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	type.string,
	// object definitions can be nested in tuples, and vice versa
	{
		coordinates: [type.number, type.number]
	}
])
```

### defaultable

A defaultable element is optional in the input. When it is missing, the output has its default.

Defaultable elements follow the prefix elements and come before any optional elements. Like optional elements, they can't be combined with postfix elements.

**string**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", "boolean = false", "number = 0"])

// ["a", false, 0]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	type.string,
	type.boolean.default(false),
	type.number.default(0)
])

// ["a", false, 0]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**tuple**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", ["boolean", "=", false], ["number", "=", 0]])

// ["a", false, 0]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

### optional

An optional element may be absent from the input and has no default.

Optional elements follow the prefix and defaultable elements, and come before a variadic element or the end of the tuple. Like in TypeScript, they can't be combined with postfix elements.

**string**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", "boolean?", "number?"])

// ["a"]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	type.string,
	type.boolean.optional(),
	type.number.optional()
])

// ["a"]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**tuple**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", ["boolean", "?"], ["number", "?"]])

// ["a"]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

### variadic

Like in TypeScript, a variadic element allows zero or more consecutive values of a type. A tuple can have at most one. Write it as `"..."` followed by an array:

**string**

```ts
// a string followed by zero or more numbers
const MyTuple = type(["string", "...", "number[]"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
// a string followed by zero or more numbers
const MyTuple = type([type.string, "...", type.number.array()])
```

### postfix

Postfix elements are required elements after a variadic element. They can't be combined with optional or defaultable elements.

**string**

```ts
// zero or more numbers followed by a boolean, then a string
const MyTuple = type(["...", "number[]", "boolean", "string"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
// zero or more numbers followed by a boolean, then a string
const MyTuple = type(["...", type.number.array(), type.boolean, type.string])
```

## dates

`Date` allows a valid `Date` instance. An invalid date, like `new Date("x")`, is rejected:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a Date (was an invalid Date)
type.Date(new Date("x"))
```

To accept invalid dates everywhere, configure [`dateAllowsInvalid`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#dateallowsinvalid).

### literals

A date literal, `d'...'` or `d"..."`, is a `Date` with an exact value. They're mostly useful as [range](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#dates-ranges) bounds.

```ts
const Literals = type({
	singleQuoted: "d'1970-01-01'",
	doubleQuoted: 'd"1970-01-01"'
})
```

A literal, like a string passed as a date limit, must be the same instant on every machine, so it can be an ISO date like `2025-01-01` (which is UTC), an ISO date-time with `Z` or an offset like `2025-01-01T12:00+01:00`, or a number of epoch milliseconds. Any other literal, like `d'notadate'` or `d'2025-01-01T12:00'`, is a `ParseError`.

### ranges

Constrain a `Date` with `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==` or `!=`. A bound is either a [date literal](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#dates-literals) or a number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	inThePast: `Date < ${Date.now()}`,
	from2000: "Date >= d'2000-01-01'",
	before2100: "Date < d'2100-01-01'"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	inThePast: type.Date.earlierThan(Date.now()),
	from2000: type.Date.atOrAfter("2000-01-01"),
	before2100: type.Date.earlierThan("2100-01-01")
})
```

The fluent methods are `laterThan`, `atOrAfter`, `earlierThan` and `atOrBefore`.

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
const tenYearsAgo = new Date().setFullYear(new Date().getFullYear() - 10)

const Recent = type(`${tenYearsAgo} <= Date < ${Date.now()}`)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const tenYearsAgo = new Date().setFullYear(new Date().getFullYear() - 10)

const Recent = type.Date.atOrAfter(tenYearsAgo).earlierThan(Date.now())
```

Descriptions and error messages write dates in UTC. A date at UTC midnight is written as its calendar date:

```ts
// "a Date and January 1, 2023 or later"
type("Date >= d'2023-01-01'").description

// "a Date and January 1, 2023, 2:30 PM UTC or later"
type("Date >= d'2023-01-01T14:30Z'").description
```

## instanceof

Most built-in classes like `Array`, `Date` and `Map` are [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#instanceof). Use `instanceof` for your own classes:

**fluent**

```ts
class MyClass {}

const Instance = type.instanceOf(MyClass)
```

**tuple**

```ts
class MyClass {}

const Instance = type(["instanceof", MyClass])
```

**args**

```ts
class MyClass {}

const Instance = type("instanceof", MyClass)
```

> **Array is the only constructor that works across realms**
>
> Constructors are compared by identity, so a value created in another realm, like an `<iframe>` or a `node:vm` context, is not an instance of the constructor in yours. `Array` is checked with `Array.isArray`, so it also matches arrays from another realm.

### keywords

The [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#instanceof) page lists every built-in class keyword, along with the subtypes of [Array](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#array) and [FormData](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#formdata).

Keywords for web platform classes, like `Blob`, `File`, `URL`, `FormData`, `Headers`, `Request` and `Response`, throw when used in a runtime that doesn't define that class, e.g. `'Blob' is unresolvable`.

# Keywords

> Every built-in keyword, from TypeScript's own types to subtypes like string.email and generics like Pick.

## TypeScript

TypeScript's built-in types are keywords, except `any` and `void`, which don't mean anything useful at runtime. If you need `any`, use `unknown.any`.

**string**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	string: "string",
	date: "Date"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	string: type.string,
	date: type.Date
})
```

These keywords are attached directly to `type`: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `undefined`, `null`, `object`, `unknown`, `true`, `false`, `never`, `Key`, `Array`, `Date`, `Record` and `arrayIndex`. Every keyword is available in `type.keywords`.

## Subtypes

A subtype keyword refines or transforms its parent, like `string.email` or `string.date.parse`. To find them in your editor, start a definition like `"string."` and let autocomplete list them.

**string**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	dateString: "string.date",
	isoDateString: "string.date.iso",
	parsedDate: "string.date.parse",
	parsedIsoDate: "string.date.iso.parse"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	dateString: type.keywords.string.date.root,
	isoDateString: type.keywords.string.date.iso.root,
	parsedDate: type.keywords.string.date.parse,
	parsedIsoDate: type.keywords.string.date.iso.parse
})
```

A keyword with subtypes, like `string.date`, is a module. Its `.root` is the keyword's own `Type`.

## All keywords

These are all the keywords `type` resolves. To define your own, see [scopes](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes).

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `Exclude` | exclude branches of a union like \`Exclude("boolean", "true")\` |

| `Merge` | merge an object's properties onto another like \`Merge(User, { isAdmin: "true" })\` |

# Expressions

> Combine, refine, transform and annotate types with operators like unions, intersections, narrows, pipes, brands and metadata.

An expression combines or modifies other definitions. Most expressions can be written four ways:

- **string**: embedded in a string definition, like `"string | number"`
- **fluent**: a method on a `Type`, like `type.string.or(type.number)`
- **tuple**: an array definition, like `["string", "|", "number"]`
- **args**: the same elements passed to `type` as arguments, like `type("string", "|", "number")`

They're interchangeable, so use whichever reads best. Where an operand is a function or a value like a symbol, use the fluent, tuple or args form.

| Expression | String | Fluent | Tuple / args |
| - | - | - | - |
| [intersection](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#intersection) | `"a & b"` | `.and(b)` | `[a, "&", b]` |
| [union](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#union) | `"a \| b"` | `.or(b)` | `[a, "\|", b]` |
| [array](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#arrays) | `"a[]"` | `.array()` | `[a, "[]"]` |
| [keyof](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-keyof) | `"keyof a"` | `.keyof()` | `["keyof", a]` |
| [brand](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#brand) | `"a#name"` | `.brand("name")` | |
| [narrow](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) | | `.narrow(fn)` | `[a, ":", fn]` |
| [filter](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#filter) | | `.filter(fn)` | |
| [pipe](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe) | | `.pipe(fn)` | `[a, "=>", fn]` |
| [to](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#to) | `"a \|> b"` | `.to(b)` | `[a, "\|>", b]` |
| [unit](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#unit) | a literal, `"'a'"` | `type.unit(value)` | `["===", value]` |
| [meta](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#meta) | | `.configure(meta)` | `[a, "@", meta]` |
| [instanceof](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#instanceof) | | `type.instanceOf(Class)` | `["instanceof", Class]` |

Optional (`?`), defaultable (`=`) and spread (`...`) definitions only apply to properties and tuple elements. They're covered on the [objects](https://arktype.io/docs/objects) page.

## Intersection

Like its TypeScript counterpart, an intersection creates a `Type` that enforces the constraints of both operands.

**string**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type("string.email & /@arktype\\.io$/")

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

**fluent**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type("string.email").and(/@arktype\.io$/)

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

**tuple**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type(["string.email", "&", /@arktype\.io$/])

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

**args**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type("string.email", "&", /@arktype\.io$/)

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

> **To combine properties, merge instead**
>
> Intersecting objects is more work to compute than [merging](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#merge) them, both when the type is created and in your editor. Unless you need overlapping keys' values intersected, merge.

### n-ary

`type.and` intersects any number of definitions:

```ts
// Type<{ foo: string; bar: number; baz: string }>
const FooBarBaz = type.and(
	{ foo: "string" },
	{ bar: "number" },
	{ baz: "string" }
)
```

## Union

A union allows a value that satisfies either operand. ArkType discriminates unions automatically: where a value like its type or a literal key tells the branches apart, it checks that first instead of trying each branch, which keeps validation fast and errors specific. Where the discriminant can't place data, like a number where every branch is an object, each branch reports its own error, as in an undiscriminated union.

**string**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type("string | number")

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type.string.or(type.number)

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

**tuple**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type(["string", "|", "number"])

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

**args**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type("string", "|", "number")

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

When no branch matches the discriminant, like a value of the wrong type here, the error's code is `discriminant`. See [errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for the fields it carries.

### n-ary

`type.or` unions any number of definitions:

```ts
// Type<string | number | { key: unknown }>
const Union = type.or(type.string, "number", { key: "unknown" })
```

> **A union that could transform the same input in different ways throws a ParseError**
>
> ```ts
> // operands overlap, but neither transforms data
> const Okay = type("number > 0").or("number < 10")
>
> // an operand transforms data, but the inputs don't overlap
> const AlsoOkay = type("string.numeric.parse").or({ box: "string" })
>
> // ParseError: An unordered union of a type including a morph and a type with overlapping input is indeterminate
> const Bad = type({ box: "string.numeric.parse" }).or({ box: "string" })
> ```
>
> To fix it, make the inputs disjoint, e.g. by narrowing a morph's input, or pipe the union of their inputs to a single morph:
>
> ```ts
> // only numeric strings are parsed, so no input reaches two branches
> const Narrowed = type("string.numeric.parse | number | null")
>
> // one morph decides how to transform each input
> const Piped = type("unknown").pipe(v => (v === null ? v : Number(v)))
> ```
>
> **Why this isn't allowed**
>
> `Bad` says two things about the same input:
>
> - if `box` is a string, parse it as a number
> - if `box` is a string, keep it as a string
>
> The order of a union's branches doesn't affect its result, so there's no way to choose between them. The same applies when the transformed keys differ: `type({ a: "string.numeric.parse" }).or({ b: "string.numeric.parse" })` throws too, since an input like `{ a: "1", b: "2" }` matches both branches and each would parse a different key.

### extract / exclude

`.extract()` keeps the branches of a union that are assignable to a definition, and `.exclude()` removes them, like TypeScript's `Extract` and `Exclude`:

```ts
const Primitive = type("string | number | boolean")

// Type<number | boolean>
const NumberOrBoolean = Primitive.extract("number | boolean")

// Type<number | boolean>
const NotString = Primitive.exclude("string")
```

In a definition, use the `Extract` and `Exclude` [generics](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords), e.g. `"Exclude<'a' | 'b' | 0, string>"`.

## Brand

A brand adds a type-only tag to a type, so the only values that satisfy it are those you validated with it.

**string**

```ts
const Even = type("(number % 2)#even")
type Even = typeof Even.infer

const good: Even = Even.assert(2)
// TypeScript: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'Brand<number, "even">'
const bad: Even = 5
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Even = type.number.divisibleBy(2).brand("even")
type Even = typeof Even.infer

const good: Even = Even.assert(2)
// TypeScript: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'Brand<number, "even">'
const bad: Even = 5
```

A brand changes nothing at runtime. The `Brand` type it infers is exported from `arktype`.

For more on branding in general, see [this article](https://www.learningtypescript.com/articles/branded-types) by [Josh Goldberg](https://github.com/joshuakgoldberg).

## Narrow

A narrow adds custom validation to a type. Return `true` to accept the value, or call `ctx.mustBe()` or `ctx.reject()` to reject it with a message. The [intro](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/adding-constraints#narrow) walks through an example.

**fluent**

```ts
const Palindrome = type("string").narrow(
	(s, ctx) => s === [...s].reverse().join("") || ctx.mustBe("a palindrome")
)

// ArkErrors: must be a palindrome (was "arktype")
Palindrome("arktype")
```

**tuple**

```ts
const Palindrome = type([
	"string",
	":",
	(s, ctx) => s === [...s].reverse().join("") || ctx.mustBe("a palindrome")
])

// ArkErrors: must be a palindrome (was "arktype")
Palindrome("arktype")
```

**args**

```ts
const Palindrome = type(
	"string",
	":",
	(s, ctx) => s === [...s].reverse().join("") || ctx.mustBe("a palindrome")
)

// ArkErrors: must be a palindrome (was "arktype")
Palindrome("arktype")
```

`ctx.reject()` can also set the error's `path` and `actual`, e.g. to report a mismatch at the right key without printing a password:

```ts
const Form = type({
	password: "string",
	confirmPassword: "string"
}).narrow(
	(data, ctx) =>
		data.password === data.confirmPassword ||
		ctx.reject({
			expected: "identical to password",
			actual: "",
			path: ["confirmPassword"]
		})
)

// ArkErrors: confirmPassword must be identical to password
Form({ password: "arktype", confirmPassword: "artkype" })
```

If a narrow's return type is a type predicate, the `Type` infers it:

```ts
// Type<`ark${string}`>
const ArkString = type("string").narrow(
	(data, ctx): data is `ark${string}` =>
		data.startsWith("ark") || ctx.reject("a string starting with 'ark'")
)
```

The [traversal API](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api) documents everything `ctx` can do.

## Filter

`filter` is like `narrow`, but checks a type's **input** instead of its output. The difference matters when the type transforms its input:

- **`narrow`** checks the **output**, after morphs run
- **`filter`** checks the **input**, before morphs run

```ts
const ShortNumeric = type("string.numeric.parse").filter(
	// s is the input string, not the parsed number
	(s, ctx) => s.length <= 10 || ctx.reject("at most 10 characters")
)

// 123
ShortNumeric("123")

// ArkErrors: must be at most 10 characters (was "12345678901")
ShortNumeric("12345678901")
```

Like `narrow`, a type predicate returned by a filter is inferred, here as the type's input.

## Pipe

A pipe transforms data after it is validated, through one or more functions called **morphs**. The [intro](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/morphs-and-more) walks through examples.

**fluent**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<string>>
const TrimStart = type("string").pipe(str => str.trimStart())
```

**tuple**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<string>>
const TrimStart = type(["string", "=>", str => str.trimStart()])
```

**args**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<string>>
const TrimStart = type("string", "=>", str => str.trimStart())
```

A morph receives the validated value itself rather than a copy, so a morph that mutates its argument mutates the caller's data. ArkType's own transforms, like defaults, copy each object they change and share every untransformed value with the input, and input nothing transforms is returned as is. The exception is an instance of a builtin class, like a `Date`, `Map` or function, which keeps its state in internal slots and is transformed in place. [`mutatesInput`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#mutatesinput) writes transforms into the data instead.

```ts
const T = type({ a: "string.trim", b: { c: "string" } })
const input = { a: " x ", b: { c: "y" } }

const out = T.assert(input)

out === input // false
out.b === input.b // true
```

### To

A morph can return `ArkErrors` to fail validation, so a `Type` works as a morph: it validates the previous output. The `to` operator pipes to a definition without wrapping it in `type`:

**string**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type("string.numeric.parse |> number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

**fluent**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type("string.numeric.parse").to("number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

**tuple**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type(["string.numeric.parse", "|>", "number % 2"])

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

**args**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type("string.numeric.parse", "|>", "number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

`.to("number % 2")` is the same as `.pipe(type("number % 2"))`.

### n-ary

`.pipe()` accepts any number of morphs and types. `type.pipe()` does the same without a `Type` to start from:

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<string>>
const TrimStartNonEmpty = type.pipe(
	type.string,
	s => s.trimStart(),
	type.string.atLeastLength(1)
)

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
TrimStartNonEmpty("   ")
```

## Unit

A [literal](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives#number-literals) is the simplest way to allow one exact primitive value. To allow a value a string can't embed, like a `symbol`, use `type.unit` or `===`:

**fluent**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValue = type.unit(mySymbol)
```

**tuple**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValue = type(["===", mySymbol])
```

**args**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValue = type("===", mySymbol)
```

## Enumerated

`type.enumerated` allows any of a list of values. With one value, it's the same as `type.unit`.

**fluent**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValueFromSet = type.enumerated(1337, true, mySymbol)
```

**tuple**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValueFromSet = type(["===", 1337, true, mySymbol])
```

**args**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValueFromSet = type("===", 1337, true, mySymbol)
```

## valueOf

`type.valueOf` allows the values of a TypeScript `enum` or an enum-like object:

```ts
enum TsEnum {
	numeric = 1
}

// Type<TsEnum.numeric>
const EnumType = type.valueOf(TsEnum)
```

It is almost the same as `type.enumerated(...Object.values(o))`. The difference is an entry whose key is another entry's numeric value, mapping back to that entry's key. That's how TypeScript compiles a numeric `enum`, so `valueOf` skips the reverse entry:

```ts
// what TsEnum compiles to
const equivalentObject = {
	numeric: 1,
	"1": "numeric"
} as const

// allows only 1, though it infers Type<1 | "numeric">
const EquivalentType = type.valueOf(equivalentObject)
```

> **Prefer enumerated**
>
> TypeScript is moving away from features that emit JavaScript, like `enum`, which [`--erasableSyntaxOnly`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#erasableSyntaxOnly) disallows. `type.valueOf` is for code that already uses `enum`. Otherwise, list values with [`type.enumerated`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#enumerated) or a literal union.

## fn

`type.fn` wraps a function so its parameters, and optionally its return value, are validated when it's called. Parameters use tuple syntax. Put a return type after `":"`.

```ts
const len = type.fn("string | unknown[]", ":", "number")(s => s.length)

len("foo") // 3
len([1, 2]) // 2

// TraversalError: value at [0] must be a string or an array (was boolean)
len(true)
// TypeScript: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | unknown[]'.
```

The result is a `TypedFn`, which is introspectable:

```ts
const len = type.fn("string | unknown[]", ":", "number")(s => s.length)

len.expression // "(string | Array) => number"
len.params.expression // "[string | Array]"
len.returns.expression // "number"
```

Parameters can be defaultable, optional or variadic:

```ts
const greet = type.fn("string = 'world'")(name => `Hello, ${name}!`)

greet() // "Hello, world!"

const join = type.fn("...", "string[]")((...parts) => parts.join(","))

join("a", "b") // "a,b"
```

Without a return type, the return type is inferred from the implementation and not validated.

## Meta

Metadata attaches information to a type. ArkType reads some of it, like `description`, which error messages use. You can read the rest from the type's `meta`.

**fluent**

```ts
const SpecialString = type("string").configure({
	description: "a special string"
})

// .describe() is shorthand for a description
const SpecialNumber = type("number").describe("a special number")

// ArkErrors: must be a special number (was a string)
SpecialNumber("five")
```

**tuple**

```ts
const SpecialString = type([
	"string",
	"@",
	{
		description: "a special string"
	}
])

// a string is shorthand for a description
const SpecialNumber = type(["number", "@", "a special number"])

// ArkErrors: must be a special number (was a string)
SpecialNumber("five")
```

**args**

```ts
const SpecialString = type("string", "@", {
	description: "a special string"
})

// a string is shorthand for a description
const SpecialNumber = type("number", "@", "a special number")

// ArkErrors: must be a special number (was a string)
SpecialNumber("five")
```

An object definition can hold its own metadata under an `"@"` key:

```ts
const User = type({
	"@": "a user",
	name: "string"
})

// ArkErrors: must be a user (was a number)
User(5)
```

A configured description, like any message you configure, takes precedence over the [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#your-own-messages), so it isn't translated.

The `keyword` key is reserved: built-in keywords set `meta.keyword` to their name so a locale can find their phrase, and configuring a description removes it. Name your own metadata something else.

To configure only some of a type's nodes, pass a selector after the metadata:

**fluent**

```ts
const Point = type({
	x: "number",
	y: "number"
}).configure(
	{ description: "a coordinate" },
	// every domain node: the object and both numbers
	"domain"
)

// ArkErrors: x must be a coordinate (was a string)
Point({ x: "1", y: 2 })
```

**tuple**

```ts
const Point = type([
	{
		x: "number",
		y: "number"
	},
	"@",
	{ description: "a coordinate" },
	// every domain node: the object and both numbers
	"domain"
])

// ArkErrors: x must be a coordinate (was a string)
Point({ x: "1", y: 2 })
```

**args**

```ts
const Point = type(
	{
		x: "number",
		y: "number"
	},
	"@",
	{ description: "a coordinate" },
	// every domain node: the object and both numbers
	"domain"
)

// ArkErrors: x must be a coordinate (was a string)
Point({ x: "1", y: 2 })
```

Selectors are documented with [`select`](https://arktype.io/docs/internals/nodes#select).

## Cast

A cast changes how a `Type` is inferred without changing what it validates:

**string**

```ts
// any string, but the editor suggests "foo" and "bar"
type AutocompletedString = "foo" | "bar" | (string & {})

const MyObj = type({
	autocompletedString: "string" as type.cast<AutocompletedString>
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
// any string, but the editor suggests "foo" and "bar"
type AutocompletedString = "foo" | "bar" | (string & {})

const MyObj = type({
	autocompletedString: type.string.as<AutocompletedString>()
})
```

## Parenthetical

Operators have the same precedence as in TypeScript, and parentheses group them the same way:

```ts
// Type<{ stringOrNumbers: string | number[]; stringsOrNumbers: (string | number)[] }>
const Groups = type({
	stringOrNumbers: "string | number[]",
	stringsOrNumbers: "(string | number)[]"
})
```

## this

`this` references the root of the definition it's in, which makes the type recursive:

```ts
const DisappointingGift = type({
	label: "string",
	"box?": "this"
})

const out = DisappointingGift({
	label: "foo",
	box: { label: "bar", box: {} }
})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: box.box.label must be a string (was missing)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// narrowed inference to arbitrary depth
	console.log(out.box?.box?.label)
	// (property) label: string | undefined
}
```

In a scope, `this` is a `ParseError`. Reference the alias by name instead, as described in [cyclic types](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes#cyclic-types):

```ts
const types = scope({
	DisappointingGift: {
		label: "string",
		"box?": "DisappointingGift"
	}
}).export()
```

# Match

> Branch on the type of a value with ArkType definitions, like a type-safe switch statement.

`match` pairs ArkType definitions with handlers. It returns a function that runs the handler of the first case its input satisfies.

## Case record API

Each key is a definition and each value is a handler. The handler's parameter is inferred from its key:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const toLabel = match({
	string: s => s,
	number: n => n.toFixed(2),
	bigint: b => `${b}n`,
	default: "assert"
})

toLabel("abc") // "abc"
toLabel(5) // "5.00"
toLabel(5n) // "5n"
// TraversalError: must be a string, a number or a bigint (was boolean)
toLabel(true)
```

Cases are checked in the order they are defined. A matcher is complete once it has a `default`.
