## Default

`default` decides what happens to input that matches no case:

| `default` | Accepts | When no case matches |
| - | - | - |
| `"assert"` | `unknown` | throws a `TraversalError` |
| `"never"` | only input the cases accept | throws a `TraversalError` |
| `"reject"` | `unknown` | returns `ArkErrors` |
| a function | `unknown` | returns the function's result |

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const sizeOf = match({
	string: s => s.length,
	number: n => n,
	default: "reject"
})

// ArkErrors: must be a string or a number (was boolean)
sizeOf(true)
```

## Fluent API

`.case(definition, handler)` adds one case at a time, which is convenient for definitions that can't be written as a key. It can follow a case record or start a chain as `match.case(...)`. `.default(...)` completes the matcher:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const sizeOf = match({
	string: s => s.length,
	number: n => n
})
	// any object with a numeric length
	.case({ length: "number" }, o => o.length)
	.default(() => 0)

sizeOf("abc") // 3
sizeOf({ name: "David", length: 5 }) // 5
sizeOf(null) // 0
```

## Input with `in`

`.in<T>()` sets the input type of a matcher: calling it with anything else is a type error, and each handler's parameter is narrowed from `T`. It does not validate at runtime.

`.in(definition)` takes a definition instead and validates input against it before any case runs:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const half = match.in("number | string").match({
	number: n => n / 2,
	default: s => s
})

half(4) // 2
// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
half(true)
// TypeScript: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'.
```

## Properties with `at`

`.at(key)` matches cases against the value of one property. Each handler receives the whole object:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

type Data = { id: 1; count: number } | { id: 2; label: string }

const describe = match
	.in<Data>()
	.at("id")
	.match({
		1: o => `${o.count} items`,
		2: o => o.label,
		default: "assert"
	})

describe({ id: 1, count: 3 }) // "3 items"
describe({ id: 2, label: "two" }) // "two"
// TraversalError: id must be 1 or 2 (was missing)
describe({ count: 3 })
// TypeScript: Property 'id' is missing in type '{ count: number; }' but required in type '{ id: 1; count: number; }'.
```

`match.at(key, cases)` does the same in one call.

## String values with `strings`

`.strings(cases)` treats each key as a string value rather than a definition, so a key needs no quotes and `number` matches the string `"number"`. It follows `.in(...)` or `.at(key)`, and a key that isn't a possible value of the input is a type error. Its types are much cheaper to check than `.match` with quoted string literals:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "square"; side: number }

const area = match
	.in<Shape>()
	.at("kind")
	.strings({
		circle: c => Math.PI * c.r ** 2,
		square: s => s.side ** 2,
		default: "assert"
	})

area({ kind: "square", side: 2 }) // 4
```

## Scoped aliases

`match` resolves the same keywords as `type`. To match on your own aliases, use the `match` method of your [scope](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes):

```ts
import { scope } from "arktype"

const $ = scope({ Id: "string", Count: "number" })

const describe = $.match({
	Id: id => `user ${id}`,
	Count: n => `${n} users`,
	default: "assert"
})

describe("42") // "user 42"
```

# Codecs

> Pair a morph with its inverse to encode output back into input.

A Type with morphs decodes input into output. A codec is a morph with an inverse, so its output can also be encoded back into input.

## Defining a codec

`codec` takes an input definition, an output definition and a function for each direction. It comes from `arktype/codecs`, which installs encoding when imported, so an app that doesn't encode doesn't ship it. Without that import, reading `.encode` throws a `ParseError`:

```ts
import { codec } from "arktype/codecs"

const EpochMs = codec("number.integer", "Date", {
	decode: n => new Date(n),
	encode: d => d.getTime()
})

// Date
const date = EpochMs(0)
// 0
const ms = EpochMs.encode(date)
```

A codec is a Type. `.encode` is a Type too, from output to input, so it validates what it receives like any other Type:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a Date (was a string)
const out = EpochMs.encode("0")
```

What `encode` returns is validated against the input definition, so encoding always produces something the codec can decode.

## Composition

Every Type has `.encode`, which inverts each of its morphs, so a codec encodes wherever it is nested: in objects, arrays and tuples, unions, intersections, pipes and cyclic scopes.

```ts
const Event = type({
	name: "string",
	at: EpochMs,
	"reminders?": EpochMs.array()
})

// { name: "launch", at: 0, reminders: [60000] }
const encoded = Event.encode({
	name: "launch",
	at: new Date(0),
	reminders: [new Date(60000)]
})
```

A Type without morphs encodes as itself.

## Defaults and unions

A defaulted key is always present in decoded output, so it is required when encoding:

```ts
const Settings = type({ since: EpochMs.default(0) })

// ArkErrors: since must be a Date (was missing)
const out = Settings.encode({})
```

A union encodes a value with a branch that accepts it, trying the branches without morphs first, so a value a branch would decode unchanged is encoded unchanged.

## Keywords

The parse keywords encode back to the string they parse: `string.date.parse`, `string.date.iso.parse` and `string.date.epoch.parse`, `string.numeric.parse`, `string.integer.parse`, `string.json.parse` and `string.url.parse`.

```ts
import "arktype/codecs"

const Event = type({
	at: "string.date.iso.parse",
	count: "string.integer.parse"
})

// { at: "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z", count: "5" }
const encoded = Event.encode({ at: new Date(0), count: 5 })
```

`string.trim`, `string.lower`, `string.upper`, `string.capitalize` and `string.normalize` encode a string already in their format as itself, and `object.json.stringify` encodes by parsing.

## Precompiling

[Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) Types encode too. The build precompiles each `codec` like any other Type, passing its `decode` and `encode` functions where you wrote them, and each `.encode` it sees read becomes an encoder of its own:

```ts
import { codec } from "arktype/codecs"

const EpochMs = codec("number.integer", "Date", {
	decode: n => new Date(n),
	encode: d => d.getTime()
})

export const Event = type({ at: EpochMs })

// precompiled to an encoder
export const encode = (event: unknown) => Event.encode(event)
```

A standalone build installs encoding itself, so `.encode` works there even if the program never imports `arktype/codecs`. A Type with a morph that has no inverse fails the build where its `.encode` is read, since arktype would throw there.

## Morphs without an inverse

Encoding is only possible if every morph has an inverse. Otherwise, accessing `.encode` throws a `ParseError`:

```ts
import "arktype/codecs"

const Length = type({ length: type("string").pipe(s => s.length) })

// ParseError: A morph must have an inverse to be encoded: (In: string) => Out<unknown>
Length.encode
```

# Scopes

> Define aliases that reference each other, then use them in definitions or export them as a module of Types.

A scope is a set of named definitions, called aliases, that can reference each other the same way they reference keywords like `string`. The `type` function you import from `arktype` is a method of ArkType's default scope.

## Defining a scope

Pass `scope` an object mapping alias names to definitions:

```ts
import { scope } from "arktype"

const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	User: { id: "Id", friends: "Id[]" },
	UsersById: { "[Id]": "User" }
})
```

Aliases are autocompleted and validated like built-in keywords. Write definitions inside a scope directly: wrapping one in `type(...)` fails, because `type` only knows built-in keywords (see [thunks](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes#thunks)).

`$.type` parses a definition that can reference the scope's aliases. Types created this way keep their scope, so chained methods can reference the aliases too:

```ts
const Group = $.type({ name: "string", members: "User[]" })

const OwnedGroup = Group.and({ ownerId: "Id" })
```

`$.match`, `$.declare`, `$.generic` and `$.fn` work like their counterparts on `type`, but also resolve the scope's aliases.

## Modules

`.export()` turns a scope into a `Module`, an object mapping each alias to its `Type`:

```ts
const types = $.export()

// ArkErrors: friends[1] must be a string (was a number)
types.User({ id: "99", friends: ["7", 8, "9"] })
```

To get a single `Type`, use `$.resolve("User")`.

`type.module` defines a scope and exports it in one call:

```ts
const types = type.module({
	Id: "string",
	User: { id: "Id", friends: "Id[]" }
})
```

A `Module` can be spread into another scope to include all of its aliases. Pass names to `.export()` to include only those:

```ts
const numbers = scope({ Three: "3", Sixty: "60", No: "'no'" })

const superScope = scope({
	...$.export(),
	...numbers.export("Three", "Sixty"),
	Saiyan: { powerLevel: "number > 9000" }
})
```

## Cyclic types

Aliases can reference themselves and each other:

```ts
const types = scope({
	Package: {
		name: "string",
		"dependencies?": "Package[]",
		"contributors?": "Contributor[]"
	},
	Contributor: {
		email: "string.email",
		"packages?": "Package[]"
	}
}).export()
```

Cyclic types are inferred to any depth, and they validate cyclic data:

```ts
type Package = typeof types.Package.infer

const packageData: Package = {
	name: "arktype",
	dependencies: [{ name: "typescript" }],
	contributors: [{ email: "david@sharktypeio" }]
}

// arktype now depends on itself
packageData.dependencies![0].dependencies = [packageData]

// ArkErrors: contributors[0].email must be an email address (was "david@sharktypeio")
types.Package(packageData)
```

A cycle must pass through an object, array or morph. An alias that resolves to itself without one, like `a` in `scope({ a: "a | string" })`, is a type error and throws a `ParseError`.

For a single recursive `Type`, you don't need a scope: use the [`this`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#this) keyword.

> **Cyclic types may display as any**
>
> TypeScript shows an anonymous cycle as `...`, or as `any` if `noErrorTruncation` is enabled. Either way, the type itself is accurate: you get completions, and accessing a property that doesn't exist is an error.

## Visibility

Aliases prefixed with `#` are private. They can be referenced in the scope, but are not exported:

```ts
const shapes = scope({
	"#BaseShape": { perimeter: "number", area: "number" },
	// reference private aliases without the "#"
	Ellipse: { "...": "BaseShape", radii: ["number", "number"] },
	Rectangle: { "...": "BaseShape", width: "number", height: "number" }
})

// shapes.type can still reference private aliases
const PartialShape = shapes.type("Partial<BaseShape>")

const shapeModule = shapes.export()
Object.keys(shapeModule) // ["Ellipse", "Rectangle"]
```

### `import()`

`.import()` is like `.export()`, but makes every alias private. Spread it into a scope to use another scope's aliases without re-exporting them:

```ts
const utilities = scope({
	"WithId<o extends object>": { "...": "o", id: "string" }
})

const userModule = type.module({
	...utilities.import(),
	Payload: { name: "string", age: "number" },
	Db: "WithId<Payload>"
})

Object.keys(userModule) // ["Payload", "Db"]
```

## Submodules

Keywords like `string.email` are grouped into submodules. To group your own aliases, assign a `Module` to an alias and reference its members with a `.`:

```ts
const ids = type.module({ User: "string", Order: "number" })

const $ = scope({
	Id: ids,
	Customer: { id: "Id.User", orderIds: "Id.Order[]" }
})
```

Submodules are parsed bottom-up: the root scope can reference a submodule's aliases, but a submodule can't reference the root scope's aliases.

### Nested

Submodules can be nested to any depth:

```ts
const store = scope({ Store: $.export() })

const OrderIds = store.type("Store.Id.Order[]")
```

### Rooted

A submodule can't be referenced as a `Type` itself unless it has an alias named `root`, the way `string` is both a keyword and the prefix of `string.email`:

```ts
const userModule = type.module({
	root: { name: "string" },
	// subaliases can reference root like any other alias
	Admin: { "...": "root", isAdmin: "true" },
	Saiyan: { "...": "root", powerLevel: "number > 9000" }
})

const types = type.module({
	User: userModule,
	// User refers to the root alias
	Group: "User[]",
	// or prefixes its subaliases
	ElevatedUser: "User.Admin | User.Saiyan"
})
```

## Thunks

A common mistake is wrapping a scoped definition in `type`:

```ts
const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	User: type({
		name: "string",
		id: "Id"
		// TypeScript: 'Id' is unresolvable
	})
})
```

`Id` exists in the scope, but `type` only knows built-in keywords. Here the wrapper is redundant, so remove it:

```ts
const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	User: {
		name: "string",
		id: "Id"
	}
})
```

To use fluent methods like `.pipe` on a scoped definition, define it as a thunk: a function that calls the `type` method of the scope you're defining.

```ts
const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	TrimmedId: () => $.type("Id").pipe(s => s.trim())
})

const types = $.export()

types.TrimmedId("  42 ") // "42"
```

A thunk can't pass a callback that receives the data, like `.narrow`'s, to a Type that references the alias the thunk defines. TypeScript would read the callback's parameter from that alias, which is still being inferred from the thunk, and reports the thunk as implicitly `any`. Write the narrow as a tuple expression instead:

```ts
const $ = scope({
	File: { name: "string" },
	Directory: {
		name: "string",
		children: [
			"(File | Directory)[]",
			":",
			children => new Set(children.map(c => c.name)).size === children.length
		]
	}
})
```

## Configuration

`scope` takes a config as its second argument. It applies to every `Type` parsed in the scope:

```ts
const $ = scope({ Even: "number % 2" }, { divisor: { expected: "even" } })

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
$.export().Even(3)
```

It accepts the same options as [global configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration), except these, which can only be configured globally: `onUndeclaredKey`, `numberAllowsNaN`, `numberAllowsInfinity`, `dateAllowsInvalid`, `keywords` and `locale`.

# Generics

> Declare definitions with parameters and instantiate them like TypeScript generics.

A generic is a definition with parameters. Instantiating it with a definition for each parameter returns a `Type`.

## Keywords

Like TypeScript's utility types, these generics are available in any definition:

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `Exclude` | exclude branches of a union like \`Exclude("boolean", "true")\` |
| `Extract` | extract branches of a union like \`Extract("0 \| false \| 1", "number")\` |
| `Merge` | merge an object's properties onto another like \`Merge(User, { isAdmin: "true" })\` |
| `Omit` | omit a set of properties from an object like \`Omit(User, "age")\` |
| `Partial` | make all named properties of an object optional like \`Partial(User)\` |
| `Pick` | pick a set of properties from an object like \`Pick(User, "name \| age")\` |
| `Record` | instantiate an object from an index signature and corresponding value type like \`Record("string", "number")\` |
| `Required` | make all named properties of an object required like \`Required(User)\` |

Instantiate one in a string, or call it from `type.keywords`:

```ts
const One = type("Extract<0 | 1, 1>")

const Unfalse = type.keywords.Exclude("boolean", "false")
```

`Record` is also available as `type.Record`. Generics like `Pick` and `Partial` have [method equivalents](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-pick-omit) on object Types, such as `User.pick("name")`.

## Syntax

### Definition

Pass a string of parameter names in angle brackets, then a definition that references them:

```ts
const BoxOf = type("<t>", { box: "t" })

// Type<{ box: string }>
const StringBox = BoxOf("string")
```

`type.generic("t")({ box: "t" })` is equivalent.

### Constraints

Constrain a parameter with `extends`. Arguments must satisfy the constraint, and the definition can use the parameter wherever its constraint is allowed, like with the `>` operator here:

```ts
const NonEmpty = type("<arr extends unknown[]>", "arr > 0")

// Type<number[]>
const NonEmptyNumbers = NonEmpty("number[]")

// ParseError: arr must be assignable to Array (was string)
NonEmpty("string")
// TypeScript: ["Invalid argument for arr", expected: unknown[]]
```

With `type.generic`, pass a `[name, constraint]` tuple: `type.generic(["arr", "unknown[]"])("arr > 0")`.

### Scoped

In a [scope](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes), declare parameters in the alias name:

```ts
const types = scope({
	"Box<t, u>": { box: "t | u" },
	BitBox: "Box<0, 1>"
}).export()

// ArkErrors: box must be 0 or 1 (was 2)
types.BitBox({ box: 2 })
```

### Recursive

A scoped generic can reference itself:

```ts
const types = scope({
	"Tree<t>": { value: "t", "children?": "Tree<t>[]" },
	NumberTree: "Tree<number>"
}).export()

// ArkErrors: children[0].value must be a number (was a string)
types.NumberTree({ value: 1, children: [{ value: "2" }] })
```

## HKT

`generic()` with an `Hkt` class wraps a type-level TypeScript function as an ArkType generic. The function transforms the arguments at runtime, and the class's `body` describes the result at the type level. This is how `Partial` is implemented:

```ts
import { generic, Hkt } from "arktype"

const Partial = generic(["T", "object"])(
	args => args.T.partial(),
	class PartialHkt extends Hkt<[object]> {
		declare body: Partial<this[0]>
	}
)

// Type<{ a?: string }>
const PartialA = Partial({ a: "string" })
```

For more examples, see the [generic tests](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/HEAD/ark/type/__tests__/generic.test.ts).

## External

To write a TypeScript function that accepts and returns Types, constrain a parameter with `type.Any`:

```ts
const createBox = <t extends string>(of: type.Any<t>) =>
	type({
		box: of
	})

// @ts-expect-error
createBox(type("number"))

// Type<{ box: string }>
const BoxType = createBox(type("string"))
```

To accept a definition instead, validate it with `type.validate` and infer the result with `type.instantiate`:

```ts
const createBox = <const def>(
	of: type.validate<def>
): type.instantiate<{ box: def }> =>
	type.raw({
		box: of
	}) as never

// Type<{ box: string }>
const BoxType = createBox("string")
```

TypeScript generics like these can be hard to get right. If yours isn't inferring as expected, see [the FAQ](https://arktype.io/docs/faq#why-isnt-my-wrapper-generic-working).

# Declare

> Define a Type that must match an existing TypeScript type exactly.

If your ArkType definitions are your source of truth, infer your TypeScript types from them: `type User = typeof User.infer`.

If the TypeScript type comes first, `type.declare` checks that a definition matches it. Object keys are autocompleted, and a definition that is too wide _or_ too narrow is a type error:

```ts
type Expected = { a: string; b?: number }

const T = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string",
	"b?": "number"
})

const Bad = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string",
	// narrower than number
	"b?": "1"
	// TypeScript: declared: number; inferred: 1;
})
```

Optionality can also be expressed in the value instead of the key:

```ts
type Expected = { a: string; b?: number }

const T = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string",
	// same as "b?": "number"
	b: "number?"
})
```

`declare` works with any definition, not only objects:

```ts
const Name = type.declare<string>().type("string")

const Entry = type.declare<[string, number]>().type(["string", "number"])
```

To reference your own aliases, use the `declare` method of your [scope](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes), like `$.declare<User>().type(...)`.

## `side`

A Type with morphs or defaults has different input and output types. For example, `string.numeric.parse` accepts a `string` and returns a `number`.

By default, `declare` compares your definition to the declared type as a whole, so a morph only matches if the declared type includes it. To compare only the input or output, pass `{ side: "in" }` or `{ side: "out" }`:

```ts
type Expected = { a: number; b?: number }

const Bad = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string.numeric.parse",
	// TypeScript: declared: number; inferred: (In: string) => To<number>;
	"b?": "number"
})

// the output must match Expected
const T = type.declare<Expected, { side: "out" }>().type({
	a: "string.numeric.parse",
	"b?": "number"
})
```

# Validation

> Check data against a Type by calling it, asserting it or testing it with allows.

## Calling a Type

A Type is a function. Call it with any data and it returns either the validated output or `ArkErrors`:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "number.integer >= 0"
})

const out = User({ name: "Alan", age: 41.5 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// age must be an integer (was 41.5)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// out is { name: string; age: number }
	console.log(out.name)
}
```

`type.errors` is the `ArkErrors` class, so `instanceof` narrows the result. Invalid data never throws unless you configure [`onFail`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#onfail). See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for what `ArkErrors` contains.

The output is the data after [morphs](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/morphs-and-more) and defaults have run, so it can differ from the input:

```ts
const Form = type({ age: "string.numeric.parse" })

// { age: 41 }
Form({ age: "41" })

// ArkErrors: age must be a well-formed numeric string (was "forty")
Form({ age: "forty" })
```

## assert

`.assert` returns the output or throws a [`TraversalError`](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#traversalerror), for when invalid data is a bug rather than something to handle:

```ts
const Form = type({ age: "string.numeric.parse" })

// { age: 41 }
const form = Form.assert({ age: "41" })

// TraversalError: age must be a well-formed numeric string (was "forty")
Form.assert({ age: "forty" })
```

## from

`.from` is `.assert` with its argument typed as the Type's input, so TypeScript checks data you write by hand:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

// { name: "David", age: 34 }
const david = User.from({ name: "David", age: 34 })

// TypeScript: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'
const typo = User.from({ name: "David", age: "34" })
```

## allows

`.allows` returns a boolean and narrows its argument, without building errors or running morphs:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

const data: unknown = { name: "David", age: 34 }

if (User.allows(data)) {
	// data is { name: string; age: number }
	console.log(data.name)
}

const Numeric = type("number | bigint")

// [0, 2n]
const numerics = [0, "one", 2n].filter(Numeric.allows)
```

On a Type with a morph, `.allows` checks only the input, so data can be allowed and still fail when the Type is called:

```ts
const AtLeast6 = type("string.numeric.parse").to("number >= 6")

// true, since "3" is a numeric string
AtLeast6.allows("3")

// ArkErrors: must be at least 6 (was 3)
AtLeast6("3")
```

## Standard Schema

Every Type implements [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), so libraries that accept one can validate with it through `~standard.validate`. ArkType validates synchronously, and a failure result is the `ArkErrors` itself, whose `issues` is an array of `ArkError`:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

const result = await User["~standard"].validate({ name: "David", age: "34" })

if (result.issues) {
	// age must be a number (was a string)
	console.log(result.issues[0].message)
} else {
	// { name: string; age: number }
	console.log(result.value)
}
```

## Custom checks

To add your own check, use [`.narrow`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow). To transform data, use [`.pipe`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe). Both receive a [`ctx`](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api) for reporting errors.

# Errors

> Read, serialize and throw the errors a Type returns for invalid data.

## ArkErrors

A Type called with invalid data returns `ArkErrors`, which holds one error for each path that failed:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "number >= 0"
})

const out = User({ name: 5, age: -1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// age must be non-negative (was -1)
	// name must be a string (was a number)
	console.error(out.summary)

	// ["age must be non-negative (was -1)",
	//  "name must be a string (was a number)"]
	out.issues.map(error => error.message)

	// { age: ["must be non-negative (was -1)"],
	//   name: ["must be a string (was a number)"] }
	flatProblemsByPath(out)
}
```

`ArkErrors` isn't an array. Its errors are in `issues`, so index them, iterate them or call array methods there.

| member | what it is |
| - | - |
| `issues` | an array with one error per path, in the order each path first failed |
| `summary`, `toString()` | every error's message, one per line |
| `count` | how many errors were added, more than `issues.length` when several failed at one path |
| `toJSON()` | an array of each error's JSON, with its `propString` |
| `toLocaleString(locale?)` | the summary in a [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#rendering-in-a-locale) |
| `throw()` | throws a [`TraversalError`](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#traversalerror) |

`arktype` exports functions that read an `ArkErrors`, most grouping it by path:

| function | what it returns |
| - | - |
| `firstIssue(out)` | the first error in `issues`, found [without the rest](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#finding-only-the-first) where it can be |
| `byPath(out)` | an object mapping each path's `propString` to its error |
| `flatByPath(out)` | like `byPath`, but each value is an array, with an `intersection` split into its errors |
| `flatProblemsByPath(out)` | like `flatByPath`, but with each error's `problem` |
| `byAncestorPath(out)` | each failed path and its ancestors, with `""` for the root, mapped to every error at or below it |
| `messageIn(error, locale)` | one error's message in a [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#rendering-in-a-locale) |

A Type that calls no narrow or morph may find its errors' issues only when they're first read, so rejecting data costs little more than the check that rejected it. The issues describe the data as it is at that read, not as it was validated: a write to it in between can change them, and data that no longer fails holds one root issue, `is invalid`. Read `summary` or `issues` before the data you validated can change, as it can when it's reactive form state or an Immer draft, or when an `await` comes before you report the errors:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string" })
const form: Record<string, unknown> = { name: 5 }

const out = User(form)
// read now: name must be a string (was a number)
const summary = out instanceof type.errors ? out.summary : ""

form.name = "Ada"
// read only now, out.summary would be "is invalid"
```

A getter or `Proxy` trap the check reads runs again at that read, and what it throws is thrown there. Each error's text is written at that first read too.

### Finding only the first

Where a form shows one error at a time, read it with `firstIssue`. Errors that haven't found their issues yet, like those of a Type that calls no narrow or morph or of a [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) validator, find only that one, reading the data until it fails, so the rest cost nothing until `issues` or `summary` is read:

```ts
import { firstIssue, type } from "arktype"

const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number >= 0" })

const out = User({ name: 5, age: -1 })

// age must be non-negative (was -1)
if (out instanceof type.errors) console.error(firstIssue(out).message)
```

It's the error `issues[0]` holds. Unlike [`errors: "first"`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#errors), it leaves the rest to be found, and it's the first a full validation finds, not whichever is cheapest.

## ArkError

Each error in `issues` is a plain object, typed as `ArkError`, describing what failed at one path:

```ts
const out = type({ age: "number >= 0" })({ age: -1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	const error = out.issues[0]

	error.code // "min"
	error.path // ["age"]
	error.propString // "age"
	error.data // -1
	error.expected // "non-negative"
	error.actual // "-1"
	error.problem // "must be non-negative (was -1)"
	error.message // "age must be non-negative (was -1)"

	// narrow by code to read its own fields
	if (error.code === "min") error.rule // 0
}
```

Its message is built from parts: `message` puts the path before `problem`, which reads "must be `expected` (was `actual`)". You can [configure each part](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#error-messages).

An error also has `meta`, the metadata of the Type that failed, and usually a `description`. It has no methods, so `JSON.stringify(error)` serializes its own keys, and `messageIn(error, locale)` writes its message in another locale.

When several checks fail at one path, they are merged into one error with the code `intersection`. `flatByPath` splits it back up:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type } from "arktype"

const out = type({ n: "number % 2 >= 2" })({ n: 1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// n (1) must be...
	//   ◦ even
	//   ◦ at least 2
	console.error(out.summary)

	// { n: ["must be even (was 1)", "must be at least 2 (was 1)"] }
	flatProblemsByPath(out)
}
```

## Error codes

An error's `code` tells you its other fields:

| code | fields |
| - | - |
| `domain` | `domain`, like `"string"` |
| `unit` | `unit`, the expected value |
| `proto` | `proto`, the expected constructor |
| `min`, `max` | `rule`, and `exclusive` when the bound is exclusive |
| `minLength`, `maxLength`, `exactLength` | `rule` |
| `divisor` | `rule` |
| `pattern` | `rule` (the regex source) and `flags` |
| `before`, `after` | `rule`, a `Date` |
| `notEqual` | `rule`, a number or `Date` |
| `notEqualLength` | `rule` |
| `predicate` | `predicate` when a narrow returns `false`; `morph` and what it threw as `cause` for `pipe.try`; `meta.keyword` and sometimes `cause` for a keyword's parse |
| `required` | `missing`, the missing value's type; `valueMeta`, its meta; and `missingValueDescription`, its English description |
| `undeclared` | none; its `data` is the value of a key `"+": "reject"` disallows |
| `discriminant` | `discriminantKind`, `cases`, `onKey` and `absent` |
| `union` | `errors`, one per branch |
| `intersection` | `errors`, one per check that failed at the path |

Each also has `data` and `path`, and `meta` unless `ctx` or `pipe.try` raised it. Built-in keywords with their own text, like `string.email`, set `meta.keyword` to their name.

`discriminant` is a miss of a union ArkType checks by switching on a domain or a literal value: branches with different domains, like `number | null`, two or more literals, like `boolean` or `"a" | "b"`, or objects with a discriminant key. Its `data` is the discriminant's value, and `cases` lists the values or domains it expected, with `"Array"` in place of `"object"` where every object it expected is an array:

```ts
const Shape = type({ kind: "'circle'", r: "number" }).or({
	kind: "'square'",
	side: "number"
})

const out = Shape({ kind: "triangle" })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	const error = out.issues[0]

	// kind must be "circle" or "square" (was "triangle")
	error.message

	// ["circle", "square"]
	if (error.code === "discriminant") error.cases
}
```

A union reports `union` instead where its discriminant can't tell the branches apart: an undiscriminated union; data that can't hold the discriminant, like `5` for a union of objects; and data matching none of the discriminant's values when some branches don't have its key, whose `errors` hold the miss beside those branches' errors.

## TraversalError

`.assert`, `.from` and `ArkErrors`' `throw()` throw a `TraversalError`, which extends `Error`. A single error's message is its summary. Several are listed on their own lines after a leading newline:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type, TraversalError } from "arktype"

try {
	type({ a: "string", b: "number" }).assert({ a: 1, b: "x" })
} catch (e) {
	if (e instanceof TraversalError) {
		// "\n  • a must be a string (was a number)\n  • b must be a number (was a string)"
		e.message

		// the ArkErrors, for structured access
		flatProblemsByPath(e.arkErrors)
	}
}
```

`arkErrors` is non-enumerable, so loggers that print an error's own properties skip it.

## ParseError

A `ParseError` is thrown when a definition is invalid, as the Type is created rather than when it validates. TypeScript reports the same mistakes in your editor, so you'll usually see one only for definitions TypeScript can't check, like strings built at runtime:

```ts
import { ParseError, type } from "arktype"

const def: string = "string | numbr"

try {
	type.raw(def)
} catch (e) {
	// ParseError: 'numbr' is unresolvable
	if (e instanceof ParseError) console.error(e.message)
}
```

# Traversal API

> The ctx argument that narrow and pipe functions receive for reading the current path and reporting errors.

Functions you pass to [`.narrow`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) and [`.pipe`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe) receive a `ctx` as their second argument. Use it to report errors that read like ArkType's own:

```ts
const Even = type("number").narrow(
	(n, ctx) => n % 2 === 0 || ctx.mustBe("even")
)

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
Even(3)
```

A narrow returns `ctx.mustBe(...)` or `ctx.reject(...)`, which add an error and return `false`. A morph returns `ctx.error(...)`, which adds an error and returns it:

```ts
const Json = type("string").pipe((s, ctx) => {
	try {
		return JSON.parse(s)
	} catch {
		return ctx.error("valid JSON")
	}
})

// ArkErrors: must be valid JSON (was "{")
Json("{")
```

`reject` and `error` take a string or the parts of an error. `relativePath` reports it below the current path:

```ts
const Range = type({ start: "number", end: "number" }).narrow(
	(range, ctx) =>
		range.start <= range.end ||
		ctx.reject({
			expected: "at least start",
			actual: `${range.end}`,
			relativePath: ["end"]
		})
)

// ArkErrors: end must be at least start (was 1)
Range({ start: 2, end: 1 })
```

To write a check outside the call, type `ctx` with `Traversal`:

```ts
import { type, type Traversal } from "arktype"

const isEven = (n: number, ctx: Traversal) => n % 2 === 0 || ctx.mustBe("even")

const Even = type("number").narrow(isEven)
```

## Members

### `path`

the path being validated or morphed

- array indices represented as numbers
- warning: mutated during traversal - use `path.slice(0)` to snapshot
- use [`propString`](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api#propstring) for a stringified version

### `root`

the original value being traversed

### `config`

configuration for this traversal

- options can affect traversal results and error messages
- defaults < global config < scope config
- does not include options configured on individual types

### `hasError`

whether `currentBranch` (or the traversal root, outside a union) has one or more errors

### `errors`

[ArkErrors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) that will be part of this traversal's finalized result

- will always be empty for a valid traversal

### `data`

the data being validated or morphed

- the value at [`path`](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api#path), as transformed by any morphs that have already run

### `propString`

a string representing [`path`](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api#path)

- uses `.access` [where allowed by JS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Property_accessors#dot_notation), falling back to `[indexAccess]`

```ts
const path = ["key1", Symbol("key2"), "key3", 4, "~key5"]
const propString = 'key1[Symbol(key2)].key3[4]["~key5"]'
```

### `reject`

add an [ArkError](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) and return `false`

- useful for predicates like `.narrow`

### `mustBe`

add an [ArkError](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) from a description and return `false`

- useful for predicates like `.narrow`
- equivalent to [`reject`](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api#reject)({ expected })

### `error`

add and return an [ArkError](https://arktype.io/docs/errors)

- useful for morphs like `.pipe`

# Configuration

> Change ArkType's defaults and error messages globally, for a scope or for a single Type.

## Levels

Config can be set at three levels. A more specific level overrides a broader one.

### Global

Call `configure` in its own file, and import that file before anything creates a Type:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ numberAllowsNaN: true })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// true
type.number.allows(Number.NaN)
```

> **Configure before any Type is created**
>
> Global config is fixed when the first Type is created, whether by a definition
> or by referencing a keyword like `type.number`, and calling `configure` after
> that throws unless it changes nothing, as when a test runner resets its
> modules and the config file runs again. Importing `"arktype"` first is fine,
> and `configure` can be imported from either `"arktype"` or `"arktype/config"`.

### Scope

Pass config as the second argument to `scope` or `type.module`. It applies to every Type parsed in that scope:

```ts
const $ = scope(
	{ User: { age: "number < 100" } },
	{ max: { actual: () => "unacceptably large" } }
)

// ArkErrors: age must be less than 100 (was unacceptably large)
$.export().User({ age: 101 })

// ArkErrors: age must be at most 100 (was unacceptably large)
$.type({ age: "number <= 100" })({ age: 101 })
```

### Type

`.configure` adds [metadata](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#meta), like a `description` or [error parts](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#error-messages), to a Type. It applies wherever that Type is referenced, but not to the Types inside it:

```ts
// don't print the password
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({ actual: "" })

const User = type({
	email: "string.email",
	password: Password
})

// ArkErrors: password must be at least length 8
User({ email: "david@arktype.io", password: "ez123" })
```

## Options

| option | default | levels |
| - | - | - |
| [`onUndeclaredKey`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#onundeclaredkey) | `"ignore"` | global, type (`"+"`) |
| [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#exactoptionalpropertytypes) | `true` | global, scope |
| [`numberAllowsNaN`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#numberallowsnan) | `false` | global |
| [`numberAllowsInfinity`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#numberallowsinfinity) | `false` | global |
| [`dateAllowsInvalid`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#dateallowsinvalid) | `false` | global |
| [`jitless`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#jitless) | `false`, or `true` where `new Function` is blocked | global, scope |
| [`onFail`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#onfail) | `null`, which returns `ArkErrors` | global, scope |
| [`errors`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#errors) | `"all"` | global, scope |
| [`mutatesInput`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#mutatesinput) | `false` | global, scope |
| [`keywords`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#keywords) | `{}` | global |
| [`locale`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#locale) | `en` | global |
| [an error code](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#by-code), like `divisor` | ArkType's messages | global, scope |
| [`toJsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#tojsonschema) | draft 2020-12, throwing for what it can't express | global, scope |

A Type's own options are its [metadata](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#meta), including the [parts of its errors](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#error-messages).

## Error messages

Each error message is built from parts. Configure the part you want to change, and ArkType keeps composing the rest, including messages for unions and intersections. `expected`, `actual`, `problem` and `message` each take a string or a function. See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for what an error contains.

### description

What follows "must be" in a message. Other parts and the Type's `.description` reuse it, so it should be your first choice:

```ts
const Even = type("number % 2").describe("an even number")

// ArkErrors: must be an even number (was 3)
Even(3)
```

### expected

Like `description`, but only for error messages, where it takes precedence. A function receives the error, so it can read `code`, `data` and `path`:

```ts
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({
	expected: ctx =>
		ctx.code === "minLength" ? `${ctx.rule} characters or more` : "a password"
})

// ArkErrors: must be 8 characters or more (was 5)
Password("ez123")

// ArkErrors: must be a password (was a number)
Password(12345678)
```

### actual

What goes inside "(was …)". An empty string omits it. A function receives the data, then the error:

```ts
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({ actual: "" })

// ArkErrors: must be at least length 8
Password("ez123")
```

### problem

The whole sentence after the path, like "must be a string (was a number)". A function receives the error, including its `expected` and `actual`. It may not apply to the errors of a union:

```ts
const Name = type("string").configure({
	problem: ctx => `${ctx.actual} isn't ${ctx.expected}`
})

// ArkErrors: a number isn't a string
Name(5)
```

### message

The whole message, including the path. A function receives the error, including its `problem`. It may not apply to the errors of a union:

```ts
const User = type({
	password: "string >= 8"
}).configure({
	message: ctx => `${ctx.propString || "(root)"}: ${ctx.problem}`
})

// ArkErrors: (root): must be an object (was a string)
User("ez123")

// .configure applies only at the root, so the nested error is unchanged
// ArkErrors: password must be at least length 8 (was 5)
User({ password: "ez123" })
```

Each function also receives the active [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#your-own-messages) as its last argument, so it can write its text in the language a message is read in.

### By code

Globally or in a scope, configure errors by their [code](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#error-codes). A function's `ctx` is typed by its code:

```ts
const mod = type.module(
	{ isEven: "number % 2" },
	{
		divisor: {
			expected: ctx => `% ${ctx.rule} !== 0`,
			problem: ctx => `${ctx.actual} ${ctx.expected}`
		}
	}
)

// ArkErrors: 3 % 2 !== 0
mod.isEven(3)
```

A key that `"+": "reject"` disallows has the code `undeclared`:

```ts
const $ = scope(
	{ User: { "+": "reject", name: "string" } },
	{ undeclared: { problem: "isn't allowed" } }
)

// ArkErrors: age isn't allowed
$.export().User({ name: "Alice", age: 42 })
```

Each kind of constraint, like `domain` or `divisor`, also takes a `description` function. It receives the constraint and changes how it is described everywhere, not only in errors.

## locale

Error messages are written in English by default. Configure a locale to write them in another language:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

configure({ locale: de })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// ArkErrors: muss eine Zeichenkette sein, ist aber eine Zahl
type.string(5)
```

`locale` can also be a function that returns a locale each time a message is read. See [i18n](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n).

## keywords

Configure built-in keywords like `string.email` by name. Each takes a description or the same options as [`.configure`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#type):

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({
	keywords: {
		string: "text",
		"string.email": {
			actual: () => "definitely fake"
		}
	}
})
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	email: "string.email"
})

// ArkErrors: email must be an email address (was definitely fake)
//            name must be text (was a number)
User({ name: 5, email: "449 Canal St" })
```

## onUndeclaredKey

Like TypeScript, ArkType ignores keys an object doesn't declare by default. There are three behaviors:

- `"ignore"` (default): allow undeclared keys and keep them in the output
- `"delete"`: allow undeclared keys and output only declared ones
- `"reject"`: fail on undeclared string keys

An undeclared symbol key passes `"reject"` and isn't in `"delete"`'s output.

Set it for one object with [`"+"`](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-undeclared), or change the default globally:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ onUndeclaredKey: "delete" })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

const UserForm = type({
	name: "string"
})

// { name: "Alice" }
UserForm({ name: "Alice", age: "42" })
```

## exactOptionalPropertyTypes

By default, ArkType treats optional keys as TypeScript does with [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#exactOptionalPropertyTypes): an optional key can be omitted, but not set to `undefined`.

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	"key?": "number"
})

// {}
MyObj({})

// ArkErrors: key must be a number (was undefined)
MyObj({ key: undefined })
```

Add `| undefined` to keys that should accept it. If your tsconfig doesn't enable `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, you can set ArkType's to `false` to match:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ exactOptionalPropertyTypes: false })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

const MyObj = type({
	"key?": "number",
	withDefault: "number = 5"
})

// { key: undefined, withDefault: 5 }
MyObj({ key: undefined, withDefault: undefined })
```

With `false`, an explicit `undefined` at a key with a default is replaced by the default, as a missing key is. Treating `null` as missing is tracked in [#1283](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/1283).

## numberAllowsNaN

`number` rejects `NaN` by default. Allow it everywhere with `numberAllowsNaN: true`, or in one Type with the `number.NaN` keyword:

```ts
const MaybeNaN = type("number | number.NaN")

// NaN
MaybeNaN(Number.NaN)
```

## numberAllowsInfinity

`number` rejects `Infinity` and `-Infinity` by default. Allow them everywhere with `numberAllowsInfinity: true`, or in one Type with the `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` keywords:

```ts
const Limit = type("number | number.Infinity")

// ArkErrors: must be a number (was Infinity)
type.number(Infinity)

// Infinity
Limit(Infinity)
```

## dateAllowsInvalid

`Date` rejects an invalid date, like `new Date("x")`, by default. Allow it with `dateAllowsInvalid: true`:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ dateAllowsInvalid: true })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// Invalid Date
type("Date")(new Date("x"))
```

## jitless

ArkType compiles each Type to optimized validation code using `new Function`. Where that's blocked, like Cloudflare Workers, it validates without compiling instead. To turn compiling off yourself, set `jitless: true`:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ jitless: true })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// will not be compiled
const MyObject = type({
	foo: "string"
})
```

Configuring `jitless` globally also skips the check for `new Function`, which a strict Content-Security-Policy would report as a violation. To validate without generating code and without shipping the parser, [precompile](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) your Types when you build.

## errors

By default, a failed validation returns an error for each check that failed. `errors` can return less:

- `"all"` (default): every error, at each path that failed
- `"first"`: the first error validation finds, where it stops
- `"none"`: one error at the root, whose message is `is invalid`

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import "arktype/errors"

configure({ errors: "none" })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

// ArkErrors: is invalid
const out = User({ name: 5, age: "5" })
```

`"first"` and `"none"` are installed by `import "arktype/errors"`, so a program choosing neither ships neither. Without it, creating a Type configured with either throws.

With `"first"`, which of the data's errors is returned isn't promised, and can differ between a Type and its precompiled validator.

With `"none"`, a failure returns one error with the code `"predicate"`, an empty path and the data. It's still an instance of `type.errors`, `.assert()` throws a `TraversalError` saying `is invalid`, and its message isn't [localized](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#locale). A narrow or morph that reads `ctx.errors` while validating sees each issue added so far written the same way, as `is invalid` at its own path.

`errors` can also be set per Scope. It applies to that Scope's Types, including where another Scope references them.

A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors) build takes `errors` as an option.

## mutatesInput

By default, a transform copies each object it changes other than a builtin like a `Date`, so the data you pass is otherwise never written. `mutatesInput` writes what a Type transforms, its defaults and its morphed values, into the data, which it returns:

- `false` (default): copies each object it changes
- `true`: writes in place where no other part of the Type can read the write, and otherwise copies
- `"always"`: writes every transform in place

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import "arktype/mutatesInput"

configure({ mutatesInput: true })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({ name: "string.trim", role: "string = 'member'" })

const data = { name: " Ada " }

// true, and data is now { name: "Ada", role: "member" }
const isData = Object.is(User(data), data)
```

`true` and `"always"` are installed by `import "arktype/mutatesInput"`, so a program choosing neither ships neither. Without it, creating a Type configured with either throws.

`true` always returns what copying would. `"always"` requires that the data hold no object at two places a transform reaches, and that a Type's functions read or return the data's objects only through the value each is passed, not `ctx.root`.

The object returned is the data, so it keeps its key order, accessors and inherited keys. Where the data holds one object at two places, a key the Type doesn't declare can hold what the other place wrote. An object a Type deletes undeclared keys from is still copied. A failed validation can leave writes in the objects of its data it found valid.

`mutatesInput` can also be set for a Scope, whose Types then transform as it says.

A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#mutatesinput) build takes `mutatesInput` as an option.

## onFail

To throw on every failed validation, or transform its result some other way, configure `onFail`. Declare its return type on `ArkEnv` so calls are typed to match:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

const config = configure({
	onFail: errors => errors.throw()
})

declare global {
	interface ArkEnv {
		onFail: typeof config.onFail
	}
}
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// string, since a failure throws instead of returning ArkErrors
const data = type.string("foo")

// TraversalError: must be a string (was a number)
type.string(5)
```

`onFail` can also be passed to a scope.

## toJsonSchema

`toJsonSchema` sets the defaults for `.toJsonSchema()`, like its target and how to handle what JSON Schema can't express. See [JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema).

## metadata

Add your own keys to the metadata Types accept by extending `ArkEnv`:

```ts
// add this anywhere in your project
declare global {
	interface ArkEnv {
		meta(): {
			// meta properties should always be optional
			secretIngredient?: string
		}
	}
}

// now types you define can specify and access your metadata
const MrPingsSecretIngredientSoup = type({
	broth: "'miso' | 'vegetable'",
	ingredients: "string[]"
}).configure({ secretIngredient: "nothing!" })
```

## prototypes

When you `.infer` a Type, ArkType walks its inferred type to extract special values like morphs, e.g. `(In: string) => Out<number>`. For some classes that walk is slow or expands the type. Declare them in `prototypes` to have them treated as opaque:

```ts
declare global {
	interface ArkEnv {
		prototypes(): MySpecialClass
	}
}

class MySpecialClass {}

// Type<MySpecialClass>
const T = type.instanceOf(MySpecialClass)
```

# i18n

> Write ArkType's error messages in another language, per app or per request.

ArkType's error messages can be written in any language. A locale supplies their text, and ArkType ships two: `en`, the default, and `de`.

## Configuring a locale

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

configure({ locale: de })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
// import your config file before arktype
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string >= 2",
	email: "string.email"
})

const out = User({ name: "A", email: "x" })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// email muss eine E-Mail-Adresse sein, ist aber "x"
	// name muss mindestens 2 Zeichen lang sein, ist aber 1 Zeichen lang
	console.log(out.summary)
}
```

Like other [global config](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#global), a locale is configured before any Type is created. It can't be set for a scope or a Type. To choose one per request, configure a [function](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#switching-locales).

Shipped locales like `arktype/locales/de` work when imported. A locale you write, or a locale function, also needs `import "arktype/i18n"` unless a shipped locale is imported. Without it, creating a Type, `toLocaleString` or `messageIn` with that locale throws. This keeps other locales out of bundles that only use `en`.

Only an error's message and its parts, `expected`, `actual` and `problem`, are localized. A Type's `description` and `expression`, JSON Schema, an error's `description` and `ParseError`s stay in English.

## Labels

A locale may name a value by its `title`. `en` ignores titles, while `de` makes them the subject of the sentence:

```ts
const Signup = type({
	name: type("string >= 2").configure({ title: "Name" })
})

// with de: „Name“ muss mindestens 2 Zeichen lang sein, ist aber 1 Zeichen lang
const out = Signup({ name: "A" })
```

## Switching locales

`locale` can also be a function, called when an `ArkErrors`' messages are first read rather than when validation fails, so errors follow your app's language even if it changed after they were created:

```ts
import type { Locale } from "arktype"
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"
import { en } from "arktype/locales/en"

const locales: Record<string, Locale> = { de, en }

let language = "en"

export const setLanguage = (next: string) => {
	language = next
}

configure({ locale: () => locales[language] })
```

On a server, the function can read the locale of the current request:

```ts
import type { Locale } from "arktype"
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import "arktype/i18n"
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from "node:async_hooks"

export const requestLocale = new AsyncLocalStorage<Locale>()

configure({ locale: () => requestLocale.getStore() })
```

```ts
import { requestLocale } from "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

const User = type({ name: "string" })

const handle = (body: unknown) =>
	requestLocale.run(de, () => {
		const out = User(body)
		// name muss eine Zeichenkette sein, ist aber eine Zahl
		if (out instanceof type.errors) return { status: 400, error: out.summary }
		return { status: 200, user: out }
	})
```

The function is called once for an `ArkErrors`, whose messages keep the locale it returned, so they never mix languages. If it returns `undefined` or throws, they're written in English.

Since messages are written when they're first read, read `summary` or `issues` inside the request. Errors returned from `requestLocale.run` and read later, like by a framework's error handler, are written in English. There, call [`toLocaleString`](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#rendering-in-a-locale) instead.

## Rendering in a locale

An `ArkErrors`' `toLocaleString` writes its summary in a locale of your choice, whatever locale is configured, and `messageIn` writes one error's message:

```ts
import { messageIn, type } from "arktype"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

const out = type({ name: "string" })({ name: 5 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// name muss eine Zeichenkette sein, ist aber eine Zahl
	out.toLocaleString(de)
	messageIn(out.issues[0], de)
	// name must be a string (was a number)
	out.issues[0].message
}
```

Called without a locale, `toLocaleString` returns the summary as configured.

## Your own messages

Any message you configure outranks the locale, which only writes what you leave out. That includes `.describe()`, `.configure()`, descriptions configured for [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#keywords) and [errors configured by code](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#by-code) in a scope or globally.

A string is shown as written in every locale. Since it may be in any language, `de` cites it rather than placing it bare in a German sentence:

```ts
const Password = type("string >= 8").describe("a secure password")

// with de: muss ein Wert gemäß der Beschreibung „a secure password“ sein, ist aber 2 Zeichen lang
const out = Password("ez")
```

If your descriptions are already German, `{ ...de, cite: text => text }` places them as written. To translate them, look each one up in `cite`, returning what follows the locale's "must be", as `de.cite` does:

```ts
import type { Locale } from "arktype"
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

const translations: Record<string, string> = {
	"a secure password": "ein sicheres Passwort"
}

const deTranslated = {
	...de,
	cite: text => translations[text] ?? de.cite(text)
} satisfies Locale.Complete

// Password("ez"): muss ein sicheres Passwort sein, ist aber 2 Zeichen lang
configure({ locale: deTranslated })
```

You can also translate your own text by writing it as a function. Every error writer you configure receives the active locale's `tag`, `list`, `plural`, `number`, `date` and `verbatim` as its last argument:

```ts
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({
	expected: (ctx, locale) =>
		locale.tag === "de" ? "ein sicheres Passwort" : "a secure password"
})

// with de: muss ein sicheres Passwort sein, ist aber 2 Zeichen lang
const out = Password("ez")
```

A writer's text isn't cited, so it should read as what follows the locale's "must be", like `de`'s `muss … sein`. The writer can also call an [i18n library](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#using-an-i18n-library).

## Changing part of a locale

A locale is an object, so you can spread it and replace what you'd like to change:

```ts
import type { Locale } from "arktype"
import { configure } from "arktype/config"
import { de } from "arktype/locales/de"

const deCompact = {
	...de,
	minLength: {
		...de.minLength,
		problem: ctx => `ist zu kurz (mindestens ${ctx.rule})`
	}
} satisfies Locale.Complete

configure({ locale: deCompact })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
// import your config file before arktype
import { type } from "arktype"

// ArkErrors: ist zu kurz (mindestens 3)
const out = type("string >= 3")("ab")
```

Spreading `de.minLength` keeps its `expected`, the fragment that unions and intersections list, like `mindestens 3 Zeichen lang`.

## Writing a locale

For a language ArkType doesn't ship, start from `en` and replace each part:

| part | writes |
| - | - |
| `tag` | the locale's BCP 47 language tag |
| `list` | a list of items joined by "or" or "and" |
| `plural` | the plural category of a number, like `"one"` or `"other"` |
| `number`, `date` | a number or a `Date` |
| `verbatim` | text shown as written, like paths and printed values |
| `cite` | expected text you wrote yourself, like a description |
| `nouns` | the name of each type, like "a string" |
| `basis` | one alternative of a missing key's value |
| `keywordPhrases` | the expected text of each keyword, like `"string.email"`, keyed by its name |
| `actual`, `message` | each part of a message, for every code that doesn't write it |
| `problem` | the sentence for a keyword's phrase or for expected text you wrote |
| `domain`, `min`, `required`, ... | one entry per [error code](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#error-codes) with its `problem` and optionally its `expected`, `actual` or `message` |

Each code's `problem` is a whole sentence without a subject, and `message` places the path or label before it. A code's `expected` is a fragment that unions and intersections list. A fragment reads as what follows the locale's "must be", like `fr`'s `doit être`:

```ts
import type { Locale } from "arktype"
import { listPattern } from "arktype/i18n"
import { en } from "arktype/locales/en"

const was = (actual: string) => actual && ` (reçu ${actual})`

const atLeast: Locale.ExpectedWriter<"min"> = (ctx, locale) =>
	`${ctx.exclusive ? "supérieur à" : "au moins"} ${locale.number(ctx.rule)}`

export const fr: Locale = {
	...en,
	tag: "fr",
	list: listPattern(
		{ two: " ou ", middle: ", ", end: " ou " },
		{ two: " et ", middle: ", ", end: " et " }
	),
	cite: text => `une valeur conforme à la description « ${text} »`,
	// for keyword phrases and text you wrote
	problem: ctx => `doit être ${ctx.expected}${was(ctx.actual)}`,
	// every subject is masculine, so "supérieur" agrees with it
	message: ctx =>
		ctx.path.length ? `le champ ${ctx.propString} ${ctx.problem}` : ctx.problem,
	min: {
		expected: atLeast,
		problem: (ctx, locale) =>
			`doit être ${atLeast(ctx, locale)}${was(ctx.actual)}`
	}
	// ...
}
```

- Until you replace them, the parts you spread from `en` write English. Most of its writers don't read `nouns`, `list` or `date`: only its `discriminant`, `required` and `union` writers and `basis` read `nouns`, and `required` and `union` also read `list`.
- Where a locale has no `expected` for a code, an error's `expected`, and so its `toJSON()`, is English. If your unions list their branches' fragments, annotate the locale with `Locale.Complete` to check that it has a fragment for every code and a phrase for every keyword. A locale without fragments can write its unions from `ctx.errors`, each with its own `problem`.
- A locale's writers receive the error and the locale. An error's `description` is English, so `expected` writers can't use it.
- `arktype/i18n` exports the helpers `de` is written with: `listPattern`, `isolate`, `groupByPath` (a union's errors by path), `labelOf` (the title of the value an error is about), `describeMissing`, `describeCause` and `writeKeywordExpected`.

Languages unlike English need a few more rules:

- `problem` has no subject, so where a predicate agrees with its subject, as in Russian, Polish or Arabic, `message` should give every subject one gender and number, like ru `Поле`/`Значение`, pl `Pole` or ar `الحقل`/`العنصر`. Particles go there too, like ja `nameは`.
- `cite`, `nouns`, `basis`, keyword phrases and fragments all read as what follows "must be", so they take its case, like the instrumental `строкой` after ru `должно быть`. Where an actual takes another case, like the nominative after ru `получено:`, write `actual` with its own forms.
- A title reaches `message` as written. Translate it there, in the form a subject takes.
- A right-to-left locale sets `verbatim: isolate`, so each path, value and name keeps its direction, in lists too.

## Using an i18n library

ArkType doesn't depend on an i18n library, but a locale's writers can call one, so you can keep ArkType's sentences in your own catalog under your own keys:

```ts
import type { Locale } from "arktype"
import { listPattern } from "arktype/i18n"
import { en } from "arktype/locales/en"
import i18next from "i18next"
import * as m from "./paraglide/messages.js"

// a namespace for ArkType's keys; escapeValue false, since messages aren't HTML
const t = (key: string, params?: object) =>
	i18next.t(key, {
		ns: "validation",
		lng: "fr",
		interpolation: { escapeValue: false },
		...params
	})

// a sentence, then the actual unless it's been suppressed
const was = (problem: string, actual: string) =>
	actual ? t("was", { problem, actual }) : problem

export const fr: Locale = {
	...en,
	tag: "fr",
	list: listPattern(
		{ two: " ou ", middle: ", ", end: " ou " },
		{ two: " et ", middle: ", ", end: " et " }
	),
	problem: ctx => was(t("mustBe", { expected: ctx.expected }), ctx.actual),
	min: {
		...en.min,
		// through locale.number, the rule is printed like the actual
		problem: (ctx, locale) =>
			was(
				t(ctx.exclusive ? "moreThan" : "min", {
					rule: locale.number(ctx.rule)
				}),
				ctx.actual
			)
	},
	// Paraglide: each message is a typed function
	required: { ...en.required, problem: () => m.required({}, { locale: "fr" }) }
}
```

With `"min": "doit être au moins {{rule}}"`, `"moreThan": "doit être supérieur à {{rule}}"` and `"was": "{{problem}} (reçu {{actual}})"` in the `validation` namespace, `type({ n: "number >= 2.5" })` reads `n doit être au moins 2.5 (reçu 1.5)` for `{ n: 1.5 }` and `n est requis` for `{}`.

- Build one locale per language and [choose one per read](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#switching-locales) with `configure({ locale: () => ... })`.
- If your library types its keys, cast ArkType's (`as never`).
- Pass numbers through `locale.number`, so a rule is printed like the actual it is compared with.
- A key your catalog lacks renders whatever the library returns for it, which for i18next is the key itself, so keep the catalog complete.

## Error codes

Writers can narrow their `ctx` by its `code`, which tells them its other fields. See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#error-codes) for every code and its fields.

# Standard Schema

> Pass a Type to any library that accepts a Standard Schema, and use other validators inside an ArkType definition.

[Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) is a small interface for TypeScript validators, written by the authors of ArkType, Zod and Valibot. A library that accepts a Standard Schema works with every validator that implements it, so it doesn't need an adapter for each one.

Every Type implements Standard Schema and its JSON Schema extension, [Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema). Wherever a library asks for either, pass the Type itself. [Integrations](https://arktype.io/docs/integrations) shows the common ones.

[Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) validators implement Standard Schema too, and Standard JSON Schema where their build's [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option sets `~standard.jsonSchema`.

## Validation

A library validates through `T["~standard"].validate`. On success, the result's `value` is the Type's output, so morphs have already run:

```ts
const Form = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "string.integer.parse"
})

Form["~standard"].validate({ name: "Ada", age: "36" })
// { value: { name: "Ada", age: 36 } }
```

On failure, the result is `{ issues }`, one for each error in the [`ArkErrors`](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) you get from calling the Type. A library printing Standard Schema issues writes each issue's `path` before its `message`, so an issue at a path is a copy of its error whose message leaves the path out:

```ts
const result = Form["~standard"].validate({ name: "Ada", age: "old" })
// { issues: [{ path: ["age"], message: 'must be a well-formed integer string (was "old")', ... }] }
```

A union's message lists each branch's path from the union's, like `b must be a string (was missing) or c must be a number (was missing)`. The issues are written as `validate` returns, so unlike an `ArkErrors` read later, they describe the data as it was validated.

ArkType always validates synchronously. The spec allows a `Promise`, which is why the return type includes one.

The spec's type helpers map to a Type's input and output:

```ts
import type { StandardSchemaV1 } from "@standard-schema/spec"

const Form = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "string.integer.parse"
})

type FormInput = StandardSchemaV1.InferInput<typeof Form>
// { name: string; age: string }, same as typeof Form.inferIn

type FormOutput = StandardSchemaV1.InferOutput<typeof Form>
// { name: string; age: number }, same as typeof Form.infer
```

## Accepting any validator

If your library validates data your users describe, accept a Standard Schema instead of depending on ArkType. Your users can then bring ArkType, Zod, Valibot or any other implementation. `@standard-schema/spec` contains only types, and validators can be async, so always `await` the result:

```ts
import type { StandardSchemaV1 } from "@standard-schema/spec"

export const parse = async <schema extends StandardSchemaV1>(
	schema: schema,
	data: unknown
): Promise<StandardSchemaV1.InferOutput<schema>> => {
	const result = await schema["~standard"].validate(data)
	if (result.issues) {
		throw new Error(result.issues.map(issue => issue.message).join("\n"))
	}
	return result.value
}

const user = await parse(type({ name: "string" }), { name: "Ada" })
// { name: string }
```

## Standard JSON Schema

Libraries that need a JSON Schema, for example to describe an API or a tool for an LLM, call `T["~standard"].jsonSchema.input` or `.output`:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

const schema = User["~standard"].jsonSchema.input({ target: "draft-2020-12" })
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"name": { "type": "string" },
		"age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
	},
	"required": ["name"]
}
```

- `target` is `"draft-2020-12"`, `"draft-07"` or `"openapi-3.0"`. Any other target throws.
- `libraryOptions` is passed to [`toJsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema) as its options, so a caller can set a `fallback` there.
- `input` and `output` differ when the Type has morphs or defaults. For `string.integer.parse`, `input` describes a string and `output` describes an integer, and a key with a default is optional with a `default` in `input` but required in `output`.

Unlike `toJsonSchema()`, these methods don't throw when part of a Type has no JSON Schema equivalent. The library calling them can't know which fallbacks your Type needs, so each such part becomes the closest schema JSON Schema can express, or `{}` if there is none:

```ts
const Event = type({
	name: "string",
	at: "Date"
})

Event.toJsonSchema() // throws ToJsonSchemaError (code "date")

const schema = Event["~standard"].jsonSchema.input({ target: "draft-2020-12" })
// { ..., properties: { at: {}, name: { type: "string" } }, required: ["at", "name"] }
```

`{}` accepts anything, so the JSON Schema is looser than the Type. Data you validate with the Type itself is still checked in full. See [Standard JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#standard-json-schema) for which parts fall back and how to write something more specific.

## Other validators in a definition

Any Standard Schema can appear in a definition, at the top level or nested. Its output is inferred and its validation runs as part of the Type:

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"
import * as v from "valibot"
import { z } from "zod"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	age: v.number(),
	address: z.object({ street: z.string(), city: z.string() })
})

type User = typeof User.infer
// { name: string; age: number; address: { street: string; city: string } }
```

ArkType can't see inside another library's schema, so it treats one as a morph from `unknown` to that schema's output. That has consequences:

- `User.expression` shows `(In: unknown) => Out<unknown>` for it.
- `toJsonSchema()` throws on it, and `~standard.jsonSchema` writes `{}`.
- It can't be a branch of a union, because its input overlaps every other branch.
- Only synchronous validators work. ArkType doesn't await the result, so a schema that returns a `Promise`, like a Zod `refine` with an async callback, throws `Standard Schema definitions must validate synchronously (zod returned a Promise)` when validation reaches it.

# Integrations

> Use a Type directly with tRPC, oRPC, Drizzle, React Hook Form, Hono, the MCP SDK and the AI SDK.

Most libraries on this page accept a [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), so you pass a Type as-is with no adapter. Where a library also publishes an ArkType-specific adapter, its section shows the Standard Schema route first.

Any other library that accepts a Standard Schema works the same way. [standardschema.dev](https://standardschema.dev/schema#what-tools-frameworks-accept-speccompliant-schemas) keeps a list.

## tRPC

[tRPC](https://trpc.io/docs/server/validators) 11 accepts a Type as a procedure's input or output:

```ts
import { initTRPC } from "@trpc/server"
import { type } from "arktype"

const t = initTRPC.create()

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

export const appRouter = t.router({
	createUser: t.procedure.input(User).mutation(({ input }) => input)
})
```

Invalid input is rejected with a `BAD_REQUEST` error before the resolver runs.

## oRPC

[oRPC](https://orpc.dev) accepts a Type the same way:

```ts
import { os } from "@orpc/server"
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

export const createUser = os.input(User).handler(({ input }) => input)
```

To generate an OpenAPI document, give oRPC's `OpenAPIGenerator` the converter from `@orpc/arktype`:

```ts
import { experimental_ArkTypeToJsonSchemaConverter } from "@orpc/arktype"
import { OpenAPIGenerator } from "@orpc/openapi"

const generator = new OpenAPIGenerator({
	schemaConverters: [new experimental_ArkTypeToJsonSchemaConverter()]
})

const spec = await generator.generate({ createUser })
```

## Drizzle

Drizzle maintains [`drizzle-arktype`](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/arktype), which creates Types from your tables:

```ts
import { createInsertSchema, createSelectSchema } from "drizzle-arktype"
import { integer, pgTable, serial, text } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core"

const users = pgTable("users", {
	id: serial().primaryKey(),
	name: text().notNull(),
	age: integer()
})

const User = createSelectSchema(users)
// Type<{ id: number; name: string; age: number | null }>

const NewUser = createInsertSchema(users)
// Type<{ name: string; id?: number; age?: number | null }>
```

`createUpdateSchema` is like `createInsertSchema` with every column optional. Integer columns also get their range, so `age` above must be a 32-bit integer.

## React Hook Form

[`@hookform/resolvers`](https://github.com/react-hook-form/resolvers) includes `standardSchemaResolver`:

```ts
import { standardSchemaResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/standard-schema"
import { type } from "arktype"
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form"

const User = type({
	name: "string > 0",
	age: "number.integer >= 0"
})

export const useUserForm = () =>
	useForm({ resolver: standardSchemaResolver(User) })
```

The form's field values are typed from the Type's input, and `handleSubmit` receives its output. If you pass type arguments to `useForm` yourself, pass all three: `useForm<typeof User.inferIn, unknown, typeof User.infer>`.

The same package exports `arktypeResolver` from `@hookform/resolvers/arktype`, which behaves the same. `@hookform/resolvers` lists `arktype@^2` as an optional peer dependency, so your package manager may warn about it with a later major version of ArkType, whichever resolver you import.

## Hono

[`@hono/standard-validator`](https://github.com/honojs/middleware/tree/main/packages/standard-validator) validates a request's `json`, `form`, `query`, `param`, `header` or `cookie`:

```ts
import { sValidator } from "@hono/standard-validator"
import { type } from "arktype"
import { Hono } from "hono"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "number.integer >= 0"
})

const app = new Hono()

app.post("/users", sValidator("json", User), c => {
	const user = c.req.valid("json")
	return c.json({ message: `${user.name} is ${user.age}` })
})
```

Invalid requests get a 400 response with the issues as JSON. [`@hono/arktype-validator`](https://github.com/honojs/middleware/tree/main/packages/arktype-validator) provides an equivalent `arktypeValidator`, with a required peer dependency on `arktype@^2`.

To generate an OpenAPI document from your routes, [`hono-openapi`](https://github.com/rhinobase/hono-openapi) has a `validator` that accepts a Type, and a `resolver` for describing responses with one.

## MCP SDK

The [MCP TypeScript SDK](https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/advanced/schema-libraries) accepts a Type as a tool's `inputSchema` or `outputSchema`:

```ts
import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server"
import { type } from "arktype"

const server = new McpServer({ name: "greeter", version: "1.0.0" })

server.registerTool(
	"greet",
	{
		description: "Greet someone by name",
		inputSchema: type({
			name: "string",
			"times?": "1 <= number.integer <= 5"
		})
	},
	async ({ name, times = 1 }) => ({
		content: [{ type: "text", text: `Hello, ${name}! `.repeat(times) }]
	})
)
```

The SDK sends clients the JSON Schema from [`~standard.jsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema#standard-json-schema) and validates arguments with the Type before your handler runs. A call with `times: 9` returns an error result, and the handler doesn't run.

This needs `@modelcontextprotocol/server`, the SDK's second major version. The first, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, accepts only Zod schemas.

## AI SDK

The [AI SDK](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/generating-structured-data) accepts a Type wherever it takes a schema. For structured output:

```ts
import { generateText, Output } from "ai"
import { type } from "arktype"

const Recipe = type({
	name: "string",
	ingredients: type({ name: "string", amount: "string" }).array(),
	steps: "string[]"
})

const { output } = await generateText({
	model: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5",
	output: Output.object({ schema: Recipe }),
	prompt: "Write a recipe for toast."
})
```

For a tool's input:

```ts
import { tool } from "ai"
import { type } from "arktype"

const weather = tool({
	description: "Get the weather in a city",
	inputSchema: type({ city: "string" }),
	execute: async ({ city }) => ({ city, celsius: 21 })
})
```

The model sees the JSON Schema from [`~standard.jsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema#standard-json-schema), and the AI SDK validates its response with the Type.
